questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 25-year-old man undergoes an elective splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis. While ligating the splenic vessels, the surgeon preserves an artery to maintain the blood supply to the stomach. Which artery is it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Short gastric artery

During splenectomy, the splenic artery and vein are ligated. The short gastric arteries, which arise from the terminal part of the splenic artery, supply the fundus of the stomach. Care must be taken to preserve them whenever possible to prevent ischemia or necrosis of the gastric fundus, especially if collateral blood supply is limited.

Why not the other options?

• A. Splenic artery: Main artery to the spleen; it is ligated during splenectomy.
• B. Left gastroepiploic artery: Also arises from the splenic artery and supplies the greater curvature, but preservation of the short gastric arteries is specifically important for the gastric fundus.
• C. Left gastric artery: Arises from the celiac trunk and supplies the lesser curvature; it is not the vessel encountered at the splenic hilum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 32-year-old male presents with acute onset colicky flank pain radiating to the groin. Non-contrast CT shows a ureteric calculus lodged at a site that is not a normal anatomical constriction of the ureter. Which of the following sites is most likely involved?
options: Crossing of ureter over iliac vessels at pelvic brim
Mid-ureter at level of L2 vertebra
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mid-ureter at level of L2 vertebra

There are three classical ureteric constrictions:

• Pelvi-ureteric junction (PUJ)
• Crossing over iliac vessels at pelvic brim
• Vesico-ureteric junction (VUJ)

These are the most common sites where ureteric calculi get lodged

Non-constriction site: Mid-ureter at L2 vertebral level is NOT a normal anatomical narrowing

Clinical correlation:

• Stones outside these constrictions are less common but possible
• Pain typically radiates from flank to groin (loin-to-groin pattern)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 38-year-old banker with a history of chronic heartburn suddenly experiences excruciating pain in the epigastric region of the abdomen. Emergency surgery is performed upon admission. Intraoperative findings reveal a ruptured ulcer located on the posterior wall of the stomach. Where will a surgeon first expect to find leaked stomach contents?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Omental bursa

The posterior wall of the stomach lies directly anterior to the lesser sac (omental bursa), a subdivision of the peritoneal cavity. When a posterior gastric ulcer perforates, the gastric contents first enter the lesser sac (omental bursa) rather than the greater sac.

Anatomical relationships:

• Anterior stomach wall → greater sac
• Posterior stomach wall → lesser sac (omental bursa)

Boundaries of the lesser sac:

• Anterior: stomach and lesser omentum
• Posterior: pancreas and posterior abdominal wall
• Communication with greater sac: through the epiploic (omental) foramen of Winslow

Other options:

• Greater peritoneal sac: involved in anterior gastric perforation.
• Cul-de-sac of Douglas: lowest peritoneal recess in females.
• Paracolic gutters: channels that allow spread of peritoneal fluid later.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 44 year old female presents to the OPD with high grade fever, pain that is constant, throbbing, and worse when sitting down with history of constipation in the past. Fluctuation is noted near the anal region. The Resident decides to drain the ischioanal abscess. Which of the following structures can be injured while draining the ischioanal abscess?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inferior rectal nerve

An ischioanal (ischiorectal) abscess occurs in the ischioanal fossa, a fat-filled space on either side of the anal canal that allows expansion during defecation. Surgical drainage of this abscess risks injury to structures passing through this space.

Boundaries of the ischioanal fossa:

• Medial: External anal sphincter and levator ani
• Lateral: Obturator internus muscle and obturator fascia
• Posterior: Sacrotuberous ligament and gluteus maximus
• Anterior: Extends into anterior recess

Important contents:

• Ischioanal fat
• Inferior rectal (anal) nerve
• Inferior rectal vessels

During incision and drainage of an ischioanal abscess, the inferior rectal nerve may be injured, potentially causing:

• Weakness of external anal sphincter
• Fecal incontinence
• Loss of perianal sensation

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45 y/o male patient presents with abdominal pain and distension. A CT scan reveals multiple appendices epiploicae, particularly prominent in the sigmoid colon. Which of the following statements regarding the anatomy of the large intestine is false?
options: The caecum is typically 8-10 cm long and is a common site for appendices epiploicae.
The sigmoid colon, which is S-shaped, leads directly into the rectum.
The total length of the large intestine in adults ranges from 1 to 1.5 meters.
Appendices epiploicae are more common in the distal colon.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The caecum is typically 8-10 cm long and is a common site for appendices epiploicae.

Appendices epiploicae are fat-filled peritoneal pouches attached to the outer surface of the colon. Key anatomical features:

• They are most numerous in the transverse and sigmoid colon.
• They are rare or absent in the cecum, appendix, and rectum.
• They can become inflamed, leading to epiploic appendagitis, which may mimic appendicitis or diverticulitis.

Large intestine facts:

• Length: about 1–1.5 meters in adults.
• Sigmoid colon: S-shaped and continues into the rectum.
• Appendices epiploicae are more common in the distal colon, especially the sigmoid colon.

Therefore, the false statement is that the cecum is a common site for appendices epiploicae.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old male with a history of smoking and NSAID use presents with multiple episodes of hematemesis and melena. He is pale and hypotensive. After stabilization, an upper GI endoscopy reveals erosion of a posterior duodenal ulcer in the first part of the duodenum with an active spurt. Which artery is most commonly responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gastro-duodenal artery

A posterior duodenal ulcer can erode into the gastroduodenal artery (GDA), leading to massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding, presenting as hematemesis, melena, hypotension, and shock. This is a surgical emergency if bleeding cannot be controlled endoscopically.

• The first part (D1) of the duodenum lies directly anterior to the gastroduodenal artery.
• A posteriorly penetrating duodenal ulcer erodes the artery, causing profuse arterial hemorrhage.

Why not the other options?

• B. Left gastroepiploic artery: Runs along the greater curvature of the stomach.
• C. Right gastroepiploic artery: Supplies the greater curvature; not related to posterior D1 ulcers.
• D. Splenic artery: Related to the pancreas and posterior stomach, not the first part of the duodenum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 63-year-old man presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and steatorrhea. CT shows a pancreatic head carcinoma compressing the gastroduodenal artery. Over the next few days, the patient develops duodenal ischemia. Which of the following arteries most directly loses its blood flow due to this compression?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery

The gastroduodenal artery (GDA) is a branch of the common hepatic artery and supplies the stomach, pancreas, and proximal duodenum. Key branches of the gastroduodenal artery:

• Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (anterior and posterior branches)
• Right gastroepiploic artery

The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery supplies the proximal duodenum and head of the pancreas and forms an important anastomosis with the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (branch of the superior mesenteric artery).

Compression of the gastroduodenal artery by a pancreatic head tumor directly reduces blood flow to the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, leading to duodenal ischemia.

Other options:

• Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery: arises from the SMA.
• Left gastroepiploic artery: branch of the splenic artery.
• Dorsal pancreatic artery: usually from the splenic artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presents with urinary retention and pelvic discomfort. A digital rectal examination reveals an enlarged prostate gland. During surgery to relieve the obstruction, the urologist must take care to avoid damaging the structures that separate the prostate from the rectum. Which of the following structures separates the prostate gland from the rectum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Denonvilliers’ fascia

The prostate gland lies anterior to the rectum, and the structure separating them is the Denonvilliers’ fascia (rectoprostatic fascia). Key features of Denonvilliers’ fascia:

• A fibrous fascial layer between the prostate/seminal vesicles anteriorly and the rectum posteriorly.
• Provides an important surgical plane during prostatectomy.
• Helps prevent direct spread of prostatic carcinoma to the rectum.

Other options:

• A. Waldeyer’s fascia: fascia related to the sacral region behind the rectum.
• B. Scarpa’s fascia: deep membranous layer of superficial fascia of the anterior abdominal wall.
• D. Camper’s fascia: fatty superficial layer of the anterior abdominal wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented to OPD with abdominal pain, jaundice, and portal hypertension. With the above symptoms identify the anastomosis seen in between veins.
options: Esophageal veins and left gastric veins
Left colic vein and middle colic veins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Esophageal veins and left gastric veins

In the given scenario of a patient with portal hypertension, anastomosis between esophageal veins and left gastric veins can be seen. In portal hypertension, increased pressure within the portal venous system may result in the dilation of portal venous tributaries and reversed flow at sites of portosystemic anastomoses.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal, located below the pectinate line, presents with palpable, tender, enlarged lymph nodes. What is the anatomical basis for this pattern of lymphatic spread?
options: Below the pectinate line drains to superficial inguinal nodes
Below the pectinate line drains to internal iliac nodes
Both above and below the pectinate line drain exclusively to internal iliac nodes
Lymphatic drainage is determined solely by arterial supply
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Below the pectinate line drains to superficial inguinal nodes

• The pectinate (dentate) line marks the embryological junction where hindgut (endoderm) meets ectoderm, and this origin dictates the distinct neurovascular and lymphatic supply above versus below the line.
• Above the pectinate line (endoderm-derived, visceral structures):

• Arterial supply: Superior rectal artery (branch of IMA)
• Venous drainage: Superior rectal vein → IMV → splenic vein → portal vein
• Innervation: Visceral (inferior hypogastric plexus, T12–L3) → painless pathology (e.g., internal hemorrhoids)
• Lymphatics: Drain to internal iliac lymph nodes
• Malignancy here is typically adenocarcinoma

• Below the pectinate line (ectoderm-derived, somatic structures):

• Arterial supply: Inferior rectal artery (branch of internal pudendal artery)
• Venous drainage: Inferior rectal vein → internal pudendal vein → internal iliac vein → common iliac vein → IVC (systemic, bypassing the portal system)
• Innervation: Somatic (pudendal nerve, S2–S4) → painful pathology (e.g., external hemorrhoids, anal fissures)
• Lymphatics: Drain to superficial inguinal lymph nodes
• Malignancy here is typically squamous cell carcinoma

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following peritoneal folds are correctly matched with their contents, except:
options: Splenorenal ligament – Splenic vessels and pancreatic tail
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gastrocolic ligament – Right gastric artery

Peritoneal ligaments are double layers of peritoneum connecting abdominal organs and usually transmit specific vessels, nerves, or ducts between them. Knowing their contents is important for abdominal surgery and imaging.

Key peritoneal folds and their contents:

• Gastrocolic ligament – Part of the greater omentum connecting the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon. It mainly contains gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) vessels, not the right gastric artery.
• Splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament – Connects the spleen to the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas.
• Transverse mesocolon – Suspends the transverse colon from the posterior abdominal wall and contains the middle colic vessels.
• Gastrosplenic ligament – Connects the stomach to the spleen and contains the short gastric vessels and left gastroepiploic vessels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following structures cross the right ureter anteriorly except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Genitofemoral nerve

Right ureter—structures crossing anteriorly:

• Terminal ileum
• Right colic and ileocolic vessels
• Vas deferens (in males)

Correct answer (exception): Genitofemoral nerve

• Lies posterior to the ureter on the psoas major
• Does not cross anteriorly

Important anatomical rule:

• Ureter runs on psoas major muscle
• Structures crossing anteriorly are mainly:

• Vessels
• Ducts (vas deferens / uterine artery)

• “Water under the bridge”:

• Ureter passes under:

• Uterine artery (female)
• Vas deferens (male)

• Important in:

• Pelvic surgeries → risk of ureter injury
• Renal colic → pain radiation along ureteric course

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During colon surgery, the inferior mesenteric artery is ligated. Which vessel maintains blood supply to the colon via collateral circulation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Middle colic artery

Inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) supplies Left colon (descending colon, sigmoid, upper rectum).

When IMA is ligated, blood supply is maintained by Middle colic artery (from SMA) via the marginal artery of Drummond.

• Important collateral pathway:

• SMA ↔ IMA anastomosis through:

• Marginal artery of Drummond (continuous arcade along colon)

• Clinical relevance:

• Preserves perfusion during:

• Colon surgery
• Aortic surgeries
•

• Weak points (watershed areas):

• Splenic flexure (Griffith’s point)
• Rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck’s point)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the sequence of muscles forming the posterior abdominal wall from medial to lateral.
options: Psoas major, Psoas minor, Transversus abdominis, Quadratus lumborum
Psoas major, Psoas minor, Quadratus lumborum, Transversus abdominis
Psoas major, Quadratus lumborum, Transversus abdominis, Psoas minor
Psoas minor, Psoas major, Quadratus lumborum, Transversus abdominis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Psoas minor, Psoas major, Quadratus lumborum, Transversus abdominis

The posterior abdominal wall muscles, arranged from medial to lateral, are psoas minor (when present), psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis. This anatomical relationship is important for interpreting cross-sectional imaging, understanding the spread of retroperitoneal infections, and performing retroperitoneal surgical approaches.

FMGE/NEET PG Pearl

• Medial → Lateral: Psoas minor → Psoas major → Quadratus lumborum → Transversus abdominis.
• Psoas minor is absent in \~40–60% of individuals and is a weak trunk flexor.
• Psoas major is the chief flexor of the hip and is innervated by L1–L3.
• Quadratus lumborum laterally flexes the trunk and fixes the 12th rib during respiration.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Level of posterior superior iliac spine:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S2

The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) is an important surface anatomical landmark on the posterior pelvis. It is visible externally as the “dimples of Venus” in the lower back.

The PSIS corresponds approximately to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2).

The S2 vertebral level is important because it corresponds to:

• Termination of the dural sac
• End of the subarachnoid space
• A landmark used in caudal epidural anesthesia

Other related landmarks:

• Iliac crest line (Tuffier’s line) → level of L4 vertebra
• Sacral hiatus → around S4

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The duodenum is derived embryologically from which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Foregut and midgut

The duodenum has a dual embryological origin:

• The proximal part (up to the opening of the bile duct) develops from the caudal foregut
• The distal part develops from the cranial midgut

Duodenum = Foregut + Midgut junction

• Foregut derivatives include: pharynx, esophagus, stomach, proximal duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas
• Midgut derivatives include: distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal 2/3 of transverse colon

The major duodenal papilla (bile duct opening) marks the transition between foregut and midgut.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fibres of the internal oblique muscle and transversus abdominus muscle contribute to which boundaries of the inguinal canal walls? i.Anterior wall ii.Roof iii.Floor iv.Posterior wall
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ii and iv

The correct answer is ii and iv (Roof and posterior wall).

Fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis arch over the spermatic cord, forming the roof of the inguinal canal.

Their aponeurotic fusion forms the conjoint tendon, which reinforces the posterior wall medially.

Anterior wall is mainly external oblique aponeurosis, and the floor is formed by the inguinal ligament, not by these muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The Space of Disse contains all of the following Expect:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Kupffer cells

The Space of Disse is the perisinusoidal space located between: Hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium

It contains:

• Blood plasma
• Microvilli of hepatocytes (for exchange)
• Stellate (Ito) cells → store vitamin A / fat

Why Kupffer cells are excluded

• Kupffer cells are macrophages
• They are located in the lining of hepatic sinusoids, not in the Space of Disse

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve is affected when there is referred pain from ureteric colic felt in the groin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Genitofemoral

Pain from ureteric colic is transmitted via sympathetic afferent fibers accompanying T11–L2 spinal segments. As the stone descends in the ureter, pain is referred along dermatomes supplied by these nerves.

Referred pain pattern:

• Upper ureter → flank (T11–T12)
• Mid ureter → lower abdomen
• Lower ureter → groin, scrotum, or labia majora

This groin pain occurs because the genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2) supplies the skin of the upper anterior thigh and genital region, producing referred pain in the groin during ureteric colic.

• Origin: L1–L2 lumbar plexus
• Divides into:

o    Genital branch → scrotum/labia majora, cremaster muscle

o    Femoral branch → skin of upper anterior thigh

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is false about Anatomy of Adrenal gland?
options: Adrenals are yellow in gross appearance
Right adrenal is semilunar in shape
Left adrenal is related medially to coeliac ganglion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right adrenal is semilunar in shape

The adrenal (suprarenal) glands are paired endocrine glands located in the retroperitoneum on the superior poles of the kidneys.

• Color: Adrenal glands appear yellowish due to their high lipid content, especially in the cortex.
• Location: They are retroperitoneal structures situated within the renal fascia above the kidneys.
• Shape difference:

• Right adrenal gland → Pyramidal/triangular in shape.
• Left adrenal gland → Semilunar (crescentic) in shape.

Important Relations:

• The left adrenal gland is medially related to the coeliac ganglion and coeliac trunk.
• The right adrenal gland is related anteriorly to the inferior vena cava and liver.

Option C states that the right adrenal is semilunar, which is incorrect. The semilunar shape belongs to the left adrenal gland, while the right adrenal gland is pyramidal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not the boundary of hepatocystic triangle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cystic artery

The hepatocystic triangle (also called hepatobiliary triangle) is an important surgical landmark used during cholecystectomy and other biliary procedures. The boundaries of the hepatocystic triangle are:

• Superior border (base): Inferior border of the liver
• Right border: Cystic duct
• Left border: Common hepatic duct

The cystic artery is not a boundary of the hepatocystic triangle but rather passes through it as content. The cystic artery typically runs within this triangular space and is an important structure that needs to be identified and ligated during cholecystectomy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles is not involved in the formation of the perineal body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Internal anal sphincter muscle

The perineal body (central tendon of the perineum) is a fibromuscular node located between the urogenital triangle and anal triangle, anterior to the anus. It serves as an important point of attachment for several perineal muscles that support the pelvic floor and maintain pelvic organ stability.

Muscles attached to the perineal body include:

• Bulbospongiosus muscle
• Superficial transverse perineal muscle
• Deep transverse perineal muscle
• External anal sphincter
• Fibers of levator ani (especially pubococcygeus)

The internal anal sphincter is not attached to the perineal body because it is a smooth muscle continuation of the circular layer of the rectum and functions involuntarily.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following spermatic cord structures is not harmed during vasectomy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ilioinguinal nerve

A vasectomy is a sterilization procedure in which the vas deferens is ligated and cut within the spermatic cord to prevent sperm from reaching the ejaculate.

The spermatic cord contains:

• Vas deferens
• Testicular artery
• Pampiniform venous plexus
• Autonomic nerve fibers (testicular plexus)
• Cremasteric artery
• Genital branch of genitofemoral nerve
• Lymphatics

During vasectomy, the vas deferens is isolated, and care is taken to avoid injury to adjacent vessels and nerves.

Structure not harmed:

• Ilioinguinal nerve runs in the inguinal canal but lies outside the spermatic cord.
• Therefore, it is not part of the spermatic cord contents and is not directly involved in vasectomy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements about the ligament of Treitz is not true?
options: It connects the duodenojejunal flexure to the right crus of the diaphragm.
It contains striated muscle fibers in its upper part.
It primarily serves as a conduit for blood supply to the small intestine.
It acts as a landmark in the diagnosis of intestinal malrotation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It primarily serves as a conduit for blood supply to the small intestine.

The ligament of Treitz (suspensory ligament of the duodenum) supports the duodenojejunal flexure and marks the transition between the duodenum and jejunum.

• Origin: Right crus of the diaphragm
• Insertion: Duodenojejunal flexure
• Structure: Contains striated muscle fibers superiorly (from diaphragm) and smooth muscle inferiorly (from duodenum).
• Function: Helps maintain the angle of the duodenojejunal junction and supports the small intestine.

Clinical importance:

• Serves as an important anatomical landmark to distinguish upper vs lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
• Used to identify intestinal malrotation in imaging and surgery.

The incorrect statement is that it serves as a conduit for blood supply, because mesenteric vessels supply the small intestine, not the ligament of Treitz.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding Cauda equina syndrome? I. Its presenting symptoms are perineal numbness, painless urinary retention and fecal incontinence. II. Urgent investigation with MRI is required. III. It is present most commonly in the 45-60 year age group. IV. Confirmed cases require early surgical decompression. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is a neurosurgical emergency caused by compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris. The most common cause is a massive central lumbar disc prolapse (usually at L4–L5 or L5–S1). Prompt diagnosis and urgent surgical decompression are essential to prevent permanent neurological deficits.

The following statements are true:

• I. Its presenting symptoms are perineal numbness, painless urinary retention and fecal incontinence: These are the hallmark features of CES:

• Saddle (perineal) anesthesia
• Painless urinary retention (earliest bladder symptom)
• Overflow incontinence
• Fecal incontinence
• Bilateral leg weakness/sciatica

• II. Urgent investigation with MRI is required: MRI of the lumbosacral spine is the gold standard investigation and should be performed urgently.
• IV. Confirmed cases require early surgical decompression: Urgent decompressive surgery (ideally within 24–48 hours) offers the best chance of recovery of bladder, bowel, and neurological function.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. It is present most commonly in the 45–60 year age group: Cauda equina syndrome can occur at any adult age, depending on the underlying cause. It is not defined by or restricted to the 45–60-year age group, making this statement incorrect.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning the liver are correct, EXCEPT:
options: Quadrate lobe drains into the right hepatic duct
The lesser omentum suspends the stomach from the visceral surface of the liver
Attachment of the hepatic veins to the IVC is the most important support of the liver
The ligamentum venosum is attached to the left branch of the portal vein in the porta hepatis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Quadrate lobe drains into the right hepatic duct

The quadrate lobe of the liver belongs functionally to the left lobe based on its vascular supply and biliary drainage.

Key anatomical facts:

• Quadrate lobe drains into the left hepatic duct, not the right hepatic duct.
• The lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments) connects the liver to the stomach and proximal duodenum.
• The hepatic veins draining into the inferior vena cava (IVC) provide the most important structural support of the liver, anchoring it to the diaphragm and posterior abdominal wall.
• The ligamentum venosum (remnant of the fetal ductus venosus) lies between the left lobe and caudate lobe and attaches near the left branch of the portal vein at the porta hepatis.

Therefore, the incorrect statement is that the quadrate lobe drains into the right hepatic duct.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures do not pass through both greater and lesser sciatic foramens?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tendon of obturator internus

The anatomical pathways of structures traversing the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, a classic integration of pelvic anatomy + clinical procedures (e.g., pudendal nerve block).

• Structures that pass through both greater AND lesser sciatic foramina (via a loop around the sacrospinous ligament):

• Pudendal nerve
• Internal pudendal vessels
• Nerve to obturator internus

Pathway:

• Exit pelvis via greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis)
• Hook around ischial spine / sacrospinous ligament
• Enter perineum via lesser sciatic foramen
• Exception (Correct answer): Tendon of obturator internus

• Originates inside pelvis
• Exits only through lesser sciatic foramen
• Does NOT pass through greater sciatic foramen

Pudendal nerve block is given near the ischial spine

• Injury/compression here can affect:

• Perineal sensation
• External anal & urethral sphincters

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 58-year-old woman was undergoing cholecystectomy. During the procedure, the resident accidentally advanced the scissors along the superior border of the epiploic foramen causing injury. Which of the following structures is likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Caudate lobe of liver

The superior border of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the caudate lobe of the liver. It is likely to be injured in this case.

Epiploic foramen is a vertical slit of about 3 cm behind the free right border of the lesser omentum. It connects the lesser sac to the greater sac.

Clinical note: Pringle maneuver (as shown below) is a technique where the free margin of the lesser omentum is compressed to obtain rapid control of bleeding from the hepatic artery and portal vein in liver trauma and surgery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient came with complaints of inability to move his 4th and 5th digit, cannot hold a pen and he was not able to hold a paper between fingers. Which of the following sites given below is the probable cause of injury to the nerve in question?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C

The given clinical situation suggests an ulnar nerve injury. The most likely site of injury would thus be medial epicondyle (marked as C)

Tests for ulnar nerve lesions are as follows:

• Card test positive
• Claw hand deformity
• Froment's sign positive
• Wartenberg sign
• Palmaris brevis sign

Positive card test is due to weakness of palmar interrosei, causing loss of adduction. As a result, the patient is unable to hold the card firmly between his or her fingers.

Option A: It is the radial groove where radial nerve runs along with profunda brachii artery.

Option D: It is the neck of humerus where axillary nerve runs around.

Option B: It is the lateral epicondyle. Fracture of this part may lead to tardy ulnar nerve palsy, but incidence is less.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A young patient presented with hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus and tetany. Which of the following marked areas in the picture is defective in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given clinical scenario of hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus, and tetany is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. It is caused by defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouch. In the image of pharyngeal pouches, "3" points to the thymus (derivative of 3rd pharyngeal pouch). Since in the above question, the thymus is absent, option 3 will be the most appropriate answer.

DiGeorge syndrome is a complex embryopathy that is caused by the hemizygous interstitial deletion of chromosome 22. It is characterized by multiple developmental defects, including conotruncal defects, hypoparathyroidism, and dysmorphic syndrome. It is also known as velocardiofacial syndrome (palate, facial, and cardiac defects).

It has variable presentations including Cleft palate, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia leading to T-cell deficiency, Cardiac defects, and Hypocalcemia secondary to parathyroid aplasia (CATCH-22).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true about grey rami communicantes except:
options: Present medial to white rami communicantes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preganglionic

The grey rami communicantes are not preganglionic fibers. They are postganglionic fibers.

The sympathetic trunks on either side of the vertebral columns consist of a series of ganglia. They are connected to the spinal nerves by white and grey rami communicantes. The cell bodies of the preganglionic sympathetic neurons are located in the lateral horn in the spinal grey matter. They leave the cord in the ventral nerve roots to form spinal nerves. These fibers enter the sympathetic trunk in white rami communicantes. They synapse with the postganglionic sympathetic neurons in the sympathetic ganglia. The axons of the postganglionic neurons return to the spinal nerve through the grey rami communicantes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Among the following, what is the function of the marked muscles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Depression

The muscle marked in the above image is the lateral pterygoid muscle and its primary function is depression of the mandible (opening of the mouth).

Bilateral contraction of the lateral pterygoid alone causes depression of the mandible (making it the primary function) whereas, protrusion is the result of bilateral contraction of both the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles.

The lateral pterygoid has the following actions:

1. Opening of the jaw (depression): Lateral pterygoid has a specialized role in mandibular opening mediated by its horizontal fibres. When left and right lateral pterygoid muscles contract together, the mandibular condyle is pulled forwards and slightly downwards. This protrusive movement alone has little or no function except in assisting the opening of the jaw (Gray's Anatomy 41st edition).
2. Side-to-side movement: When the lateral pterygoid contracts unilaterally along with the adjacent medial pterygoid the jaw is pulled medially. This is used for grinding food between teeth of the same side. This action is mediated by the inferior head of the lateral pterygoid.

Levator ani is formed by:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure passing through the foramen marked.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abducens nerve

The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure and the abducens nerve passes through it.

The abducens nerve is the 6th cranial nerve and arises from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction. It runs through the Dorello's canal which is present at the medial most end of the petrous ridge and then enters the cavernous sinus where it lies lateral to the internal carotid artery. It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the common tendinous ring and supplies the lateral rectus.

Other options:

Spinal accessory nerve passes through the foramen magnum along with the medulla oblongata and the verterbral arteries

Ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal along with the optic nerve.

Middle meningeal artery and vein pass through the foramen spinosum along with the meningeal branch of mandibular nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure marked with the asterisk in the electron micrograph indicates _____________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Secretory vesicles

The structure marked with the asterisk in the electron micrograph indicates presynaptic secretory vesicles. The structure marked with the arrowhead is postsynaptic density.

The secretory vesicles are synthesized by the neurons and are involved in electrochemical signalling in the brain and neuromuscular junctions.

On electron microscopy:

• Mitochondria appear as round or elliptical bodies of 0.5-2.0 micron long on an electron microscope, consisting of an outer and an inner mitochondrial membrane, cristae, and mitochondrial matrix.

• Golgi bodies (or Golgi apparatus) appear as stacks of flatenned membranous cisternae surrounded by clusters of vesicles.

• Ribosomes may be attached to the membrane of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (as shown in the image below), or else, they may exist as monosomes or as a chain of granular structures called polyribosomes associated with mRNA.

The inferior vena cava passes through the central tendon of the diaphragm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The talocalcaneonavicular joint is a ________type of joint.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ball and Socket

The talocalcaneonavicular joint is a ball and socket joint.

• The ball part is formed by the rounded head of the talus.
• The socket is formed by 3 structures:

• Posterior surface of the navicular
• Anterior articular surface of the calcaneus
• Upper surface of the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament (spring ligament).

Cremasteric reflex is mediated by L1 and L2. In this reflex, there is ipsilateral elevation of the testicle following stroking of the medial thigh.

The cremasteric reflex's afferent and efferent branches:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What represents the marked area in the given histology of lymph node?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mantle zone

The area marked in the image is the mantle zone of a lymph node.

Lymph node has primary follicle composed of small, quiescent lymphocytes, and a secondary follicle with germinal centre composed mainly of antigen-stimulated B cells.

The mantle zone is produced as surrounding cells are marginalised by the rapidly growing germinal centre. It is populated by mainly quiescent B cells with condensed heterochromatic nuclei and little cytoplasm (hence the deeply basophilic staining of this region in routine preparations), a few helper T cells, Follicular Dendritic cells and macrophages.

In peripheral lymph nodes, the marginal zone are often inapparent because they are mixed with the mantle zone cells. And often not well developed in lymph nodes.

The paracortex lies between the cortical follicles and the medulla and is populated mainly by T cells, which are not organised into follicles

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is connected to the structure marked as A in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Striate cortex

The structure marked A is the splenium of the corpus callosum and it is connected to the striate cortex.

The body of the corpus callosum arches posteriorly and ends as the thickened posterior portion called the splenium. The fibers from the splenium form the forceps major and arch backward into the occipital lobe (striate cortex).

The hippocampus is not connected directly to the splenium, but situated inferior to the splenium.

The image given below shows the parts of the corpus callosum.

questions.explanation:

The histopathological image marked ‘B’ represents the sebaceous gland, which is a type of holocrine gland.

Holocrine secretions are produced in the cytoplasm of the cell and released by the rupture of the plasma membrane, which destroys the cell and results in the secretion of the product into the lumen.

Examples of holocrine glands are

• Sebaceous glands of the skin and
• Meibomian glands of the eyelid

Image C: Mammary gland - Apocrine gland; apical part sheds to secrete

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to you with inability to form words but can make noises. He also knows what he wants to say. What area of the brain has been damaged in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Broca’s area

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Broca's aphasia in which the Broca's area will be affected.

In Broca's aphasia/ Motor aphasia / Non-fluent aphasia, areas 44 and 45 in the prefrontal and premotor facial regions of the cerebral cortex are affected. The affected individuals will have difficulty forming verbal or written words. The comprehension aspect of speech is preserved but the person cannot repeat or name the words and lacks fluency.

Patients in whom the area is severely affected may have very few words to express all of their emotions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following take part in the formation of the wrist joint, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Distal end of ulna

The distal end of the ulna does not take part in the formation of the radiocarpal joint.

The radiocarpal joint (Wrist joint) is a synovial, biaxial, and ellipsoid joint formed by the articulation of:

• The distal end of the radius
• Articular disc of the triangular fibrocartilage
• Scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum

In the neutral position of the wrist, only the scaphoid and lunate are in contact with the radius and articular disc; the triquetrum comes into apposition with the disc only in full adduction of the wrist joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the cranial nerve that passes through the marked foramen marked in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oculomotor nerve

The marked structure is the superior orbital fissure and the oculomotor nerve passes through this fissure.

Superior orbital fissure is divided into three compartments by the common tendinous ring. The oculomotor nerve passes through its intermediate compartment.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Inferior thyroid artery is the branch of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thyrocervical trunk

Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of thyrocervical trunk, which in turn, is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. The inferior thyroid artery loops upwards anterior to the medial border of the scalenus anterior, turns medially just below the sixth cervical transverse process, and then descends on longus colli to the lower border of the thyroid gland.

Relations between the terminal branches and recurrent laryngeal nerve are very variable and of considerable surgical importance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ligamentum flavum has high levels of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Elastin fibres

Ligamentum flavum has high levels of elastin fibres.

The ligamenta flava are a series of ligaments that connect the ventral parts of the laminae of adjacent vertebrae. They predominantly contain elastic tissue and form part of the posterior surface of the vertebral canal. The high content of elastin allows it to be stretched by 80% without damage. The ligamentum flava resist separation of the laminae in flexion and assist in extension back to the anatomical position.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Loss of flexion at the interphalangeal joint of thumb after supracondylar fracture is due to the involvement of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anterior interosseous nerve

Loss of flexion at the interphalangeal (IP) joint of the thumb, is due to the involvement of the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN).

Flexion of thumb occurs at 2 joints:

1. IP joint: Flexor pollicis longus (FPL) supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve (a branch of the median nerve, C7 and C8).
2. MCP joint: Flexor pollicis brevis (FPB) supplied by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve.

Other options:

• Deep branch of ulnar nerve > ulnar claw hand

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Meissner corpuscles are present in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Papillary dermis

Meissner corpuscles are present in the papillary dermis. These corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors particularly sensitive to the movement of objects over the skin's surface and low-frequency vibrations. Their acute sensitivity plays a crucial role in tasks such as reading Braille text.

It is an elongated encapsulated nerve ending of a large myelinated sensory nerve fiber (type Aβ). Each corpuscle consists of a connective tissue capsule and a central core composed of stacked modified Schwann cells. Meissner's corpuscles are found in nonhairy areas of the skin, especially in fingertips, lips, and other regions where spatial touch perception is highly developed.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Neurovascular bundle is absent in which compartment of the leg?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior superficial compartment

Posterior superficial compartment of the leg does not contain any neurovascular bundle.

The posterior compartment of the leg is divided into the deep and superficial parts by the transverse intermuscular septum.

The contents of the posterior superficial compartment are gastrocnemius, plantaris, and soleus muscle.

Neurovascular components in various compartments of leg are as follows:

• Anterior compartment: Anterior tibial artery and Deep fibular/peroneal nerve
• Posterior deep compartment: Tibial nerve and posterior tibial vessels in the deep plane.
• Lateral Compartment: Superficial peroneal/fibular nerve and peroneal/fibular vessel. Peroneal artery is a branch of posterior tibial artery.

Note: MRI is the best imaging modality for evaluating the soft tissues of the leg.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Purkinje cells of cerebellum relay into _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dentate nucleus

Purkinje cells of the cerebellum relay into the dentate nucleus which is one of the deep cerebellar nuclei.

The input to the Purkinje cells come from the climbing fibres. The output of Purkinje cells is inhibitory to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

Options A and B: Caudate and lentiform nuclei are part of the basal ganglia.

Option D: Red nucleus receives afferents from the cerebellum and plays a role in modulating signals to the upper motor neurons of the cerebral cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the main action of the muscle marked below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Elevation

The muscle marked in the image is the temporalis and its main action is elevation of the mandible.

Other actions are:

• It helps in the side-to-side grinding movements of the mandible.
• The posterior fibres which are horizontal, help in the retraction of the mandible.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which muscle is not involved in the inversion of foot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Peroneus longus

Peroneus longus muscle is not involved in the inversion of the foot. It causes eversion and plantar flexion.

Inversion of the foot is a movement in which the medial border of the foot is elevated so that the sole faces medially.

• Tibialis anterior - Causes dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot
• Tibialis posterior - Causes plantar flexion and inversion of the foot
• Extensor hallucis longus - Causes extension of the great toe, dorsiflexion of the foot, and inversion of the foot (minimal action)

Eversion of the foot is a movement where the lateral border of the foot is elevated so that the sole faces laterally. Peroneus longus, peroneus brevis, and peroneus tertius are the muscles involved.

These movements take place, mainly at the talocalcaneal and the talocalcaneonavicular joints, and partly at the transverse tarsal joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries does not supply the corresponding region of the dura mater?
options: Middle meningeal artery – Anterior cranial fossa
Accessory meningeal branch of maxillary artery – Middle cranial fossa
Meningeal branch of internal carotid artery – Posterior cranial fossa
Meningeal branch of anterior and posterior ethmoid artery – Anterior cranial fossa
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meningeal branch of internal carotid artery – Posterior cranial fossa

The meningeal branch of the internal carotid artery (ICA) does not supply the posterior cranial fossa. It supplies the anterior cranial fossa.

The dura mater is supplied by meningeal arteries that pass along the inner periosteum (endosteum) of the skull over the endosteal layer of the dura and supply the following regions.

Region
Arteries

Anterior cranial fossa

• Meningeal branches of anterior and posterior ethmoid arteries
• Meningeal branches of internal carotid arteries
• A branch of the middle meningeal artery

Middle cranial fossa

• Middle meningeal artery and accessory meningeal branches of the maxillary artery
• A branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery
• Branches of the internal carotid artery
• A recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery

Posterior cranial fossa

• Meningeal branches of the occipital artery
• Posterior meningeal branches of the vertebral artery
• Dorsal meningeal and tentorial arteries arising from the meningohypophyseal trunk

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is normally seen in lumbar spine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lordosis

Lordosis is normally seen in lumbar spine.

In adults,

• The cervical curve is a lordosis (convex forwards),
• The thoracic curve is a kyphosis (convex dorsally),
• The lumbar curve is also a lordosis,
• The pelvic curve is concave anteroinferiorly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is the most conspicuous sign of breast cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peau d'orange

The most conspicuous sign of breast cancer is Peau d’ orange appearance.

Peau d'orange (orange peel like texture), is the edematous swollen and pitted breast skin due to obstruction of the subcutaneous lymphatics.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nerves is not involved in olfaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypoglossal nerve

The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor cranial nerve and is not involved in olfaction.

The other three cranial nerves—trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves are mixed cranial nerves and contribute to olfaction.

Vagal nerve stimulation modifies the electrical activity of the olfactory bulb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following sensations is not perceived by the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Proprioception

Proprioception is perceived by the mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve, not the spinal nucleus.

The trigeminal nerve consists of 4 nuclei: 3 sensory (Mesencephalic, spinal, and principal sensory nucleus) and 1 motor.

Nucleus
Location
Function

Mesencephalic Nucleus
Composed of a column of unipolar nerve cells situated in the midbrain and extends inferiorly into the pons as far as the main sensory nucleus
Receives the sensation of proprioception from the muscles of mastication and from the facial and extraocular muscles

Principal sensory nucleus
Posterior part of the pons lateral to the motor nucleus

Receives the sensations of touch and pressure from the face

Spinal nucleus
Continuous superiorly with the main sensory nucleus and extends inferiorly the whole of the medulla oblongata till the 2nd Cervical Segment
Receives the sensation of pain and temperature from the face and some fibers of touch

Motor nucleus
The pons medial to the main sensory nucleus
Supplies the muscles of mastication, the tensor tympani, the tensor veli palitini and the mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric muscle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following veins drain into brachiocephalic vein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left superior intercostal vein

The left superior intercostal vein drains into the left brachiocephalic vein.

Tributaries of the brachiocephalic vein:

• Left and right internal thoracic veins
• Left and right inferior thyroid veins
• Left superior intercostal vein drains into the left brachiocephalic vein.

The right superior intercostal vein drains into the azygos vein.

Option A - Hemiazygous vein drains into the azygous vein.

Option B - Superior thyroid veins drain directly into internal jugular veins.

Option C - Right superior intercostal vein drains into the azygous vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A lesion of the structure marked in the image below causes?

The structure marked in the image is the pyramid containing the pyramidal tracts. A lesion here leads to contralateral hemiplegia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following form the marked structure except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2nd Palmar interossei

The structure marked in the image is the dorsal digital expansion of the middle finger. Palmar interossei do not attach to the middle finger and therefore it does not contribute to the dorsal digital expansion of the middle finger.

Palmar interossei are unipennate muscles originating from their own metacarpal bone. Their function is adduction. The middle finger does not need adduction and hence does not have palmar interossei.

Dorsal interossei are bipennate muscles originating from the adjacent metacarpal bone. They attach to the middle three fingers on both sides and do not attach on the thumb and little finger. Their function is abduction. The thumb and little finger have other muscles for abduction.

The lateral 2 lumbricals are unipennate and medial 2 lumbricals are bipennate. Their function is flexion at metacarpophalangeal joints.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following supply the marked structure except :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diagonal artery

The structure marked is the right ventricle. It is not supplied by the diagonal artery.

The diagonal artery is a branch of the anterior interventricular artery supplying the left ventricle. This is present in about 30-50% of the population.

The right ventricle is mostly supplied by the right coronary artery and its branches such as the marginal artery.

The anterior interventricular artery gives off 1-2 anterior right ventricular branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the image given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ulnar artery

The structure marked in the image is the ulnar artery, seen contributing to the superficial palmar arch.

It passes deep to the Guyon's canal in the wrist and contributes to the superficial and deep palmar arch.

Correct answer: C. A-5, B-3, C-2, D-1

The image shows a cut and reflected section of the heart.

The ventricles can be identified based upon the wall thickness. Left ventricle has thicker walls. The correct match is:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Lesion of the structure marked 'A' causes:
options: Loss of sensation of the nail of index finger
Loss of sensation at the tip of radial tubercle
Loss of sensation of the 4th interdigital cleft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of sensation of the nail of index finger

The structure marked 'A' in the diagram is median nerve in the cubital fossa. A lesion of the median nerve causes loss of sensation of the nail of the index finger.

Median nerve cutaneous supply:

• Lateral 2/3rd of the palm by superficial cutaneous branch
• Lateral 3½ fingers (palmar aspect and dorsal aspect of nailbeds) by palmar digital nerves

Contents of cubital fossa: (From medial to lateral) - “MBBR”

• Median nerve
• Brachial artery
• Biceps brachii tendon
• Radial nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Marked structure is derived from the______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endocardial cushions

The structure marked is the membranous part of the interventricular septum. It is derived from endocardial cushions.

Endocardial cushions are soft tissue masses that protrude in the atrioventricular and conotruncal regions.

• Atrioventricular cushions are derived from overlying endocardial cells.
• The conotruncal cushions are derived from the neural crest cells.

Endocardial cushions contribute to the formation of:

• Atrial septa
• Ventricular septa (membranous portion)
• Atrioventricular canals
• Atrioventricular valves
• Aortic and pulmonary channels

Defects in endocardial cushion formation can result in cardiac malformations, including ASDs, VSDs, and defects involving the great vessels (transposition of the great vessels, common truncus arteriosus, and tetralogy of Fallot).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The action of the muscle attached to the marked area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abduction

The image shows the greater trochanter and the muscle fibers of the gluteus medius and the gluteus minimus attach(insert) here and their function is to abduct the thigh and their anterior fibers rotate the thigh medially.

Both are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve  (L4, L5, S1)

Greater and Lesser trochanters:

• Greater trochanter

• Large and quadrangular
• Junction of the neck and shaft

• Lesser trochanter

• Conical projection
• Posteromedial to shaft
• Posteroinferior to junction with the neck.

• Surface marking: Greater trochanter lies approximately a hand’s breadth below the iliac tuberculum, the surface is palpable, especially when the muscles are relaxed, Lesser trochanter is not palpable.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The blood supply to the structure marked in the image is by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior cerebral artery

The marked structure is fornix which is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.

The anteromedial central branches from the anterior cerebral artery supply the fornix along with optic chiasma, lamina terminalis, hypothalamus, para-olfactory areas, and cingulate gyrus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The region marked corresponds to the surface marking for which of the following structures:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right atrium

The region marked corresponds to the surface marking for the right atrium.

The costal margin, xiphoid process, and the mid-clavicular line are seen in this image. The examiner draws a laterally convex line that extends from a level below the 2nd costal cartilage (as clued in by the sternal angle) i.e., 3rd costal cartilage to about 3 spaces below i.e., the 6th costal cartilage. This line is about 1.2 cms lateral to the sternal edge. These suggest that the region marked corresponds to the surface marking for the right atrium.

The projection of the cardiac borders, of an average adult, onto the anterior thoracic wall forms a trapezoid.  This can be mapped out using the percussion method by looking for cardiac dullness.

The varying heart borders and the corresponding surface markings are as follows:

• Upper border: Slopes gently from the second left costal cartilage to the third right costal cartilage. It corresponds to the left atrium.
• Right border: Convex to the right and runs from the third to the sixth right costal cartilages, 1–2 cm lateral to the sternal edge. It corresponds to the right atrium.
• Inferior border or acute border: Runs leftwards from the 6th right costal cartilage to the cardiac apex which is located approximately 9 cm lateral to the midline, often in the left 5th intercostal space or level with the 5th or 6th rib. It corresponds to the right ventricle.
• Left border or obtuse border: Convex laterally on the left. It extends superomedially from the cardiac apex to meet the second left costal cartilage about 1 cm from the left sternal edge. It corresponds to the left ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure that divides the liver in Couinaud's classification system is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Portal vein

The structure that divides the liver in Couinaud's classification system is the portal vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The wrong statement regarding the levator ani muscle is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Attached to pelvic brim

Levator Ani Muscle is not attached to the pelvic brim. It takes its origin from the body of the pubis, the arcus tendinous of the levator ani (a thickened part of the obturator fascia), and the ischial spine.

• Insertion :- The coccyx and the anococcygeal raphe or ligament.
• Nerve supply :- The branches of the anterior rami of sacral nerves S3 and S4 and the perineal branch of the pudendal nerve.
• Supports and raises the pelvic floor.
• Consists of the puborectalis, pubococcygeus, and iliococcygeus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: True regarding the lesion of the structure marked by the arrow is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wrist drop

The structure marked in the image is the radial nerve demonstrated in the cubital fossa. A lesion of the radial nerve leads to a wrist drop.

Ape thumb deformity is seen in a lesion of the median nerve.

Claw hand deformity is seen in a lesion of the ulnar nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the nerve supply of the structure marked in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trochlear nerve

The structure marked in the image is the superior oblique muscle. It is innervated by the trochlear nerve.

There are seven extraocular muscles present in the eye. They are:

• Levator palpebrae superioris - Which elevates the upper eyelids
• Four recti muscles - Superior, inferior, medial, and lateral recti
• Two obliques - Superior and inferior oblique

The muscles originate from the back of the orbit in a common tendinous ring called the annulus of Zinn and are inserted into the sclera.

All the extraocular muscles are innervated by the oculomotor (III) nerve except:

• Lateral rectus which is supplied by abducens (VI) nerve
• Superior oblique which is supplied by trochlear (IV) nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following finger has two dorsal interossei muscles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Middle finger

The Middle Finger has two Dorsal interossei as seen in the image below.

Dorsal Interossei causes Abduction of fingers from the Middle/3rd finger:

Muscle
Palmar  Interossei
Dorsal Interossei

Origin
First arises from the base of 1st metacarpal; Other three from the anterior surface of shafts of 2nd, 4th, and 5th metacarpals
Contiguous sides of shafts of metacarpal bones

Insertion
Proximal phalanges of thumb and index, ring, and little fingers and dorsal extensor expansion of each finger
Proximal phalanges of index, middle, and ring fingers and dorsal extensor expansion

Deep branch of the ulnar nerve

Palmar interossei adduct fingers toward the center of the third finger & flexes  the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend interphalangeal joints

Dorsal interossei abduct fingers from the center of the third finger flexes metacarpophalangeal joints and extend interphalangeal joints

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is related to the marked area in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stomach

The marked area in the image of the left kidney is related to the stomach.

The anterior relations of the right kidney:

Intraperitoneal

• Right lobe of liver
• Small intestine

Retroperitoneal

• Right suprarenal gland
• 2nd part of duoednum
• Hepatic flexure of colon

The anterior relations of the left kidney:

Intraperitoneal

• Stomach
• Jejunum
• Spleen

Retroperitoneal

• Left suprarenal gland
• Pancreas
• Splenic vessels
• Splenic flexure and beginning of descending colon

The posterior relations of the kidneys:

• One vessel - subcostal vessels
• Two ligaments - medial and lateral arcuate ligaments
• Three nerves - subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves
• Four muscles - diaphragm, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transverse abdominis.
• The right kidney is related to the 12th rib and the left kidney is related to the 11th and 12th ribs

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscle is not supplied by the structure marked A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superior oblique

The structure marked in the image is the oculomotor nerve and it does not supply the superior oblique muscle. Superior oblique muscle is supplied by the trochlear nerve.

All the extraocular muscles are innervated by the oculomotor (III) nerve except:

• Lateral rectus which is supplied by abducens (VI) nerve
• Superior oblique which is supplied by trochlear (IV) nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures given below is related to the structure highlighted (red) in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pudendal nerve

The structure marked in red is the ischial spine and the pudendal nerve is related to it.

The pudendal nerve originates from the sacral plexus S2-S4. It exits out of the pelvis by passing through the greater sciatic foramen. It then enters the perineum below the pelvic floor by passing around the ischial spine. The ischial spine is used as a landmark for pudendal nerve block.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures of brachial plexus do not give branches?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Divisions

The divisions in the brachial plexus do not give any branches.

However, the roots, trunks, and cords of the brachial plexus give out direct branches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A muscle is attached to the area marked in the given image. What is the action of this muscle on the hip joint?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Extension and lateral rotation

The area marked in the given image is the gluteal tuberosity. The muscle that is inserted here is the gluteus maximus which causes extension and lateral rotation of the hip joint.

Gluteus maximus inserts onto iliotibial tract (3/4th part) and deep fibers (1/4th) attach on gluteal tuberosity (marked in image). It is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve. It is the chief extensor of the lower limb at the hip joint. It additionally also causes lateral rotation, abduction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient is unable to abduct his arm. Which of the following root values is likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:

The inability to abduct the arm is most likely due to a lesion of the C5 root.

The deltoid muscle is the main muscle involved in the abduction of the arm. It is innervated by the C5 root of the axillary nerve. So, a lesion involving the C5 causes inability to abduct the arm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with paradoxical respiration. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. D

Paradoxical respiration occurs due to the damage of the phrenic nerve, which is marked as D, in the given image.

The structures marked in the image are:

A. Right vagus nerve

B. Left vagus nerve

C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve

D. Right phrenic nerve

Paradoxical movements in the chest are as follows:

• Paradoxical respiration - the abnormal movement of the chest wall or abdominal wall, where they move in during inspiration instead of moving out. It is seen in flail chest.
• Paradoxical movement of the diaphragm - normally, the diaphragm moves down during inspiration. However, in cases of phrenic nerve palsy, the affected side of the diaphragm moves upward (paradoxical respiration) due to diaphragmatic paralysis. The gold standard investigation to detect this is the electrical or magnetic stimulation of the phrenic nerve with a recording of the compound muscle action potential and/or the transdiaphragmatic pressure. This can be observed on ultrasound or fluoroscopy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are the contents of the carotid sheath except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sympathetic chain

The sympathetic chain is not the content of the carotid sheath. It lies posterior to the carotid sheath and anterior to the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae in the neck.

The carotid sheath is a layer of loose connective tissue formed by adjacent portions of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, the pretracheal fascia, and the prevertebral fascia.

Contents of carotid sheath:

• Common and internal carotid arteries,
• Internal jugular vein,
• Vagus nerve
• Ansa cervicalis

Note: The glossopharyngeal, accessory, and hypoglossal nerves lie within the upper part of the carotid sheath.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following nerves are involved in the movement of the eyeball except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

The nerve marked as 'A' is the optic nerve (II CN), and is not involved in the movement of the eyeball.

The nerves marked in the image are:

1. Optic nerve (II CN)
2. Oculomotor nerve (III CN)
3. Abducens nerve (VI CN)
4. Trochlear nerve (IV CN)

Extraocular muscles involved in the movement of the eyeball:

• Superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique, and levator palpebrae superioris muscles - supplied by the oculomotor (III) nerve.
• Lateral rectus - supplied by abducens (VI) nerve.
• Superior oblique - supplied by trochlear (IV) nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle occurs at which level?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Midbrain

The decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle occurs in the midbrain, at the level of the inferior colliculus.

The midbrain has four decussations:

• At the level of the superior colliculus:

• Ventral tegmental decussation of the rubrospinal tract
• Dorsal tegmental decussation of the tectospinal tract

• At the level of the inferior colliculus:

• Decussation of superior cerebellar peduncles
• Decussation of trochlear nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Given is a model of embryological development of the heart. Which structure develops from the area marked as "A" ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Infundibulum

The structure marked is conus cordis (middle part of bulbus cordis). The infundibulum of the heart develops from this structure.

The model shows the embryologic stage of the heart at which both the heart tubes have fused and are undergoing dextro-looping or bending. This happens around day 23 of intrauterine life.

Heart tube and its derivatives

Part of the heart tube
Derivative structure in the heart

Bulbus cordis

• Proximal 1/3

• Middle 1/3 (conus cordis)

• Distal 1/3 (truncus arteriosus)

• Trabeculated part of Rt.ventricle

• Outflow tract of Rt. and Lt.ventricles

• Root and proximal portions of aorta and pulmonary artery

Primitive ventricle

• Trabeculated part of the Lt.ventricle

Primitive atrium

• The common atrium that splits to Rt. and Lt.atrium

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the foramen marked in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Foramen rotundum

The image shows the sphenoid bone. The foramen marked is the foramen rotundum. Maxillary branch of trigeminal nerve passes through it.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the level of the cross-section shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. T3 - T4

The cross-section shown in the image is at the level of T3-T4.

The cross-section shows a large vascular opening of the arch of the aorta, along with three small openings corresponding to the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery and left subclavian artery. This suggests that the section was taken at the level between T3 and T4.

Options A, B: In cross-sections at the levels of T1-T2 and T2-T3, only the small vascular openings of the branches arising from the arch of aorta would be visible.

Option D: In cross-section at the level of T4-T5, where, the arch of the aorta begins and ends, bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk is visible.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Medial lemniscus is a continuation of which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fasciculus gracilis

Medial lemniscus is a continuation of fasciculus gracilis.

Posterior column–medial lemniscal pathway:

First-order axons carrying discriminative touch and vibration sensations enter the dorsal horn and continue traveling upward in the posterior white column as the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus.

Fibers of these fasciculi synapse on the second-order neurons of the ipsilateral nuclei gracilis and cuneatus in the medulla oblongata, respectively.

Axons of these second-order neurons then cross over as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus in the contralateral medulla.

These second-order axons ascend through the brainstem to reach the third-order neuronal cell bodies in the ventral posterior lateral nucleus of the thalamus. Axons from the third-order neurons then project through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to reach the primary somatosensory cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Neurotransmitter secreted by the area marked in the given image is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dopamine

The area marked in the given image is substantia nigra (meaning- dark substance). The neurotransmitter secreted by this area is dopamine.

Substantia nigra is a part of the nigrostriatal pathway. Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons is implicated in Parkinson's disease.

Other dopaminergic pathways include:

• Mesocortical
• Mesolimbic
• Tuberoinfundibular

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Reticular fibres are not present in which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thymus

Reticular fibres are not present in the thymus.

Reticular fibres are fine, anastomosing fibres composed of mainly type III collagen. They differ from type I collagen fibres in that, they are finer and are arranged in the form of a network (reticulum). The fibres appear black in colour on staining with silver impregnation. Due to this affinity to silver salts, they are also known as argentophil fibres.

Reticular fibres are mainly found in:

• All lymphoid organs like spleen, lymph node, and bone marrow (except thymus).
• Glands, liver and kidneys.
• The basement membrane of all epithelia.
• Smooth muscle and nerve cells.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The middle radioulnar joint is an example of a:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fibrous joint

The middle radioulnar joint is an example of a fibrous joint (syndesmosis).

The radius and ulna are united with each other by three joints:

• Proximal (superior) radioulnar joint
• Middle radioulnar joint
• Distal (inferior) radioulnar joint

Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot joints (synovial) and are involved in pronation and supination movements of the forearm.

The middle radioulnar joint is a fibrous joint (syndesmosis). The radius and ulna, in the middle, are connected by two syndesmoses namely:

• The oblique cord - extends from the lateral side of the ulnar tuberosity to the radius, distal to the radial tuberosity.
• Interosseous membrane - a broad, thin collagenous structure, which runs perpendicular to the oblique cord. It extends distomedially between the interosseous borders of the radius and ulna.

Based on the structure, joints are classified into three types:

• Fibrous joints

• Sutures
• Syndesmosis
• Gomphosis

• Cartilaginous joints

• Primary cartilaginous joints or synchondrosis
• Secondary cartilaginous joints or symphysis

• Synovial joints

• Ball-and-socket or spheroidal joints
• Sellar or saddle joints
• Condylar or bicondylar joints
• Ellipsoid joints
• Hinge joints
• Pivot or trochoid joints
• Plane joints

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia encloses all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sternocleidomastoid

All the above structures are enclosed by the pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia except sternocleidomastoid. It is enclosed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.

The deep cervical fascia of the neck is organized into the following layers:

• The investing layer, which surrounds all structures in the neck
• The prevertebral layer, which surrounds the vertebral column and the deep muscles associated with the back.
• The pretracheal layer, which encloses the viscera of the neck
• The carotid sheath, which receives a contribution from the other three fascial layers

In the neck, the pretracheal fascia covers the strap muscles i.e sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid. It splits to enclose the thyroid gland. It also surrounds the trachea and the esophagus including the recurrent laryngeal nerve present in the groove between them.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structures marked in the image below are found in the epithelial lining of all of the following sites, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epididymis

The image shows an arrow mark pointing towards the cilia. All the structures given in the options have a ciliated lining epithelium except epididymis, which is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia.

The given image is a histological section of the epididymis showing the pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia.

Cilia are minute hair-like projections, while stereocilia are very long, thick microvilli measuring about 5–10 μm in length.

Ciliated epithelium:

• The epithelium bears cilia, which moves in a coordinated fashion, and help in the movement of the mucus, or propel the movement of any other structures such as ova or spermatozoa.
• The ciliated columnar epithelium is found in most of the respiratory tract, the uterus, and the uterine tube (oviduct), efferent ductules of the testis, parts of the middle ear and auditory tube; the ependyma lining the central canal of the spinal cord and the ventricles of the brain.
• The pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium is seen in the trachea and in large bronchi.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The type of fibers present in the fornix are:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Association and commisural fibers

The fibers present in the fornix are association fibers except for the hippocampal commissure of fornix which has commissural fibers. Hence the most appropriate answer is option A. i.e both association and commissural fibers.

Association fibers connect various cortical regions within the same hemisphere whereas commissural fibers connect corresponding regions of two hemispheres.

Fornix arises from the hippocampus and ends in the mamillary body of the hypothalamus. It is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.

Note: The function of the commissure of the fornix is to connect the hippocampal formations of the two sides.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the action of the muscle at the hip, which is attached to the marked area in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Extension and lateral rotation

The image shows the posterior surface of the femur, and the structure marked is gluteal tuberosity, to which the gluteus maximus muscle is attached. It causes extension and lateral rotation at the hip joint.

The femur can be divided into:

• The proximal femur - Consists of the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters. The intertrochanteric line is present on the anterior surface at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur while the intertrochanteric crest is present on the posterior surface.
• The shaft of the femur - Consists of linea aspera (bony crest present on the posterior surface), gluteal tuberosity, and pectineal line
• The distal femur - Consists of the medial condyle, lateral condyle, intercondylar fossa, and patellar surface

The image below shows attachments of various muscles over the posterior surface of the right femur.

Gluteus maximus muscle:

Origin:

• Posterior aspect of the dorsal ilium, posterior to the posterior gluteal line
• Posterior superior iliac spine
• Posterior aspect of sacrum and coccyx
