• Sacrotuberous ligament.

Insertion - It is inserted mainly in fascia lata at the iliotibial band and also into the gluteal tuberosity on the posterior femoral surface.

Action:

• Major extensor of the hip joint
• Lateral rotation of the hip joint
• Active in powerful abduction of the thigh

Arterial Supply - Inferior and superior gluteal arteries and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery.

Nerve Supply- Inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1 and S2).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Where are the Ito cells in the liver located?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Space of disse

Ito cells/Hepatic stellate cells are located in the space of Disse. They are mesenchymal in origin.

The space of Disse or the perisinusoidal space (or space of Disse) is a location in the liver between hepatocytes and the liver sinusoid.

Significance of Ito cells:

Ito cells are in a dormant state for the majority of the duration. They store the fat-soluble vitamin A in their lipid droplets and are a signiﬁcant source of growth factors involved in liver homeostasis and regeneration.

When there is liver injury, Ito cells get activated. They replace damaged hepatocytes with collagenous scar tissue and secrete intralobular matrix components, including collagen type III (reticular) ﬁbres. This leads to hepatic ﬁbrosis.

Note: A narrow space which separates limiting plate (a sleeve of modified hepatocytes) from the connective tissue of the portal area is known as space of moll.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries passes in close proximity to the area marked by the arrow in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Middle meningeal artery

The area marked by an arrow in the given image is pterion and the artery that passes in close proximity to this area is the middle meningeal artery.

The pterion is an H shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull:

• Frontal bone
• Squamous part of the temporal bone
• Greater wing of the sphenoid bone
• Parietal bone.

It is an important structure as it overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery and lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere. The bone in this area is thin and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following bony structures is present behind the marked area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lesser wing of sphenoid

The structure marked in the image is pterion, and the bony structure that is present behind it is the lesser wing of the sphenoid.

The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull:

1. Frontal bone
2. Squamous part of the temporal bone
3. Greater wing of the sphenoid bone
4. Parietal bone

The pterion overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery and lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere. The bone in this area is thin and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.

The pterion also corresponds to the site of the anterolateral (sphenoidal) fontanelle of the neonatal skull, which closes in the third month after birth.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following features differentiates the exocrine pancreas from the parotid gland?
options: Basal lamina lining the serous acini
Presence of serous acini with acidophilic tip
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absence of striated duct

Absence of striated duct in exocrine pancreas differentiates it from the parotid gland.

The exocrine pancreas is comprised entirely of serous acini. Hence, its general structure is similar to that of the parotid gland, but the two are easily distinguished by:

• The parotid gland has striated and intercalated intralobular ducts, whereas the pancreas has only the intercalated type.
• The excretory ducts of the parotid gland are striated columnar, whereas the excretory duct of the pancreas is a simple columnar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following marked structures does not form part of the laryngeal skeleton?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

The structure marked as 'A', is the hyoid bone, which is not a part of the laryngeal skeleton.

The structures marked in the image are:

1. Hyoid bone
2. Thyroid cartilage
3. Epiglottis
4. Cricoid cartilage

The laryngeal skeleton is formed by a series of cartilages that are connected by ligaments and fibrous membranes:

• The thyroid, cricoid, and the greater part of the arytenoid cartilages consist of hyaline cartilage.
• The corniculate, cuneiform, tritiate, and epiglottic cartilages and the apices of the arytenoid cartilage consist of elastic cartilage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles is attached to the area marked in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Opponens pollicis

The area marked in the image is the palmar aspect of the first metacarpal. The opponens pollicis muscle is inserted at this site.

Opponens pollicis:

Origin:  Tubercle of the trapezium and flexor retinaculum

Insertion: Whole length of the lateral border and adjoining lateral half of the palmar aspect of the first metacarpal.

Action: Flexes the metacarpal bone of the thumb.

The image below shows various intrinsic muscles of the hand.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles is not involved in the overhead abduction of the arm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pectoralis major

Pectoralis major is mainly involved in adduction and medial rotation of the arm and is not involved in the abduction of the arm.

Glenohumeral abduction is about 120° or more. The glenohumeral arthrodesis restricts the abduction at about 45°. Further abduction occurs at the sterno and acromioclavicular articulations, and contralateral vertebral flexion.

Muscles involved in the abduction of the shoulder:

• The first 15° of abduction is initiated by the supraspinatus muscle.
• 15° to 90° of abduction is carried out mainly by the middle fibers of the deltoid muscle.
• Abduction of the arm, beyond 90°, is carried out by the movement of the shoulder girdle caused by the action of trapezius and serratus anterior.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 1-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for mass in the neck. The parents noticed a small area of nontender swelling in the neck a month ago. Over the last few days, it has enlarged and become painful, and the patient has a fever. Examination shows a mobile, tender, fluctuant, and warm mass approximately 2 cm in diameter that is located at the right mandibular angle. There is purulent drainage from the skin surface just anterior to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. This patient's clinical findings are most likely due to which of the following embryologic processes?
options: Failed descent of a pharyngeal pouch structure
Failed neural crest migration into a pharyngeal arch
Inadequate fusion of the mandibular prominences
Incomplete obliteration of a pharyngeal groove
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Incomplete obliteration of a pharyngeal groove

A branchial cleft (pharyngeal groove) cyst or fistula occurs due to failure of obliteration of the second pharyngeal cleft during embryologic development. These lesions commonly present in children or young adults as a lateral neck swelling along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Typical features:

• Located anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle
• Mobile, fluctuant neck mass
• May become painful, infected, and drain purulent material
• Often appears near the mandibular angle

Normally, the second pharyngeal arch overgrows the third and fourth arches, forming the cervical sinus, which later obliterates.

Failure of this obliteration leads to branchial cleft cysts, sinuses, or fistulas.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 50-year-old patient experiences numbness in the area around the neck following a cervical block performed for neck surgery. Which of the following is not a branch of the cervical plexus?
options: Transverse Cutaneous Nerve of the Neck
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phrenic Nerve

The cervical plexus is formed by the anterior rami of spinal nerves C1–C4 and provides sensory and some motor innervation to the neck region.

Cutaneous (sensory) branches of the cervical plexus:

• Lesser occipital nerve (C2)
• Greater auricular nerve (C2–C3)
• Transverse cervical (transverse cutaneous) nerve of neck (C2–C3)
• Supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4)

Motor branches include:

• Ansa cervicalis (C1–C3) → infrahyoid muscles
• Phrenic nerve (C3–C5) → diaphragm

Although the phrenic nerve originates mainly from C3–C5, it is considered a separate motor nerve rather than a typical branch supplying the neck region, making it the exception in this context.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy was diagnosed with urethral stricture. He underwent visual internal urethrotomy in the lithotomy position with stirrups supporting both popliteal fossa and proximal parts of tibia. No ankle support was used. On the first postoperative day, the patient complained of decreased sensation on the lateral aspect of right leg, the lateral border of his right foot and difficulty in dorsiflexion of the right foot due to compression of a particular nerve of the lower limb. Which of the following muscles is supplied by the nerve involved in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extensor Digitorum Longus

Compression at the popliteal region or fibular neck in the lithotomy position can injure the common peroneal (fibular) nerve, which is particularly vulnerable where it winds around the neck of the fibula.

Clinical features of common peroneal nerve injury:

• Foot drop due to loss of dorsiflexion
• Weak toe extension
• Sensory loss over:

• Lateral leg
• Dorsum of foot
• Lateral border of foot

The common peroneal nerve divides into:

1. Deep peroneal nerve (anterior compartment):

• Tibialis anterior
• Extensor hallucis longus
• Extensor digitorum longus
• Fibularis tertius

These muscles perform dorsiflexion of the foot and extension of toes.

2. Superficial peroneal nerve (lateral compartment):

• Fibularis longus
• Fibularis brevis

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 2-week-old boy is brought to the clinic by his parents for evaluation of his umbilicus. The parents report that since the umbilical cord stump separated 2 days ago, there has been serous pale drainage from the umbilicus that increases when the patient cries. He is exclusively breastfed and continues to have normal wet diapers and stool output. Laboratory results are as follows: • Hemoglobin: 14 g/dL • Platelets: 240,000/mm3 • TLC: 11,000/mm3 • Neutrophils: 60% • Lymphocytes: 32% Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's umbilical findings?
options: Incomplete closure of anterior abdominal wall
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Persistence of allantois remnant

Persistent serous fluid discharge from the umbilicus that increases with crying in a neonate suggests a patent urachus, which occurs due to persistence of the allantois remnant.

• The allantois connects the developing bladder to the umbilicus during fetal life.
• Normally it obliterates after birth and forms the urachus → median umbilical ligament.
• Failure of obliteration leads to urachal anomalies, most importantly patent urachus.

Clinical clue:

• Urine-like serous discharge from the umbilicus
• Discharge increases with crying or abdominal pressure
• Normal stool and urine output otherwise

Types of urachal anomalies:

1. Patent urachus – complete connection between bladder and umbilicus (urine leaks from umbilicus)
2. Urachal cyst
3. Umbilical urachal sinus
4. Vesicourachal diverticulum

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of right-sided facial weakness and sound intolerance. Three days ago, he hit the right side of his head in a motor vehicle collision. He neither lost consciousness nor sought medical attention. Sensation over the face is not impaired. Impedance audiometry shows an absence of the acoustic reflex in the right ear. Which of the following muscles is most likely paralyzed in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stylohyoid

This patient has right-sided facial weakness with hyperacusis (sound intolerance) after head trauma, indicating facial nerve (CN VII) injury. Facial nerve functions:

• Motor supply to muscles of facial expression
• Innervates stapedius muscle in the middle ear
• Supplies stylohyoid and posterior belly of digastric

Explanation of symptoms:

• Hyperacusis occurs because the stapedius muscle (innervated by CN VII) normally dampens excessive vibration of the stapes.
• Paralysis of stapedius → increased sound sensitivity.
• Loss of acoustic reflex on impedance audiometry confirms facial nerve involvement.

Among the options, the muscle supplied by CN VII is Stylohyoid.

Other options:

• A. Tensor tympani: Trigeminal nerve (V3)
• B. Posterior cricoarytenoid: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (CN X)
• C. Stylopharyngeus: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 30 y/o athlete reports sudden pain in the back of his left leg and an inability to push off the ground while sprinting. Examination reveals a significant weakness in plantar flexion. Which muscle is primarily responsible for the action of plantar flexion in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gastrocnemius

Plantar flexion of the ankle is mainly produced by the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, which together form the triceps surae.

Gastrocnemius:

• Origin: Medial and lateral condyles of the femur
• Insertion: Calcaneus via the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon
• Actions:

• Powerful plantar flexion of the foot
• Flexion of the knee

Clinical relevance:

• Sudden pain in the posterior leg with inability to push off while running often suggests gastrocnemius strain or Achilles tendon injury.
• This leads to weakness in plantar flexion.

Other options:

• A. Tibialis anterior: Dorsiflexion of the ankle.
• C. Tibialis posterior: Plantar flexion and inversion but not the primary powerful plantar flexor.
• D. Fibularis longus: Assists in plantar flexion and eversion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with inability to extend his wrist and fingers. O/E, he exhibits a wrist drop with loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the dorsum of the hand. Triceps muscle strength is fully intact and there is no sensory loss over the posterior arm. Elbow flexion in the mid-prone position is weak, and the brachioradialis tendon is not palpable on resisted flexion. Based on these findings, at which level is the radial nerve likely injured?
options: Posterior interosseous nerve at the forearm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. At the spiral groove

Reasoning from the localising signs

| Finding | What it tells you

| ------- | -----------------

| Wrist drop (loss of wrist + finger extension) | Radial nerve affected proximal to the extensor compartment supply

| Triceps fully intact | Branches to triceps arise in/proximal to the spiral groove → lesion is at or below the groove, not in the axilla

| No sensory loss over posterior arm | Posterior cutaneous nerve of arm arises in the axilla → intact ⇒ excludes an axillary lesion

| Sensory loss over lateral dorsum of hand | Superficial branch of radial nerve is involved ⇒ excludes a pure PIN lesion (PIN is purely motor)

→ Below axilla + sensory branch involved = spiral groove (radial groove of humerus)

Other options:

| Option | Why it fails

| ------ | ------------

| A. Axilla | Would cause triceps paralysis (loss of elbow extension) + sensory loss over posterior arm. Both are explicitly negative — the classic "crutch palsy" pattern.

| B. Spiral groove | Triceps spared, posterior cutaneous n. of arm spared, superficial radial involved. Textbook Saturday-night / honeymoon palsy.

| C. Lateral epicondyle | Radial divides here into superficial + deep branches. Would give wrist drop + sensory loss — but brachioradialis and ECRL would be spared, and wrist drop is typically incomplete/with radial deviation.

| D. PIN in forearm | Purely motor → finger drop (loss of MCP extension) with preserved wrist extension in radial deviation and NO sensory loss. The stem's sensory deficit rules this out outright.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents to the physician with a 3-month history of pain in her right shoulder. She is physically active and regularly plays tennis. The pain is reproduced when the shoulder is externally rotated against resistance. Injury of which of the following tendons is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Infraspinatus

The infraspinatus muscle is one of the rotator cuff muscles responsible for external rotation of the shoulder. Pain reproduced with external rotation against resistance indicates injury to the infraspinatus tendon, commonly seen in overhead athletes such as tennis players.

Thus, isolated pain with resisted external rotation localizes the pathology to the infraspinatus tendon.

Why not other options:

B. Pectoralis major: Causes adduction & internal rotation, not external rotation.

C. Subscapularis: Main internal rotator of shoulder.

D. Supraspinatus: Responsible for abduction initiation (0–15°).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 39-year-old man comes to the clinic with 2 weeks of severe low back pain radiating down the lateral aspect of his right thigh and leg to the dorsum of the foot. He reports tripping frequently because his foot “slaps the ground” while walking. The pain worsens when sitting for long periods. On examination, there is weakness of foot dorsiflexion and toe extension. Sensation is decreased over the dorsum of the right foot. The patellar (knee jerk) and Achilles reflexes are normal. Which of the following intervertebral discs is most likely herniated in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. L4–L5

This clinical picture is classic for L5 radiculopathy, most commonly due to L4–L5 intervertebral disc herniation.

• Pain distribution: Radiates along lateral thigh → leg → dorsum of foot
• Motor deficit:

• Weakness of dorsiflexion (foot drop)
• Weakness of toe extension (EHL)

→ “Foot slap gait”

• Sensory loss: Over dorsum of foot
• Reflexes: Usually normal (no reliable deep tendon reflex for L5)
• In lumbar disc herniation:

• Disc herniates posterolaterally
• Compresses the traversing (lower) nerve root

Thus: L4–L5 disc → compresses L5 nerve root

Why not other options:

A. L2–L3: Affects anterior thigh, not dorsum foot

B. L3–L4:

• Affects knee extension
• ↓ patellar reflex

D. L5–S1:

• Affects S1 root
• Weak plantarflexion
• ↓ Achilles reflex

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 40 year old female presents with symptoms of cavernous sinus thrombosis, including severe headache, visual disturbances, and facial swelling. Which of the following is not a tributary of the cavernous sinus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Deep facial vein

The cavernous sinus is a dural venous sinus located on either side of the sella turcica. It receives venous blood from the orbit, brain, and superficial facial regions. Tributaries of the cavernous sinus include:

• Superior ophthalmic vein
• Inferior ophthalmic vein
• Sphenoparietal sinus
• Superficial middle cerebral vein

Deep facial vein is not a direct tributary of the cavernous sinus. Instead:

• It drains into the pterygoid venous plexus.
• The pterygoid plexus communicates with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins.

Clinical relevance:

• Infections from the “danger triangle of the face” can spread to the cavernous sinus through connections between the facial vein → angular vein → superior ophthalmic vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 40 year old male patient presents with a shoulder injury following a fall. During a physical examination, the physician palpates the brachial artery to assess the blood supply to the arm. At which anatomical landmark does this artery begin as a continuation of the axillary artery?
options: Lower border of the teres minor
Upper border of the teres major
Lower border of the teres major
Upper border of the teres minor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lower border of the teres major

The brachial artery is the continuation of the axillary artery. Anatomical transition:

• The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of the teres major muscle.
• The brachial artery then travels down the arm in the medial bicipital groove and eventually divides into the radial and ulnar arteries at the level of the neck of the radius in the cubital fossa.

Clinical relevance:

• The brachial artery pulse can be palpated in the medial aspect of the arm.
• It is commonly used for blood pressure measurement and arterial catheterization.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 40-year-old man with a history of tobacco chewing presented with a non-healing ulcer over the tip of the tongue. Biopsy revealed squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following would be the sentinel lymph nodes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Submental lymph nodes

• Lymphatic drainage of the tongue is region-specific, and the first lymph node group receiving lymph (sentinel node) is important in the spread of carcinoma of the tongue.
• A carcinoma located at the tip of the tongue will first drain to the submental lymph nodes, making them the sentinel lymph nodes.

Lymphatic Drainage of Different Parts of Tongue:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of progressively worsening headaches and fatigue. She has also had a 5-kg weight loss in the same time period. MRI of the head shows a hyperintense mass with extension into the right foramen rotundum. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?
options: Decreased sensation over the cheekbone, nasolabial fold, and the upper lip
Hemiatrophy of the tongue with right-sided deviation when protruded
Abnormal taste of the distal tongue and decreased sensation behind the ear
Absent corneal reflex and decreased sensation of the forehead
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased sensation over the cheekbone, nasolabial fold, and the upper lip

The foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (V2), the purely sensory division of the trigeminal nerve. A lesion extending into the foramen rotundum therefore affects V2 sensory distribution.

Sensory supply of V2 (maxillary nerve):

• Lower eyelid
• Cheek (zygomatic region)
• Side of the nose and nasolabial fold
• Upper lip
• Upper teeth and maxillary sinus

Compression of V2 leads to loss or decrease of sensation in the midface. Therefore, a tumor involving the foramen rotundum will most likely cause decreased sensation over the cheekbone, nasolabial fold, and upper lip.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old male undergoes ligation of the femoral artery proximal to the profunda femoris due to trauma. Despite this, blood supply to the distal femur remains adequate through collateral circulation around the hip. Which arterial network is most responsible for restoring blood flow in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cruciate anastomosis

The cruciate anastomosis is an important arterial network around the upper thigh that provides collateral circulation when the femoral artery is occluded proximal to the profunda femoris. It is located in Posterior aspect of the upper femur near the lesser trochanter.

Arteries forming the cruciate anastomosis:

• Transverse branch of medial circumflex femoral artery
• Transverse branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery
• Ascending branch of the first perforating artery (from profunda femoris)
• Descending branch of the inferior gluteal artery

Allows blood from the internal iliac artery (via inferior gluteal artery) to reach the profunda femoris and distal femoral circulation when the femoral artery is ligated above the profunda femoris.

Other networks:

• Trochanteric anastomosis: mainly supplies the head and neck of the femur.
• Genicular anastomosis: around the knee joint.
• Obturator arcade: related to pelvic circulation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old male undergoes surgery for a retroperitoneal tumor compressing the inferior vena cava (IVC). During dissection, a large vein is identified draining directly into the IVC from the right kidney, while its counterpart on the left side drains into another vein before reaching the IVC. Which of the following veins directly drains into the IVC on both sides?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lumbar veins

This question tests knowledge of asymmetry in venous drainage into the IVC and identification of exceptions that are symmetric on both sides.

• Asymmetrical drainage (high-yield):

• Gonadal veins:

• Right → directly into IVC
• Left → into left renal vein

• Suprarenal veins:

• Right → directly into IVC
• Left → into left renal vein

• Renal veins:

• Both drain into IVC, but left renal vein receives tributaries (gonadal, suprarenal)

• Lumbar veins (important exception):

• Drain directly into IVC on both sides
• Form part of posterior abdominal wall venous system

• Clinical relevance:

• Important in retroperitoneal surgeries
• Lumbar veins can cause significant bleeding if injured

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is undergoing evaluation for palpitations. ECG reveals a supraventricular tachycardia with HR of 190/min. An echocardiogram reveals hypertrophy of the right ventricle and enlargement of the right ventricular outflow tract. Which structure separates the inflow and outflow tracts in the right ventricle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Supraventricular crest

The right ventricle has two functional parts:

• Inflow tract (sinus part) → receives blood from the tricuspid valve
• Outflow tract (infundibulum or conus arteriosus) → leads to the pulmonary trunk

These two parts are separated by a muscular ridge called the supraventricular crest.

Key anatomical features:

• Supraventricular crest: Separates the inflow tract from the outflow tract of the right ventricle.
• Crista terminalis: Ridge in the right atrium, separating smooth and rough parts.
• Moderator band (septomarginal trabecula): Carries part of the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle.
• Interventricular septum: Separates right and left ventricles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident with severe head trauma. His GCS is 5. On examination, there is a loss of sensation below the level of the neck and flaccid paralysis of all four limbs. Which of the following structures pass through the same cranial foramen as the structure involved in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spinal root of accessory nerve

The spinal root of the accessory nerve (CN XI) enters the skull through the foramen magnum, ascends briefly into the cranial cavity, and then exits the skull with the cranial root of CN XI through the jugular foramen. Structures passing through the foramen magnum:

• Medulla oblongata
• Spinal roots of the accessory nerve (CN XI)
• Vertebral arteries
• Anterior and posterior spinal arteries
• Meninges

Why others are incorrect:

A. Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) → passes through the hypoglossal canal.

B. Cranial root of accessory nerve → exits through the jugular foramen.

D. Middle meningeal artery → enters through the foramen spinosum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents to the clinic with symptoms of urinary incontinence. She reports a sensation of urgency followed by involuntary loss of urine. Her medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Upon further evaluation, you consider the role of the detrusor muscle in her condition. In understanding the embryological origins of muscles, which of the following muscles is not derived from the paraxial mesoderm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Detrusor

Muscles of the body develop from different embryological mesodermal sources. Most skeletal muscles arise from the paraxial mesoderm (somites), whereas smooth muscle of viscera develops from splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm of the lateral plate.

Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, which differentiate into myotomes that give rise to skeletal muscles. Examples in the options:

• Genioglossus → skeletal muscle of tongue (derived from occipital somites)
• Superior oblique → extra-ocular skeletal muscle
• Biceps brachii → skeletal muscle of upper limb

All are skeletal muscles derived from paraxial mesoderm.

Exception:

• Detrusor muscle → smooth muscle of the urinary bladder wall
• Derived from splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm of lateral plate mesoderm, not paraxial mesoderm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 52-year-old male undergoes carotid endarterectomy for carotid artery stenosis. Postoperatively, he develops difficulty in swallowing, loss of gag reflex, and impaired ability to sense changes in blood pressure via carotid sinus reflex. However, his facial movements and laryngeal functions remain intact. Which pharyngeal arch derivative is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Third pharyngeal arch

Third pharyngeal arch → Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

• Supplies:

• Stylopharyngeus muscle
• Afferent limb of gag reflex
• Carotid sinus & carotid body (baro- and chemoreceptors)

Clinical correlation:

• Dysphagia + loss of gag reflex (afferent) + impaired carotid sinus reflex

• Indicates CN IX involvement
• Hence, 3rd pharyngeal arch derivative

Other Options:

A. 1st arch (CN V3): mastication

B. 2nd arch (CN VII): facial expression

D. 4th arch (CN X): laryngeal function (intact here → rules it out)

| Arch | Nerve | Cartilage | Muscle | Artery | Internal pouch | External cleft

| ---- | ----- | --------- | ------ | ------ | -------------- | --------------

| 1st Mandibular | Trigeminal (Mandibular branch V3) nerve | •      Meckel's: Maxilla
·       Malleus & Incus | •      Mylohyoid
•      Anterior digastric
•      Tensor tympani
•      Tensor veli palatini
·       Muscles of mastication | 1st aortic arch: maxillary artery | •      Eustachian tube
•      Middle ear cleft
·       Medial surface of TM | •      External auditory meatus
·       Lateral surface of TM

| 2nd Hyoid | Facial nerve | •      Reichert's: Lesser cornu + upper body of hyoid
•      Stapes superstructure
·       Styloid process | •      Muscles of facial expression
•      Posterior belly of digastric
•      Platysma
·       Stapedius | 2nd aortic arch: stapedial artery | Palatine tonsil | Grows over remaining grooves

| 3rd | Glossopharyngeal nerve | Greater cornu + lower body of hyoid | •      Stylopharyngeus
·       Superior & middle constrictor | 3rd aortic arch | •      Inferior parathyroid glands
·       Thymic duct | Obliterated

| 4th | Vagus - Superior laryngeal nerve | Thyroid lamina | Cricothyroid | 4th aortic arch: arch of aorta | Superior parathyroid glands | Obliterated

| 6th | Vagus - Recurrent laryngeal nerve | •      Cricoid cartilage
·       Arytenoid cartilages | •      Inferior constrictor
·       Intrinsic muscles of larynx | 6th aortic arch: ductus arteriosus | Ultimobranchial body (forms parafollicular C cells of thyroid) | Obliterated

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 55-year-old male undergoes esophagectomy for carcinoma of the middle third of the esophagus. Postoperatively, he develops milky white fluid in the chest drain with high triglyceride content. Imaging confirms injury to a lymphatic structure in the posterior mediastinum. Which of the following best describes the anatomical course of the injured structure?
options: Ascends on the right side and drains into right venous angle
Ascends on the left side throughout and drains into left subclavian vein
Ascends on the right, crosses to the left at T5 level, and drains into left venous angle
Ascends on the left, crosses to the right at T8 level, and drains into right venous angle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ascends on the right, crosses to the left at T5 level, and drains into left venous angle

This question tests understanding of thoracic duct anatomy and its clinical relevance in chyle leak (chylothorax) after thoracic surgery.

• Thoracic duct injury → chylothorax

• Milky pleural fluid
• High triglyceride content

• Anatomical course of thoracic duct:

• Originates from cisterna chyli (L2)
• Ascends in posterior mediastinum on the right side
• Crosses to the left at T5 level
• Drains into left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular + subclavian vein)

• Clinical relevance:

• Vulnerable during esophageal and thoracic surgeries
• Injury → chyle leak → nutritional and immunological compromise

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 55-year-old man develops intracranial meningeal bleeding secondary to skull base osteomyelitis. Different regions of the dura mater are involved, and angiography shows distinct arterial sources depending on the cranial fossa involved. Which combination best identifies the major arterial supply to the dura mater in the three cranial fossae?
options: Anterior cranial fossa – Middle meningeal artery; Middle cranial fossa – Ascending pharyngeal artery; Posterior cranial fossa – Ophthalmic artery
Anterior cranial fossa – Ethmoidal arteries; Middle cranial fossa – Middle meningeal artery; Posterior cranial fossa – Meningeal branches of vertebral & occipital arteries
Anterior cranial fossa – Ascending pharyngeal artery; Middle cranial fossa – Ophthalmic artery; Posterior cranial fossa – Middle meningeal artery
Anterior cranial fossa – Deep temporal artery; Middle cranial fossa – Ascending palatine artery; Posterior cranial fossa – Maxillary artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior cranial fossa – Ethmoidal arteries; Middle cranial fossa – Middle meningeal artery; Posterior cranial fossa – Meningeal branches of vertebral & occipital arteries

The dura mater receives arterial supply from different arteries in each cranial fossa, mainly branches of the internal carotid and external carotid systems. Major arterial supply:

• Anterior cranial fossa:

o    Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (branches of the ophthalmic artery from the internal carotid artery)

• Middle cranial fossa:

o    Middle meningeal artery (branch of the maxillary artery from the external carotid artery)

o    Enters the skull through the foramen spinosum

• Posterior cranial fossa:

o    Meningeal branches of the vertebral and occipital arteries

The middle meningeal artery is the most clinically important because its rupture can cause an epidural hematoma, often associated with temporal bone fractures.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 56-year-old man with peripheral arterial disease undergoes femoral arterial catheterization for angiography. After passing the catheter through the femoral artery and advancing distally, the interventional radiologist notes that the artery disappears from the anterior medial thigh view on fluoroscopy and reappears in the popliteal fossa without forming a visible collateral branch in between. Which anatomical structure has the catheter just traversed?
options: Adductor hiatus in the adductor magnus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Adductor hiatus in the adductor magnus

The femoral artery travels through the anterior and medial thigh and enters the popliteal fossa after passing through the adductor hiatus. Adductor hiatus:

• An opening in the tendon of the adductor magnus muscle.
• Located at the distal end of the adductor canal.
• Allows the femoral artery and vein to pass from the anterior thigh to the posterior knee region.

After passing through the adductor hiatus:

• Femoral artery → becomes the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa.

Other structures:

• Femoral triangle: proximal region where the femoral vessels first enter the thigh.
• Adductor longus tendon: forms part of the medial boundary of the femoral triangle.
• Vastoadductor membrane: covers the adductor canal but is not the opening where the artery exits.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant presents with stridor, recurrent respiratory infections, and difficulty feeding with choking episodes. Imaging reveals a vascular ring encircling both the trachea and esophagus. Which of the following embryological abnormalities best explains this condition?
options: Persistence of right 4th aortic arch and caudal part of right dorsal aorta
Persistence of left dorsal aorta only
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Persistence of right 4th aortic arch and caudal part of right dorsal aorta

Double aortic arch is the most common cause of a complete vascular ring

• Caused by persistence of right 4th aortic arch + right dorsal aorta
• Leads to encirclement of trachea and esophagus

Clinical features:

• Stridor
• Recurrent respiratory infections
• Feeding difficulty, choking

Embryological concept:

• Normally, the right dorsal aorta regresses
• Persistence → forms a ring around foregut structures

Differentials to remember:

• Right aortic arch with aberrant left subclavian → incomplete ring
• 3rd arch abnormalities → carotid system, not vascular ring

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 6-year-old child falls from his bicycle and injures his hand. On X-ray, a fracture of the first metacarpal bone is noticed. Where is the epiphysis of the affected bone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. At the base

Metacarpal bones have secondary ossification centers (epiphyses) that differ between the first metacarpal and the other metacarpals.

Ossification pattern of metacarpals:

• 1st metacarpal (thumb):

• Epiphysis at the base

• 2nd–5th metacarpals:

• Epiphysis at the head

The first metacarpal behaves developmentally like a phalanx, therefore its secondary ossification center appears at the base rather than the head.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 60-year-old female undergoes right lower lobe resection for a tumor. Which statement about bronchopulmonary segments is true?
options: Each segment shares a bronchus with adjacent segments.
Segments are supplied by segmental arteries and share venous drainage.
Each segment has independent arterial and venous supplies.
The shape is pyramidal with the base at the hilum.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Segments are supplied by segmental arteries and share venous drainage.

A bronchopulmonary segment is a functionally independent subdivision of a lung lobe supplied by a segmental (tertiary) bronchus and its accompanying branch of the pulmonary artery. Key features:

• Each segment has its own segmental bronchus and segmental pulmonary artery.
• Pulmonary veins run in the intersegmental planes, so venous drainage is shared between adjacent segments.
• Segments are separated by connective tissue septa, allowing surgical resection of individual segments (segmentectomy).
• Each segment is pyramidal in shape, with the apex toward the hilum and base toward the lung surface.

Incorrect statements:

A. Segments do not share bronchi.

C. Venous drainage is not completely independent.

D. The base is at the pleural surface, not at the hilum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with persistent headaches that change location depending on intracranial irritation. MRI shows localized pachymeningitis affecting different cranial fossae at different times. The neurologist explains that each cranial fossa has a different primary sensory innervation of the dura, which helps explain the variation in referred pain patterns. Which combination correctly identifies the major nerve distribution to the dura mater in the three cranial fossae?
options: Anterior cranial fossa – V2; Middle cranial fossa – C1–C3; Posterior cranial fossa – V1
Anterior cranial fossa – V3; Middle cranial fossa – V1; Posterior cranial fossa – C1–C3
Anterior cranial fossa – V1; Middle cranial fossa – V3 (meningeal branches); Posterior cranial fossa – C1–C3
Anterior cranial fossa – V2; Middle cranial fossa – V3 via auriculotemporal nerve only; Posterior cranial fossa – V1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior cranial fossa – V1; Middle cranial fossa – V3 (meningeal branches); Posterior cranial fossa – C1–C3

The dura mater of the cranial cavity receives sensory innervation from branches of the trigeminal nerve and upper cervical nerves, which explains the pattern of referred headache pain depending on which cranial fossa is involved. Major sensory innervation of cranial fossae:

•

Anterior cranial fossa:

• Mainly supplied by ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve (V1)
• Especially via anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves

•

Middle cranial fossa:

• Supplied mainly by meningeal branches of the mandibular division (V3)
• Includes the nervus spinosus (meningeal branch of V3)

•

Posterior cranial fossa:

• Supplied primarily by upper cervical nerves (C1–C3)
• Also contributions from vagus and hypoglossal nerves

Irritation of different dural regions produces distinct headache referral patterns because of these different sensory nerve supplies.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 65-year-old hypertensive man develops sudden weakness of the right face, arm, and leg. Sensation is preserved. MRI shows a lacunar infarct involving the genu and adjacent posterior limb of the left internal capsule. Which vessel is most likely occluded?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Charcot artery

| Structure involved | Deficit

| ------------------ | -------

| Genu | Contralateral lower facial weakness

| Posterior limb | Contralateral hemiplegia

| Vessel | Lenticulostriate branch of MCA (Charcot artery)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 66-year-old man hospitalized 3 days ago for left lower lobe pneumonia is evaluated for persistent fever. He has been receiving the appropriate intravenous antibiotics as determined by antibiotic susceptibility testing of his sputum cultures. The patient has a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F) and pulse is 87/min. Examination shows dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds over the left lower lung. Imaging studies reveal a loculated, left-sided pleural effusion. A tube is placed to drain the fluid via an incision at the 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line. Which of the following muscles is most likely to be dissected during the procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serratus anterior

A chest tube for pleural drainage is commonly inserted in the 5th intercostal space at the midaxillary line (within the “safe triangle” of thoracostomy).

Layers encountered during insertion:

Skin → superficial fascia → Serratus anterior muscle → intercostal muscles → parietal pleura → pleural cavity.

The serratus anterior lies on the lateral thoracic wall in the midaxillary line, so it is typically dissected when inserting a chest tube at this site.

Other options:

• External oblique: located in the abdominal wall, not the thoracic insertion site.
• Latissimus dorsi: forms the posterior boundary of the safe triangle but is usually avoided.
• Pectoralis major: located anteriorly on the chest wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A medical student was yawning during his afternoon anatomy lecture. His jaw got arrested while yawning. Which muscle aids in relocation of the jaw?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Temporalis

Excessive yawning can cause anterior dislocation of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). In this condition, the mandibular condyle moves anterior to the articular tubercle of the temporal bone, and the mouth remains open.

The temporalis muscle is responsible for:

• Elevation of the mandible
• Retraction (pulling the mandible backward)

During TMJ dislocation, retrusion of the mandible by the temporalis muscle helps move the mandibular condyle back into the mandibular fossa, aiding in relocation of the jaw.

Comparison with other muscles:

• Lateral pterygoid → protrudes and depresses mandible
• Medial pterygoid → elevates mandible
• Masseter → powerful elevator of mandible

Only temporalis significantly retracts the mandible, which is needed to reduce the dislocation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A muscle that adducts and medially rotates the arm at the shoulder is found arising from the inferior angle of the scapula and inserted into the medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. Which nerve supplies it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lower subscapular nerve

The muscle described is teres major.

• Origin: Inferior angle of the scapula
• Insertion: Medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
• Actions:

o    Adduction of the arm

o    Medial rotation of the arm

o    Assists in extension of the shoulder

Nerve supply: Lower subscapular nerve (C5–C6) from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

Teres major forms part of the posterior axillary fold and the lower boundary of the quadrangular and triangular spaces in the axillary region.

Other options:

• Thoracodorsal nerve: supplies latissimus dorsi.
• Dorsal scapular nerve: supplies rhomboids and levator scapulae.
• Axillary nerve: supplies deltoid and teres minor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A neonate has isolated paralysis of a single tongue muscle, yet the hypoglossal nerve conduction study is completely normal. Swallowing is mildly affected and gag reflex is slightly diminished. MRI shows a small developmental defect in the muscle located at the junction of the palate and tongue. All remaining intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles appear normal. Which embryological structure most likely failed to develop properly?
options: Occipital myotomes derived from paraxial mesoderm
Neural crest mesenchyme surrounding the stomodeum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fourth pharyngeal arch mesoderm

Most tongue muscles (intrinsic and extrinsic) develop from occipital myotomes derived from paraxial mesoderm and are innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). However, the palatoglossus muscle is an exception.

Palatoglossus:

• Located at the junction of the soft palate and tongue
• Derived from the 4th pharyngeal arch mesoderm
• Innervated by the vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus, not the hypoglossal nerve

Clinical implication:

• A developmental defect affecting the 4th pharyngeal arch can cause isolated palatoglossus dysfunction with normal hypoglossal nerve conduction.
• This may cause mild swallowing difficulty and slight gag reflex changes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. An abdominal X-ray shows signs of bowel obstruction. Intraoperatively, the surgeon finds multiple fibrous bands with the cecum on the left side and the small intestine on the right side. What is the most likely underlying anomaly?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nonrotation of the midgut

During embryonic development, the midgut normally rotates 270° counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) before returning to the abdominal cavity.

Nonrotation of the midgut:

• Occurs when this normal rotation fails to occur.
• As a result:

• Small intestine lies predominantly on the right side
• Colon (including cecum) lies on the left side

Clinical features:

• Bilious vomiting
• Abdominal distension
• Intestinal obstruction
• Presence of fibrous peritoneal bands (Ladd bands) that may compress the duodenum.

Other conditions:

• Incomplete rotation (malrotation): predisposes to midgut volvulus.
• Reversed rotation: colon lies posterior to the SMA.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient has suffered a stroke caused by occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery. This patient is most likely to present with:
options: A loss of pain and temperature sensations in the left leg
Drooping of the corner of the mouth on the left
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A loss of pain and temperature sensations in the left leg

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA. supplies the medial surface of the brain, including the areas of the primary motor and sensory cortices responsible for the lower limb. An occlusion of the right ACA affects the contralateral side (in this case, the left leg) due to the decussation of motor and sensory pathways.

• The loss of pain and temperature sensations results from disruption of the sensory pathways supplying the contralateral lower limb.
• Additionally, motor deficits such as weakness or paralysis of the contralateral lower limb can occur, but this is not the best fit based on the options provided.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with right-sided hemiparesis and hemisensory loss of the leg and foot. He is unable to correctly identify objects and has significant personality changes. The occlusion of which of the following arteries could be responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior cerebral artery

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the paracentral lobule, which represents the motor and sensory areas for the lower limb (leg and foot).

Clinical features of ACA occlusion:

• Contralateral weakness of the leg and foot
• Contralateral sensory loss in the leg
• Behavioral and personality changes due to medial frontal lobe involvement
• Possible abulia (lack of motivation) and impaired judgment

Why other options are incorrect:

• Middle cerebral artery (MCA): affects face and upper limb, aphasia or neglect.
• Posterior cerebral artery (PCA): mainly causes visual deficits (contralateral homonymous hemianopia).
• Internal carotid artery: produces combined ACA and MCA deficits.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis presents with ulnar deviation of fingers at MCP joints. Which type of joint is primarily involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Condyloid joint

Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints are condyloid (ellipsoid) joints

• Movements allowed:

• Flexion–extension
• Abduction–adduction
• Circumduction

Clinical correlation:

• In rheumatoid arthritis, synovial inflammation leads to:

• Ulnar deviation of fingers at MCP joints
• Due to ligament laxity and joint destruction

High-yield differentiation:

• Hinge joint: elbow, interphalangeal joints (flexion–extension only)
• Pivot joint: atlantoaxial joint (rotation)
• Saddle joint: first carpometacarpal joint (thumb opposition)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A pedestrian crossing the road is met with a road traffic accident. He has presented to the emergency with left foot drop. Power in tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, and extensor hallucis longus is 0/5. While power in tibialis posterior, gastrocnemius is 4/5. What is the likely site of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fracture neck of left fibula

Foot drop is characterized by inability to dorsiflex the foot, resulting in a high-stepping gait (steppage gait). It most commonly occurs due to injury to the common peroneal (fibular) nerve. The common peroneal nerve winds superficially around the neck of the fibula, making it highly vulnerable to injury in fractures at this site.

The common peroneal nerve divides into deep and superficial peroneal nerves:

• Deep peroneal nerve → supplies dorsiflexors of the foot

• Tibialis anterior
• Extensor hallucis longus
• Extensor digitorum longus

In the question, these muscles have power 0/5, explaining the foot drop.

Muscles Spared:

• Tibialis posterior
• Gastrocnemius

These are supplied by the tibial nerve, which remains intact, explaining their preserved power (4/5).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A postpartum woman presents with headache, papilledema, and increased intracranial pressure. MR venography shows superior sagittal sinus thrombosis. Which finding best explains her symptoms?
options: Impaired CSF absorption due to blocked arachnoid villi
Increased CSF drainage to spinal veins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Impaired CSF absorption due to blocked arachnoid villi

The superior sagittal sinus receives cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) through arachnoid villi (arachnoid granulations).

• CSF produced by the choroid plexus circulates through the ventricles and subarachnoid space.
• It is absorbed into the venous system via arachnoid villi projecting into the superior sagittal sinus.

In superior sagittal sinus thrombosis:

• Venous outflow is obstructed.
• Arachnoid villi cannot drain CSF into the sinus.
• This causes impaired CSF absorption, leading to increased intracranial pressure (ICP).

Clinical features:

• Headache
• Papilledema
• Signs of raised intracranial pressure

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A right trochlear nerve lesion causes:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right SO palsy

The trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies the superior oblique (SO) muscle of the eye.

• It is the only cranial nerve that exits dorsally from the brainstem.
• Its fibers decussate (cross) within the brainstem before exiting.
• Therefore, each trochlear nerve innervates the superior oblique muscle on the same side after crossing.

A right trochlear nerve lesion results in right superior oblique muscle palsy.

Function of superior oblique:

• Intorsion
• Depression of the adducted eye
• Abduction

Clinical signs:

• Vertical diplopia
• Difficulty looking down while reading or descending stairs
• Compensatory head tilt away from the affected side

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A soccer player twists his ankle after inversion of a plantar-flexed foot. He develops pain and swelling over the lateral aspect of the ankle. Which ligament is most commonly injured in this type of ankle sprain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL)

• The ATFL is the most commonly injured ligament in an ankle sprain.

• Mechanism: Inversion + plantar flexion
• Type: Lateral/“low” ankle sprain
• Most commonly injured: ATFL
• High ankle sprain: Involves the AITFL (syndesmosis) and typically occurs with external rotation ± dorsiflexion.

High-yield: Inversion + plantar flexion → ATFL

• The squeeze test (compressing the tibia and fibula together above the ankle, reproducing distal pain at the syndesmosis) is specific for high ankle sprains and is typically negative in isolated ATFL injuries.
• Mnemonic: "High tibiofibular ligament, high tide" — helping distinguish the AITFL/high ankle sprain from the far more common ATFL/low ankle sprain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A surgeon identifies a structure passing through the central tendon of the diaphragm at T8. Which additional structure is most likely found at this site?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right phrenic nerve

Contents of Caval Opening

• Inferior vena cava (IVC)
• Right phrenic nerve

Why other options are wrong

• A. Thoracic duct → passes through aortic hiatus (T12)
• D. Azygos vein → passes through aortic hiatus (T12)
• C. Left phrenic nerve pierces the muscular part of the diaphragm independently

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A surgeon inadvertently injured the middle trunk of the brachial plexus while removing a Pancoast tumor. Which of the following nerve functions can be impaired?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thoracodorsal nerve

The middle trunk of the brachial plexus is formed by the anterior ramus of C7. Knowledge of which nerves ultimately carry C7 fibers helps predict deficits when this trunk is injured (e.g., during surgery for a Pancoast tumor at the lung apex).

The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord and carries fibers from C6–C8 (especially C7). Therefore, injury to the middle trunk (C7) can impair the thoracodorsal nerve, affecting the latissimus dorsi muscle.

Function affected: Latissimus dorsi

• Extension of the arm
• Adduction of the arm
• Medial rotation of the arm

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Medial pectoral nerve → arises from the medial cord (C8–T1).
• Nerve to subclavius → arises from the upper trunk (C5–C6).
• Suprascapular nerve → also arises from the upper trunk (C5–C6).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true about grey rami communicants except:
options: Present medial to white rami communicants
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preganglionic

Gray rami communicants are branches that connect the sympathetic trunk (paravertebral ganglia) to the spinal nerves and carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers to the body wall.

• Unmyelinated fibers
• Contain postganglionic sympathetic fibers
• Connect the sympathetic chain ganglion to the spinal nerve
• Present at all spinal levels (C1–Co)
• Located medial to the white rami communicants

| Feature | White rami | Gray rami

| ------- | ---------- | ---------

| Fiber type | Myelinated | Unmyelinated

| Fibers carried | Preganglionic sympathetic | Postganglionic sympathetic

| Levels present | T1–L2 only | All spinal levels

| Direction | Spinal nerve → sympathetic trunk | Sympathetic trunk → spinal nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following tracts pass through inferior cerebellar peduncle except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior spinocerebellar

The inferior cerebellar peduncle (restiform body) connects the medulla to the cerebellum and mainly carries afferent (sensory) fibers to the cerebellum involved in proprioception and coordination.

Major Tracts Passing Through the Inferior Cerebellar Peduncle:

• Posterior (dorsal) spinocerebellar tract

• Carries unconscious proprioception from trunk and lower limbs.

• Cuneocerebellar tract

• Carries unconscious proprioception from upper limbs.

• Olivocerebellar fibers

• Arise from the inferior olivary nucleus and play an important role in motor learning and coordination.

Anterior (ventral) spinocerebellar tract passes through the superior cerebellar peduncle, not the inferior peduncle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An 8 year old child presents to the pediatric clinic with recurrent ear infections and complaints of ear pain, especially after upper respiratory infections. What is the most likely reason for this child's increased susceptibility to ear infections?
options: The Eustachian tube's shorter length allows for quicker drainage of secretions from the middle ear.
The more horizontal orientation of the Eustachian tube in children impairs proper ventilation and drainage of the middle ear.
The Eustachian tube opens more frequently during normal activities in children, causing increased exposure to environmental allergens.
The Eustachian tube is typically narrow in children, which facilitates the entry of pathogens from the nasopharynx.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The more horizontal orientation of the Eustachian tube in children impairs proper ventilation and drainage of the middle ear.

Children are more prone to otitis media because the Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube differs anatomically from that of adults.

In children, the Eustachian tube is:

• Shorter
• More horizontal
• Relatively wider

The more horizontal orientation makes ventilation and drainage of the middle ear less efficient and allows nasopharyngeal secretions and pathogens to reflux into the middle ear, especially during upper respiratory infections. This predisposes children to recurrent middle ear infections.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An 82-year-old woman is sent to the hospital from a nursing home after 2 days of fever, confusion, and lethargy. The patient has a history of mild dementia, hypertension, and osteoarthritis. Her temperature is 38.8°C (102°F), blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, and pulse is 116/min. She has mild suprapubic and right costovertebral angle tenderness. Her leukocyte count is 18,000/mm³, and urinalysis is consistent with acute cystitis. A femoral venous access is planned for administration of intravenous fluids and antibiotics. The femoral artery pulsation is palpable immediately below the inguinal ligament. Which of the following describes the optimal cannulation site for the femoral vein?
options: Immediately lateral to the femoral artery
Immediately medial to the femoral artery
Midway between the iliac crest and the femoral artery
Superior and medial to the pubic tubercle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immediately medial to the femoral artery

The femoral vein lies medial to the femoral artery within the femoral triangle, just inferior to the inguinal ligament. Therefore, when the femoral artery pulse is palpated, the optimal site for femoral venous cannulation is immediately medial to the artery.

Arrangement of structures in the femoral triangle (lateral → medial)

NAVEL mnemonic:

• N – Femoral Nerve
• A – Femoral Artery
• V – Femoral Vein
• E – Empty space (femoral canal)
• L – Lymphatics

Clinical correlation

• Femoral venous access is used in shock, sepsis, or emergency resuscitation when rapid central access is needed.
• The needle is inserted just medial to the palpable femoral artery pulse below the inguinal ligament to access the femoral vein safely.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An infant presents with progressive macrocephaly, a bulging fontanelle, and impaired upward gaze ("sunset eyes"). MRI shows marked dilation of the lateral and third ventricles, with a normal-sized fourth ventricle. Where is the site of CSF flow obstruction, and which structure is compressed to cause the impaired upward gaze?
options: Obstruction at the foramen of Magendie; compression of the inferior colliculi
Obstruction at the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius; compression of the superior colliculi (dorsal midbrain/Parinaud syndrome)
Obstruction at the interventricular foramina of Monro; compression of the pineal gland alone, unrelated to eye movements
Obstruction at the foramina of Luschka; compression of the cerebellum causing eye movement abnormality
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Obstruction at the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius; compression of the superior colliculi (dorsal midbrain/Parinaud syndrome)

• Normal CSF flow: lateral ventricles → 3rd ventricle (via foramina of Monro) → 4th ventricle (via cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius) → subarachnoid space (via foramina of Luschka [lateral] and Magendie [medial]).
• Since the lateral and third ventricles are dilated but the fourth ventricle is normal-sized, the obstruction must lie between the third and fourth ventricles — i.e., at the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius (classic aqueductal stenosis, the most common cause of congenital/obstructive hydrocephalus).
• The resulting dilation of the third ventricle and adjacent structures compresses the dorsal midbrain (tectum), specifically the superior colliculi, which coordinate upward gaze — producing Parinaud syndrome ("sunset eyes," paralysis of upward gaze).
• Obstruction at the foramen of Magendie/Luschka (distal to the 4th ventricle) would cause dilation of all four ventricles including the 4th; obstruction at the foramen of Monro would cause isolated lateral ventricle dilation, sparing the third ventricle — neither matches this imaging pattern.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arrange in sequence the structures involved in the direct pathway: 1. Striatum 2. Globus pallidus 3. Substantia nigra 4. Thalamus 5. Cortex 6. Subthalamic nucleus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5, 1, 2, 3, 4

The direct pathway of the basal ganglia facilitates initiation and execution of voluntary movement by reducing inhibitory output from the basal ganglia to the thalamus.

Sequence of the direct pathway:

1. Cortex stimulates the striatum (caudate + putamen).
2. Striatum inhibits the globus pallidus internus / substantia nigra pars reticulata.
3. This reduces inhibitory output from the basal ganglia to the thalamus.
4. Thalamus then excites the motor cortex, promoting movement.

Correct sequence: Cortex → Striatum → Globus pallidus → Substantia nigra → Thalamus, which corresponds to: 5 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arrange the events in the development of the thyroid gland in the correct sequence: 1. Fusion with caudal pharyngeal complex. 2. Formation of pharyngeal arches 3. Thyroglossal duct formation 4. Tuberculum impar is formed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2, 4, 3, 1

The thyroid gland develops from an endodermal thickening in the floor of the primitive pharynx near the foramen cecum of the tongue.

Correct developmental sequence:

1.     Formation of pharyngeal arches

2.     Formation of the tuberculum impar in the developing tongue

3.     Thyroglossal duct formation as the thyroid primordium descends from the foramen cecum

4.     Fusion with the caudal pharyngeal complex (ultimobranchial body contributing C cells)

Persistence of the thyroglossal duct can lead to thyroglossal duct cysts, typically located in the midline of the neck and moving with swallowing or tongue protrusion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arrange the following fibers of the internal capsule in order from posterior to anterior: 1. Frontopontine fibers 2. Corticonuclear tract 3. Corticospinal tract 4. Sublentiform fibres
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 4 → 3 → 2 → 1

The internal capsule is organized from anterior to posterior as follows:

• Anterior limb → Frontopontine fibers
• Genu → Corticonuclear fibers
• Posterior limb → Corticospinal fibers
• Retrolenticular part → Occipitopontine fibers

Reversing this order gives posterior → anterior:

Occipitopontine → Corticospinal → Corticonuclear → Frontopontine

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During a submandibular surgical approach, after reflecting the mylohyoid muscle, a surgeon identifies the hyoglossus muscle. Two nerves are seen running superficial to hyoglossus, one lying closer to the oral mucosa (more superior) and the other lying closer to the hyoid bone (more inferior) before entering the tongue region. Which combination correctly identifies the two nerves based only on their anatomical position relative to hyoglossus?
options: Superior – Hypoglossal nerve; Inferior – Lingual nerve
Superior – Lingual nerve; Inferior – Hypoglossal nerve
Superior – Marginal mandibular nerve; Inferior – Lingual nerve
Superior – Glossopharyngeal nerve; Inferior – Hypoglossal nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superior – Lingual nerve; Inferior – Hypoglossal nerve

The hyoglossus muscle is an important anatomical landmark in the floor of the mouth used to identify nearby nerves and vessels. Structures related to the hyoglossus muscle:

Superficial (lateral) to hyoglossus:

• Lingual nerve (more superior, closer to oral mucosa)
• Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) (more inferior, closer to the hyoid bone)
• Submandibular duct

Deep (medial) to hyoglossus:

• Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
• Lingual artery

During submandibular gland or floor-of-mouth surgery, recognizing these relations helps avoid injury to the lingual and hypoglossal nerves, which could cause loss of tongue sensation or motor function.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During dissection of the posterior leg compartment, a medical student encounters a long, thin structure extending from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the femur all the way down to the calcaneus. Because of its slender appearance, it is often mistaken for a nerve (called freshman’s nerve). Which muscle has the longest tendon in the body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Plantaris

The plantaris muscle is a small muscle of the posterior compartment of the leg known for having the longest tendon in the human body.

• Origin: Lateral supracondylar line of the femur
• Insertion: Posterior surface of the calcaneus (often via the Achilles tendon)
• Tendon: Very long and thin, extending from the knee to the heel

Because of its slender tendon, it is often called the “freshman’s nerve”, as it can be mistaken for a nerve during dissection.

Function:

• Weak plantar flexion of the ankle
• Weak flexion of the knee

The plantaris tendon is sometimes harvested for tendon grafts because its removal has minimal functional effect.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During early embryonic development, the neural tube differentiates into primary and secondary brain vesicles, which later give rise to specific adult brain structures and ventricular components. Which of the following vesicle–derivative–ventricle combinations is correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mesencephalon → Midbrain → Cerebral aqueduct

During early embryonic brain development, the neural tube forms primary brain vesicles, which later divide into secondary brain vesicles. Each vesicle gives rise to specific adult brain structures and ventricular cavities.

Correct relationship:

• Mesencephalon → Midbrain → Cerebral aqueduct

Why others are incorrect:

A. Telencephalon → Thalamus → Third ventricle: Thalamus comes from diencephalon.

B. Diencephalon → Cerebral hemispheres → Lateral ventricles: Hemispheres come from telencephalon.

D. Myelencephalon → Pons → Fourth ventricle: Pons develops from metencephalon.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During embryological development, the buccopharyngeal (or oropharyngeal) membrane separates the primitive mouth from the foregut and later ruptures to establish continuity. This membrane is formed by the fusion of which of the following germ layers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ectoderm and endoderm

• Buccopharyngeal (or oropharyngeal) membrane:

• Formed by direct contact of ectoderm and endoderm
• No intervening mesoderm
• Separates stomodeum (primitive mouth) from foregut

• Developmental event:

• Membrane ruptures around 4th week
• Establishes communication between oral cavity and pharynx

• Other similar membrane:

• Cloacal membrane → also ectoderm + endoderm (no mesoderm)

Most body structures have mesoderm between layers, but these membranes are exceptions

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During laparoscopic surgery near the diaphragm, a surgeon encounters brisk bleeding from a vessel supplying the inferior surface of the diaphragm and adjacent pleura. This vessel typically arises directly from which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Abdominal aorta

Inferior phrenic arteries:

• Supply the inferior surface of diaphragm
• Also contribute to adjacent pleura and suprarenal glands
• Most commonly arise directly from the abdominal aorta (may also arise from celiac trunk occasionally)

Other diaphragmatic supply (high-yield differentiation):

• Superior phrenic arteries → from thoracic aorta
• Pericardiacophrenic & musculophrenic arteries → from internal thoracic artery

Clinical relevance:

• Important source of bleeding during upper abdominal/laparoscopic surgery
• Can be involved in collateral circulation in liver disease

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During surgery on a 56-year-old man for a squamous cell carcinoma of the neck, the surgeon notices profuse bleeding from the deep cervical artery. Which of the following arteries must be ligated immediately to stop bleeding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Costocervical trunk

The deep cervical artery is a branch of the costocervical trunk, which itself arises from the subclavian artery. Therefore, severe bleeding from the deep cervical artery can be controlled by ligation of the costocervical trunk, the parent vessel supplying it.

• Subclavian artery branches (relevant here):

o    Thyrocervical trunk

o    Costocervical trunk

• Costocervical trunk branches:

o    Deep cervical artery – supplies deep muscles of the neck and participates in anastomosis with the descending branch of the occipital artery.

o    Superior intercostal artery

Since the deep cervical artery originates from the costocervical trunk, ligating the costocervical trunk will effectively control hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During surgery, the surgeon notices an additional thyroid vein, known as the Kocher’s vein, which drains into the internal jugular vein. The surgeon carefully ligates this additional vein to avoid any postoperative complications. What is the most likely origin of this additional vein?
options: Between the middle and inferior thyroid veins
Between the superior and inferior thyroid veins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Between the middle and inferior thyroid veins

Kocher’s vein is an additional thyroid vein that may be present as an anatomical variation during thyroid surgery.

• It usually drains into the internal jugular vein.
• It most commonly arises between the middle and inferior thyroid veins.
• It may drain blood from the posterolateral surface of the thyroid gland.

Clinical importance:

• Important during thyroidectomy because if unrecognized it can lead to significant intraoperative bleeding.
• Surgeons must identify and ligate it carefully during dissection near the internal jugular vein.

| Vein | Origin | Drainage

| ---- | ------ | --------

| Superior Thyroid Vein | Upper pole of the thyroid | Internal jugular vein

| Middle Thyroid Vein | Middle of the thyroid lobe | Internal jugular vein

| Inferior Thyroid Vein | Lower border of the isthmus | Plexus in front of trachea → Left brachiocephalic vein

| Kocher’s Vein (Fourth Thyroid Vein) | Between middle and inferior veins | Internal jugular vein

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Following statements concerning the structures that leave the pelvis are correct, except:
options: The sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen
The piriformis muscle leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen
The external iliac artery passes beneath the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery
The obturator nerve leaves the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The obturator nerve leaves the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen

Several important nerves, muscles, and vessels exit the pelvis through specific foramina or openings.

• Sciatic nerve: Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below the piriformis muscle).
• Piriformis muscle: Exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and divides it into suprapiriform and infrapiriform compartments.
• External iliac artery: Passes beneath the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery in the thigh.
• Obturator nerve: Leaves the pelvis through the obturator canal, not the lesser sciatic foramen.

Lesser sciatic foramen transmits:

• Pudendal nerve
• Internal pudendal vessels
• Nerve to obturator internus
• Tendon of obturator internus

Therefore, the incorrect statement is that the obturator nerve leaves through the lesser sciatic foramen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: GSE fibres are present in cranial nerves:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. III, IV, VI, XII

General Somatic Efferent (GSE) fibers are motor fibers that supply the skeletal muscles derived from somites. These fibers are involved in voluntary motor control. The cranial nerves that contain GSE fibers and their respective muscles include:

• Cranial Nerve III (Oculomotor nerve): Innervates most of the extraocular muscles, including the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique, as well as the levator palpebrae superioris.
• Cranial Nerve IV (Trochlear nerve): Supplies the superior oblique muscle of the eye.
• Cranial Nerve VI (Abducens nerve): Innervates the lateral rectus muscle of the eye.
• Cranial Nerve XII (Hypoglossal nerve): Supplies the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue.

These cranial nerves have motor nuclei that are classified as GSE.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: How many papillary muscles are present in the left ventricle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2

The left ventricle contains two papillary muscles:

• Anterior papillary muscle
• Posterior papillary muscle

In contrast:

• The right ventricle has three papillary muscles:

• Anterior
• Posterior
• Septal

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: If the development of the endoderm is negatively affected and fails to normally differentiate, which of the following glands would not be affected by this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior pituitary

During embryonic development, many endocrine glands arise from the endoderm, particularly from the pharyngeal pouch endoderm and foregut endoderm.

Endoderm-derived glands:

• Follicular cells of the thyroid → derived from endoderm of the primitive pharynx.
• Parathyroid glands → develop from 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouch endoderm.
• Pancreas → develops from foregut endoderm (dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds).

Exception:

• The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) develops from oral ectoderm (Rathke’s pouch), not from endoderm. Therefore, endodermal developmental defects would not affect the anterior pituitary.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In which layer of the cerebral cortex is the outer band of Baillarger seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Internal granular layer

The bands of Baillarger are horizontal layers of myelinated fibers seen in the cerebral cortex.

There are two bands:

• Outer band of Baillarger → located in Layer IV (Internal granular layer)
• Inner band of Baillarger → located in Layer V (Internal pyramidal layer)

Functional significance:

• The outer band corresponds to thalamocortical input fibers, which terminate mainly in layer IV.
• In the primary visual cortex (area 17), the outer band is highly developed and appears as the stria of Gennari.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In which of the following chambers can one palpate a muscular ridge, which is the site of origin of pectinate muscles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right atrium

The pectinate muscles are parallel muscular ridges present mainly in the right atrium, especially within the right auricle.

These muscles originate from a prominent vertical ridge called the crista terminalis, which separates two parts of the right atrium:

• Posterior smooth part (sinus venarum) – derived from the sinus venosus
• Anterior rough part with pectinate muscles – derived from the primitive atrium

Clinical correlation:

• The crista terminalis serves as an important landmark for cardiac conduction pathways.
• It corresponds externally to the sulcus terminalis.

The left atrium is mostly smooth, with pectinate muscles confined only to the left auricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Persistent left superior vena cava is due to failure of regression of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left anterior cardinal vein

During embryological development of the venous system, the anterior cardinal veins drain blood from the cranial part of the embryo. Normal development:

• The right anterior cardinal vein and right common cardinal vein form the superior vena cava (SVC).
