• The left anterior cardinal vein normally regresses, leaving the ligament of Marshall and contributing to the coronary sinus.

Persistent left superior vena cava (PLSVC):

• Occurs when the left anterior cardinal vein fails to regress.
• The persistent vessel usually drains into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.
• Often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally.
• Important during central venous catheterization, pacemaker placement, or cardiac surgery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Regarding typical and atypical ribs, all of the following statements are correct except:
options: The head of a typical rib has two articular facets
The tubercle of a rib articulates with the transverse process of a vertebra
The 11th and 12th ribs possess necks and tubercles
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The 11th and 12th ribs possess necks and tubercles

Ribs are classified into typical and atypical based on anatomical features.

Typical ribs (3–9):

They are curved and consist of a shaft with anterior and posterior ends.

• The anterior end attaches to costal cartilage
• The posterior end has a head, neck, and tubercle
• They articulate with vertebrae at three sites:

• Head → has two facets (articulates with two vertebral bodies)
• Tubercle → articulates with the transverse process

Atypical ribs (1, 2, 10, 11, 12):

They show variations from the typical pattern:

• 1st rib → flat, head has single facet, superior surface has scalene tubercle
• 2nd rib → has rough area for serratus anterior attachment
• 10th rib → head has single facet
• 11th & 12th ribs → head has single large facet and lack neck and tubercle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Sequential arrangement of secretomotor pathway to lacrimal gland: 1. Pons 2. Nerve of pterygoid canal 3. Geniculate ganglion 4. Nervus intermedius 5. Lacrimal nerve 6. Greater petrosal nerve 7. Pterygopalatine ganglion 8. Zygomaticotemporal nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 4, 3, 6, 2, 7, 8, 5

The secretomotor (parasympathetic) supply of the lacrimal gland originates from the facial nerve (CN VII) and follows a specific sequence through the pterygopalatine ganglion before reaching the gland.

Sequential pathway

1. Pons – Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arise from the superior salivatory nucleus.
2. Nervus intermedius – Parasympathetic root of the facial nerve carries these fibers.
3. Geniculate ganglion – Sensory ganglion; fibers pass through without synapse.
4. Greater petrosal nerve – Carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers.
5. Nerve of pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve) – Formed by the union of greater petrosal nerve + deep petrosal nerve.
6. Pterygopalatine ganglion – Synapse occurs here.
7. Zygomaticotemporal nerve (branch of V2) – Postganglionic fibers hitchhike.
8. Lacrimal nerve (branch of V1) – Carries fibers to the lacrimal gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Struthers syndrome results from compression of:
options: Radial nerve in the radial tunnel
Median nerve beneath a ligament from supracondylar process to medial epicondyle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Median nerve beneath a ligament from supracondylar process to medial epicondyle

Struthers syndrome is a rare condition caused by compression of the median nerve beneath the ligament of Struthers.

• The ligament of Struthers is a fibrous band extending from the supracondylar process of the humerus to the medial epicondyle.
• The median nerve and sometimes the brachial artery pass beneath this ligament.

Clinical features:

• Median nerve compression symptoms, similar to proximal median neuropathy:

o    Pain or paresthesia in the lateral 3½ fingers

o    Weakness of forearm flexors and thenar muscles

Important distinction:

• Struthers syndrome: compression above the elbow by ligament of Struthers.
• Carpal tunnel syndrome: compression at the wrist under the flexor retinaculum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The blood oxygen saturations measured from different fetal vessel samples are 71%, 64%, 62%, 55%, and 43%. The sample with the greatest oxygen saturation was most likely obtained from which of the following blood vessels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inferior vena cava

In fetal circulation, the highest oxygen saturation is found in blood returning from the placenta through the umbilical vein. After passing through the ductus venosus, this relatively well-oxygenated blood enters the inferior vena cava (IVC) before reaching the right atrium.

Approximate descending order of oxygen saturation:

1. Umbilical vein → highest (\~80%)
2. Inferior vena cava → \~65–70% (mixture of oxygenated placental blood and systemic venous blood)
3. Right atrium / left atrium mixture
4. Pulmonary trunk / ductus arteriosus
5. Descending aorta → lower due to mixing with deoxygenated blood

The IVC carries blood from the ductus venosus that bypassed the fetal liver, so it contains the most oxygenated blood among the listed options.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The Burn’s space (suprasternal space) is located in which anatomical region?
options: Between the two layers of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Between the two layers of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia

Burns’ space (suprasternal space) is a small potential space in the lower anterior neck.

• Situated between the two layers of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia
• Located just above the manubrium of the sternum, between the sternal heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscles

Contents:

• Jugular venous arch
• Interclavicular ligament
• Occasionally fat and lymph nodes

Clinical relevance:

• Can act as a pathway for spread of infection in the anterior neck.
• Important surgical landmark during tracheostomy or neck dissections.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The first pharyngeal arch gives rise to all of the following muscles Expect:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Levator veli palatini

The 1st pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch) forms:

• Muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial & lateral pterygoids)
• Mylohyoid
• Anterior belly of digastric
• Tensor tympani
• Tensor veli palatini

Levator veli palatini is not derived from the 1st arch

• It develops from the 4th pharyngeal arch
• Supplied by vagus nerve (pharyngeal plexus)

| Arch | Nerve | Cartilage | Muscle | Artery | Internal pouch | External cleft

| ---- | ----- | --------- | ------ | ------ | -------------- | --------------

| 1st Mandibular | Trigeminal (Mandibular branch V3) nerve

• Meckel's: Maxilla
• Malleus & Incus

• Mylohyoid
• Anterior digastric
• Tensor tympani
• Tensor veli palatini
• Muscles of mastication

| 1st aortic arch: maxillary artery

• Eustachian tube
• Middle ear cleft
• Medial surface of TM

• External auditory meatus
• Lateral surface of TM

| 2nd Hyoid | Facial nerve

• Reichert's: Lesser cornu + upper body of hyoid
• Stapes superstructure
• Styloid process

• Muscles of facial expression
• Posterior belly of digastric
• Platysma
• Stapedius

| 2nd aortic arch: stapedial artery | Palatine tonsil | Grows over remaining grooves

| 3rd | Glossopharyngeal nerve | Greater cornu + lower body of hyoid

• Stylopharyngeus
• Superior & middle constrictor

| 3rd aortic arch

• Inferior parathyroid glands
• Thymic duct

| Obliterated

| 4th | Vagus - Superior laryngeal nerve | Thyroid lamina | Cricothyroid | 4th aortic arch: arch of aorta | Superior parathyroid glands | Obliterated

| 6th | Vagus - Recurrent laryngeal nerve

• Cricoid cartilage
• Arytenoid cartilages

• Inferior constrictor
• Intrinsic muscles of larynx

| 6th aortic arch: ductus arteriosus | Ultimobranchial body (forms parafollicular C cells of thyroid) | Obliterated

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What mechanism occurs within the zona pellucida of an oocyte to prevent the entry of multiple sperm cells after the initial fertilization?
options: Increased membrane potential of the oocyte
Decreased membrane potential of the oocyte
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cortical reaction

After the first sperm fertilizes the oocyte, mechanisms are activated to prevent polyspermy (entry of multiple sperm).

The cortical reaction is the main mechanism in humans:

• Fertilization triggers Ca²⁺ release inside the oocyte.
• Cortical granules beneath the oocyte membrane release enzymes into the zona pellucida.
• These enzymes modify the zona pellucida (zona reaction) and inactivate sperm-binding receptors (ZP3).
• This prevents additional sperm from binding or penetrating the oocyte.

Other options:

A. Acrosomal reaction: occurs in the sperm before fertilization to penetrate the zona pellucida.

B. and D. Membrane potential changes: important in some species but not the primary block in humans.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Where does esophageal venous drainage go?
options: Azygous, Inferior thyroid and left gastric vein
Azygous, Inferior thyroid and right gastric vein
Superior thyroid, inferior thyroid, azygous and hemiazygous
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Azygous, Inferior thyroid and left gastric vein

The esophagus has segmental venous drainage corresponding to its cervical, thoracic, and abdominal parts. These veins ultimately drain into both the systemic venous system and the portal venous system, forming an important portosystemic (porto-caval) anastomosis.

1. Cervical part

• Drains into the inferior thyroid veins → brachiocephalic veins.

2. Thoracic part

• Drains mainly into the azygos vein and hemiazygos vein → superior vena cava.

3. Abdominal part

• Drains into the left gastric vein → portal vein.

At the lower end of the esophagus, there is a portosystemic anastomosis between:

• Left gastric vein (portal circulation)
• Azygos system (systemic circulation)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which among the following is incorrect regarding Sibsons's fascia?
options: Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Attached to the inner border of 2nd rib

Sibson’s fascia (suprapleural membrane) is a thickened extension of the endothoracic fascia that forms a protective fibrous layer over the apex of the lung at the thoracic inlet.

• Medial: Transverse process of C7 vertebra
• Lateral: Inner border of the 1st rib and its costal cartilage

Therefore, the statement “attached to the inner border of the 2nd rib” is incorrect.

Relations and functions:

• Covers the cervical pleura and the apex of the lung
• Reinforced by fibers from the scalenus minimus muscle (when present)
• Provides support and protection to the lung apex during respiration

Major vessels such as the subclavian artery and vein pass above the suprapleural membrane.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which among the following is wrong about the venous drainage of the heart?
options: Coronary sinus is guarded by the thebesian valve
Middle cardiac vein lies in the posterior atrioventricular groove
Great cardiac vein accompanies left anterior descending artery
Anterior cardiac vein opens into RA directly
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Middle cardiac vein lies in the posterior atrioventricular groove

The middle cardiac vein (posterior interventricular vein) runs in the posterior interventricular groove, accompanying the posterior interventricular artery (PDA), and drains into the coronary sinus.

Key points of cardiac venous drainage:

• Coronary sinus drains most cardiac veins into the right atrium and is guarded by the Thebesian valve.
• Great cardiac vein runs in the anterior interventricular groove with the left anterior descending (LAD) artery.
• Anterior cardiac veins drain the right ventricle directly into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus.

The middle cardiac vein does NOT lie in the posterior atrioventricular groove; it lies in the posterior interventricular groove.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which among the following statements is true regarding the course of the mandibular nerve? 1. Auriculotemporal nerve is a branch from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve, and it emerges from behind the temporomandibular joint. 2. Buccal branch is a branch from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve, and it emerges from behind the mandibular ramus. 3. Lingual nerve is a branch from the posterior division of the mandibular nerve, and it arcs around the submandibular duct. 4. Ophthalmic nerve is a branch from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve, and it arises in the middle cranial fossa.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2, 3

The mandibular nerve (V3) is the third division of the trigeminal nerve and is the only division with both sensory and motor fibers. After passing through the foramen ovale, it divides into anterior and posterior divisions in the infratemporal fossa.

Anterior division (mainly motor) branches include:

• Masseteric nerve
• Deep temporal nerves
• Nerve to lateral pterygoid
• Buccal nerve (long buccal) – sensory branch that passes behind the mandibular ramus to supply the cheek mucosa and skin.

Posterior division (mainly sensory) branches include:

• Auriculotemporal nerve
• Lingual nerve
• Inferior alveolar nerve

Important anatomical points:

• Lingual nerve loops around the submandibular duct in the floor of the mouth.
• Auriculotemporal nerve arises from the posterior division, not the anterior division.
• Ophthalmic nerve (V1) is a separate division of the trigeminal nerve, not a branch of V3.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which is not a branch of the vessel known as the Anesthetist’s artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mental

The “Anesthetist’s artery” refers to the facial artery because it is commonly encountered and sometimes compressed during regional anesthesia and facial procedures.

Branches of the facial artery (in the face):

• Inferior labial artery → supplies the lower lip
• Superior labial artery → supplies the upper lip and nasal septum
• Lateral nasal artery → supplies the side of the nose
• Angular artery → terminal branch at the medial angle of the eye

Mental artery is not a branch of the facial artery. It arises from the inferior alveolar artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, and emerges through the mental foramen to supply the chin and lower lip.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which muscle is physically in the back but functionally in the thorax?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Levator costae

The levator costarum muscles are anatomically located in the back (posterior thoracic region) but are functionally part of the thoracic wall because they assist in respiration by elevating the ribs.

• Origin: Transverse processes of C7–T11 vertebrae
• Insertion: Rib below the corresponding vertebra (between tubercle and angle)
• Action: Elevate ribs → assist inspiration
• Innervation: Posterior rami of thoracic spinal nerves

Although these muscles lie in the posterior back region, their action on ribs during breathing places them functionally with thoracic muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following areas is not a part of anterior neck?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subclavian triangle

The anterior triangle of the neck is bounded by:

• Anterior border of sternocleidomastoid
• Midline of the neck
• Inferior border of mandible

It is subdivided into four smaller triangles:

1.     Submental triangle

2.     Digastric (submandibular) triangle

3.     Carotid triangle

4.     Muscular triangle

The subclavian triangle (also called the omoclavicular or supraclavicular triangle) is not part of the anterior triangle. It belongs to the posterior triangle of the neck.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following brainstem nuclei is not derived from the alar plate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypoglossal

During embryonic development of the neural tube, the sulcus limitans divides it into:

• Alar plate (dorsal) → gives rise to sensory nuclei
• Basal plate (ventral) → gives rise to motor nuclei

Brainstem nuclei derived from the alar plate (sensory):

• Inferior olivary nucleus
• Dentate nucleus
• Many other sensory relay nuclei

Hypoglossal nucleus:

• A motor nucleus of cranial nerve XII
• Derived from the basal plate, not the alar plate

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following branches of internal Carotid artery are given off in the cervical region?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. None of the above

The internal carotid artery (ICA) has no branches in the cervical region.

Course of the ICA:

1.     Cervical part → from common carotid bifurcation to carotid canal

o    No branches

2.     Petrous part → gives caroticotympanic branches

3.     Cavernous part → gives cavernous branches

4.     Cerebral part → gives major intracranial branches such as:

o    Ophthalmic artery

o    Posterior communicating artery

o    Anterior choroidal artery

o    Anterior cerebral artery

o    Middle cerebral artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following combinations forms the principal arterial anastomosis around the scapula?
options: Posterior circumflex humeral, anterior circumflex humeral, profunda brachii
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Suprascapular, dorsal scapular, circumflex scapular

The scapular anastomosis is an important arterial network that provides collateral circulation between the subclavian artery and axillary artery, especially when the axillary artery is occluded proximal to the subscapular artery.

Principal arteries involved:

• Suprascapular artery (branch of the thyrocervical trunk from the subclavian artery)
• Dorsal scapular artery (from the subclavian artery)
• Circumflex scapular artery (branch of the subscapular artery from the axillary artery)

Location of anastomosis: Around the scapula, especially near the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae and medial border of the scapula.

Maintains blood flow to the upper limb if the axillary artery is ligated or obstructed proximal to the subscapular artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the role of Sertoli cells during spermatogenesis?
options: They induce spermatogonial stem cells to initiate spermatogenesis.
They stimulate Leydig cells to produce testosterone.
They secrete androgen-binding proteins and support germ cells.
They transform type A spermatogonia into spermatids.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. They secrete androgen-binding proteins and support germ cells.

Sertoli cells are supporting cells of the seminiferous tubules that play a crucial role in spermatogenesis. Key functions:

• Provide structural and nutritional support to developing germ cells.
• Secrete androgen-binding protein (ABP), which maintains high testosterone concentration in seminiferous tubules necessary for sperm development.
• Form the blood–testis barrier through tight junctions.
• Secrete inhibin, which regulates FSH secretion.
• Phagocytose residual cytoplasm during spermiogenesis.

Hormonal control:

• FSH stimulates Sertoli cells, while Leydig cells (stimulated by LH) produce testosterone.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following descending tracts in the spinal cord remains uncrossed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vestibulospinal tract

Major Descending Tracts and Their Crossing

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a Y-shaped ligament that connects the calcaneum to the cuboid and navicular bone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chopart

The Y-shaped ligament connecting the calcaneus to the navicular and cuboid bones is the bifurcate ligament, commonly associated with the Chopart joint.

The bifurcate ligament arises from the anterior process of the calcaneus and divides into two limbs forming a Y-shape:

1. Calcaneonavicular ligament → attaches to the navicular bone
2.

Calcaneocuboid ligament → attaches to the cuboid bone

3.

Stabilizes the midtarsal (transverse tarsal) joint, also called the Chopart joint.

4. Helps maintain integrity of the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• A. Lisfranc ligament → connects medial cuneiform to base of 2nd metatarsal (tarsometatarsal joint).
• B. Spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) → supports head of talus and medial longitudinal arch.
• D. Deltoid ligament → strong medial ligament of the ankle joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of pressure epiphysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Head of femur

Epiphyses are classified based on their function and role in bone development. One important type is the pressure epiphysis, which is involved in weight transmission and articulation at joints.

Pressure Epiphysis:

• Located at articular ends of long bones.
• Transmits body weight and mechanical pressure across joints.
• Usually covered by articular cartilage.
• Develops secondary ossification centers.

Example: Head of femur – articulates with the acetabulum and transmits body weight at the hip joint.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Tubercles of humerus → Traction epiphysis (site of muscle attachment).
• Coracoid process of scapula → Atavistic epiphysis (represents a bone that was separate in lower animals).
• Trochanters of femur → Traction epiphysis (muscle attachment sites).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not a content in the 4th compartment of extensor retinaculum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Extensor pollicis brevis

The extensor retinaculum at the wrist forms six osteofibrous compartments that transmit the extensor tendons.

Fourth compartment contents:

• Extensor digitorum tendons
• Extensor indicis tendon
• Posterior interosseous nerve (terminal branch of radial nerve)

Extensor pollicis brevis is not present in the 4th compartment. It lies in the 1st extensor compartment along with abductor pollicis longus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not accurate regarding pericardial sinuses?
options: Transverse sinus is between arterial and venous pericardial reflection.
Oblique sinus lies behind left atrium
Transverse sinus lies behind ascending aorta
Oblique sinus allows a surgeon to ligate the pulmonary vessels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oblique sinus allows a surgeon to ligate the pulmonary vessels

The pericardial sinuses are spaces formed by reflections of the serous pericardium around the great vessels of the heart.

1. Transverse pericardial sinus

• Lies between arterial and venous ends of the heart.
• Anterior: Ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk
• Posterior: Superior vena cava
• Clinical importance: A surgeon can pass a finger or clamp through this sinus to control or ligate the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk during cardiac surgery (e.g., cardiopulmonary bypass).

2. Oblique pericardial sinus

• A blind recess behind the left atrium.
• Formed by reflections around the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava.
• No surgical use for ligating vessels because it is a cul-de-sac.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about the cavernous sinus thrombosis?
options: Loss of sensation around the orbit
Infection spreads to cavernous sinus from the danger area of face via inferior ophthalmic vein
Superior ophthalmic vein serves as a both incoming as well as outgoing channel to cavernous sinus because it is valveless
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Loss of jaw jerk

Cavernous sinus thrombosis typically affects the cranial nerves that run within the cavernous sinus, leading to characteristic neurological deficits. Structures commonly involved include:

• CN III (Oculomotor)
• CN IV (Trochlear)
• CN V1 (Ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve)
• CN V2 (Maxillary division of trigeminal nerve)
• CN VI (Abducens nerve)
• Internal carotid artery

Clinical Features:

• Loss of sensation around the orbit → due to involvement of CN V1 (ophthalmic division).
• Infection from the “danger area” of the face can spread to the cavernous sinus via facial vein → angular vein → superior/inferior ophthalmic veins, because these veins are valveless.
• Superior ophthalmic vein acts as both inflow and outflow channel because it lacks valves.

Jaw jerk reflex is mediated by the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3) via the mesencephalic nucleus. CN V3 does NOT pass through the cavernous sinus, so jaw jerk is not affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about the location of otic ganglia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial- Mandibular nerve

The otic ganglion is a small parasympathetic ganglion in the infratemporal fossa, located just below the foramen ovale and medial to the mandibular nerve (V3).

Relations of the otic ganglion:

• Superior (roof): Foramen ovale
• Lateral: Mandibular nerve (V3)
• Medial: Tensor veli palatini muscle
• Posterior: Middle meningeal artery

Parasympathetic pathway:

• Preganglionic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (via the lesser petrosal nerve) synapse in the otic ganglion.
• Postganglionic fibers travel through the auriculotemporal nerve to supply the parotid gland.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is part of the complete syndrome triad associated with Anterior Choroidal Artery Syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Contralateral hemisensory loss

Anterior choroidal artery syndrome classically presents with a triad due to infarction of structures supplied by the anterior choroidal artery, a branch of the internal carotid artery.

Classic triad:

1. Contralateral hemiplegia → due to involvement of the posterior limb of internal capsule (corticospinal tract).
2. Contralateral hemisensory loss → due to involvement of thalamocortical sensory fibers.
3. Contralateral homonymous hemianopia → due to damage to the optic tract or lateral geniculate body.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Bilateral hemiplegia: Not typical; the deficit is contralateral and unilateral.

C. Bitemporal hemianopia: Occurs with optic chiasm lesions (e.g., pituitary tumors).

D. Ipsilateral homonymous hemianopia: Visual field loss is contralateral to the lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is/are incorrectly matched? 1. Sternoclavicular joint – Plane synovial joint 2. Wrist and knuckle joints – Hinge variety of synovial joints 3. Middle tibiofibular joint – Syndesmosis 4. Calcaneocuboid joint – Saddle synovial joint 5. Elbow and ankle joint – Ellipsoid synovial joint
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 5

Evaluation of the pairs:

1. Sternoclavicular joint – Plane synovial joint

• Incorrect. The sternoclavicular joint is a saddle-type synovial joint (with an articular disc), allowing movements like elevation, depression, protraction, and rotation of the clavicle.

2. Wrist and knuckle joints – Hinge synovial joints

• Incorrect.
• Wrist joint (radiocarpal) → Ellipsoid (condyloid) joint.
• Knuckle joints (metacarpophalangeal joints) → Condyloid joints, allowing flexion, extension, abduction, and adduction.

3. Middle tibiofibular joint – Syndesmosis

• Correct.
• The interosseous membrane between tibia and fibula forms a fibrous syndesmosis joint.

4. Calcaneocuboid joint – Saddle synovial joint

• Correct.
• This joint is part of the transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint and has saddle-like articular surfaces.

5. Elbow and ankle joint – Ellipsoid synovial joint

• Incorrect.
• Both the elbow and ankle (talocrural) joints are hinge synovial joints, permitting mainly flexion and extension.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscle causes opening of laryngeal inlet?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroepiglotticus

The laryngeal inlet (aditus of the larynx) is the opening that connects the pharynx to the larynx. Its size is regulated by specific intrinsic laryngeal muscles that either widen or narrow the inlet during breathing and swallowing.

Muscle Responsible for Opening the Laryngeal Inlet: Thyroepiglotticus muscle

• It is an extension of the thyroarytenoid muscle.
• Action: Pulls the epiglottis anteriorly and upward, thereby widening (opening) the laryngeal inlet.
• Helps facilitate air passage during respiration.

Other Muscles:

• Vocalis → Fine adjustment of vocal cord tension for phonation.
• Cricoarytenoid muscles → Mainly control abduction or adduction of vocal cords, not the laryngeal inlet directly.
• Thyroarytenoid → Relaxes vocal cords and narrows the laryngeal vestibule.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles is unipennate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2nd palmar interossei

Palmar interossei are unipennate muscles, meaning their fibers attach obliquely to one side of a tendon.

In contrast:

• Dorsal interossei are bipennate → fibers attach on both sides of a central tendon
• Medial two lumbricals (3rd & 4th) are also bipennate
• Lateral two lumbricals (1st & 2nd) are unipennate

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following sinuses is not located between the meningeal and endosteal layers of the dura mater?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Straight sinus

Most dural venous sinuses are located between the periosteal (endosteal) and meningeal layers of the dura mater and drain venous blood from the brain. Examples include:

• Superior sagittal sinus
• Transverse sinus
• Sigmoid sinus

However, the straight sinus is formed at the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli, where two folds of the meningeal layer meet, rather than between the meningeal and endosteal layers.

Formation of the straight sinus:

• Union of inferior sagittal sinus + great cerebral vein (vein of Galen).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements about cardiac jelly is incorrect?
options: Provide structural support during early heart development
Facilitates end-systolic occlusion, improving pumping efficiency
Store elastic energy during systole for the refilling phase of the heart.
Cellular matrix secreted by the endocardium in the developing heart.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cellular matrix secreted by the endocardium in the developing heart.

Cardiac jelly is a gelatinous extracellular matrix located between the endocardium and myocardium during early heart development. Functions:

• Provides structural support to the developing heart tube.
• Helps in endocardial cushion formation, which later contributes to heart valves and septa.
• Aids early pumping efficiency by allowing end-systolic occlusion of the heart lumen.

Origin:

• Cardiac jelly is secreted primarily by myocardial cells, not by the endocardium.

Therefore, the statement “Cellular matrix secreted by the endocardium in the developing heart” is incorrect.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements about the scalenus anterior muscle is incorrect?
options: The phrenic nerve lies anteriorly to the muscle.
The thoracic duct arches laterally on the right side.
The brachial plexus is posterior to the muscle.
The lateral part of the carotid sheath contains the internal jugular vein.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The thoracic duct arches laterally on the right side.

The scalenus anterior muscle is an important landmark in the root of the neck, arising from the transverse processes of C3–C6 and inserting on the first rib.

• Phrenic nerve runs anterior to scalenus anterior on its surface.
• Brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass posterior to scalenus anterior (between anterior and middle scalene muscles).
• Subclavian vein lies anterior to scalenus anterior.
• In the carotid sheath, the internal jugular vein lies laterally, common carotid artery medially, and vagus nerve posteriorly.

Thoracic duct relation:

• The thoracic duct arches laterally and empties into the venous angle on the LEFT side, not the right.

Therefore, the incorrect statement is that the thoracic duct arches laterally on the right side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements about the structures within the parotid gland are accurate? 1. The external carotid artery enters the parotid gland through the posteromedial surface. 2. The maxillary artery exits through the posterior surface of the gland. 3. The superficial temporal artery branches into the transverse facial artery and emerges from the anterior part of the superior surface. 4. The superficial temporal vein and maxillary vein unite to form the retromandibular vein, which divides into anterior and posterior divisions near the apex of the gland. 5. The facial nerve enters the parotid gland and passes behind the retromandibular vein.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Only 1, 3 and 4

The parotid gland contains several important structures arranged from superficial to deep: Order of structures (lateral → medial):

1.     Facial nerve (CN VII)

2.     Retromandibular vein

3.     External carotid artery

Key anatomical facts:

• The external carotid artery enters the gland through its posteromedial surface and divides into maxillary and superficial temporal arteries within the gland.
• The superficial temporal artery gives off the transverse facial artery and emerges from the upper anterior part of the gland.
• The superficial temporal vein and maxillary vein unite to form the retromandibular vein, which divides into anterior and posterior divisions near the apex of the gland.

Incorrect statement: The facial nerve lies superficial to the retromandibular vein, not behind it.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements with respect to histology of alveoli is incorrect?
options: The most abundant cell type lines form 70-90% of the alveolar surface and are of simple squamous type.
Type II alveolar epithelial cells are microvilli-containing cells which secrete surfactant similar to that of Clara cells.
In some alveolar area, basement membrane of the endothelium fuses with that of the alveolar epithelium.
Type I alveolar epithelial cells are involved in replacing the damaged type II alveolar cells.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Type I alveolar epithelial cells are involved in replacing the damaged type II alveolar cells.

The alveoli are the primary sites of gas exchange in the lungs and are lined by two types of pneumocytes. Cell types in alveoli:

• Type I pneumocytes:

o    Simple squamous cells

o    Cover 70–90% of the alveolar surface

o    Responsible for gas exchange

• Type II pneumocytes:

o    Cuboidal cells with microvilli

o    Secrete pulmonary surfactant (similar functionally to Clara/club cells)

o    Act as stem cells, capable of dividing and differentiating into Type I pneumocytes to repair alveolar lining.

Alveolar-capillary barrier:

• In many areas, the basement membrane of the alveolar epithelium fuses with that of the capillary endothelium, minimizing diffusion distance.

The incorrect statement is that Type I cells replace damaged Type II cells, because actually Type II cells regenerate both Type I and Type II pneumocytes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures is not derived from the septum transversum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ligamentum teres

The septum transversum is a mesodermal structure that contributes to the formation of several peritoneal ligaments of the liver and the central tendon of the diaphragm.

Structures derived from the septum transversum:

• Falciform ligament
• Coronary ligament
• Lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments)
• These ligaments help attach the liver to the anterior abdominal wall, diaphragm, and stomach/duodenum.

Exception:

• Ligamentum teres hepatis is not derived from the septum transversum.
• It is the fibrous remnant of the left umbilical vein from fetal circulation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which statement correctly describes the representation of body parts in the motor and sensory homunculi?
options: In the motor homunculus, finer motor control areas like arms and legs have larger cortical regions.
The sensory homunculus shows body parts with higher acuity, like fingertips, having smaller cortical areas.
Both homunculi are in the precentral gyrus and represent the same body parts.
The motor homunculus in the precentral gyrus has larger areas for fine motor parts like hands and face.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The motor homunculus in the precentral gyrus has larger areas for fine motor parts like hands and face.

The motor homunculus represents the somatotopic organization of the primary motor cortex located in the precentral gyrus.

• The size of cortical representation depends on the precision of control, not the physical size of the body part.
• Body parts requiring fine motor control (e.g., hands, fingers, face, tongue) occupy larger cortical areas.

Sensory homunculus:

• Located in the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex).
• Highly sensitive areas such as lips, tongue, and fingertips have larger cortical representation.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Arms and legs do not have the largest motor representation—hands and face do.
• High sensory acuity areas have larger, not smaller, cortical areas.
• Motor and sensory homunculi are in different gyri (precentral vs postcentral).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: You should not insert the needle below which level in midaxillary line so as not to damage the liver?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 10th rib

• In the midaxillary line, the inferior border of the lung reaches the 8th rib, while the inferior border of the pleura extends to the 10th rib.
• The liver lies just below the diaphragm on the right side, roughly at the level of the 10th rib in the midaxillary line.
• Therefore, inserting a needle below the 10th rib risks penetrating the diaphragm and injuring the liver.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents with intermittent mucoid discharge from a small opening along the lower third of the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle since childhood. This congenital anomaly most commonly results from the persistence of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Second pharyngeal cleft

A branchial (pharyngeal) cleft cyst or sinus is the most common congenital anomaly of the branchial apparatus and usually results from persistence of the second pharyngeal cleft. Patients typically present with a mucoid discharge from an external opening located along the lower third of the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle. A complete second branchial fistula extends from the skin to the tonsillar fossa, passing between the internal and external carotid arteries.

• This is the most common branchial cleft anomaly, accounting for approximately 95% of branchial cleft defects.

Why not the other options?

• A. First pharyngeal cleft: Rare; presents near the external auditory canal, parotid gland, or angle of the mandible, and may involve the facial nerve.
• C. Third pharyngeal cleft: Very rare; tract opens into the piriform sinus and may present with recurrent lower neck infections or suppurative thyroiditis.
• D. Fourth pharyngeal cleft: Extremely rare; usually presents with recurrent left-sided suppurative thyroiditis due to communication with the apex of the piriform sinus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 3-month-old infant is scheduled for cleft lip repair. During the surgical procedure, which of the following muscles is primarily corrected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Orbicularis oris

Cleft lip results from failure of fusion of the maxillary prominence with the medial nasal prominence, disrupting the orbicularis oris muscle.

Orbicularis oris forms the sphincter of the mouth and is essential for lip seal and feeding.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn presents with hypoplasia of the zygomatic bones, micrognathia, malformed external ears, and downward-slanting palpebral fissures. The condition results from abnormal development of which of the following pharyngeal arches?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. First and second pharyngeal arches

The clinical features described are characteristic of Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis), an autosomal dominant disorder caused most commonly by mutations in the TCOF1 gene, resulting in defective neural crest cell migration into the first and second pharyngeal arches. This leads to abnormal development of facial bones and external ears.

The patient has the classic features of Treacher Collins syndrome:

• Hypoplasia of the zygomatic bones
• Micrognathia (mandibular hypoplasia)
• Malformed external ears (microtia)
• Downward-slanting palpebral fissures

Why not the other options?

• A. First pharyngeal arch only: Although the mandible and zygoma are first arch derivatives, external ear abnormalities also involve the second arch.
• B. Second pharyngeal arch only: Does not explain the marked mandibular and zygomatic hypoplasia.
• D. Third and fourth pharyngeal arches: These primarily contribute to the hyoid bone, laryngeal cartilages, pharyngeal muscles, and cranial nerves IX and X, not the facial skeleton.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Covering of an omphalocele is derived from which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Amnion

In omphalocele, herniated abdominal contents are covered by a membrane composed of amnion externally and peritoneum internally.

This differentiates it from gastroschisis, where there is no covering membrane.

Endoderm and mesoderm form gut and body wall structures, not the external covering.

| Feature | Omphalocele | Gastroschisis

| ------- | ----------- | -------------

| Midline | Yes | Usually right-sided

| Covered by sac | Yes | No

| Sac layer | Amnion | None

| Associated anomalies | Common | Rare

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During surgery for a gastric ulcer, the prepyloric vein of Mayo is accidentally injured, resulting in bleeding. This vein is an important landmark for the pylorus and is closely related to the lesser omentum at the pyloric end. It drains into which of the following veins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right gastric vein

The prepyloric vein of Mayo is a constant venous landmark that runs vertically over the anterior surface of the pylorus, making it an important intraoperative guide to identify the pyloroduodenal junction during gastric and duodenal surgery. It usually drains into the right gastric vein, which subsequently drains into the portal vein.

Why is C correct?

• The prepyloric vein (vein of Mayo) lies on the anterior aspect of the pylorus.
• It is a reliable landmark used during procedures such as vagotomy, pyloroplasty, and gastrectomy.
• It empties into the right gastric vein.

Why not the other options?

• A. Portal vein: The prepyloric vein drains indirectly into the portal vein through the right gastric vein.
• B. Superior mesenteric vein: Does not directly receive the prepyloric vein.
• D. Splenic vein: Drains the spleen and part of the stomach but is not the drainage site of the prepyloric vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Epiblast first migration lead to formation of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endoderm

The correct answer is Endoderm.

During gastrulation, the first wave of epiblast cell migration displaces the hypoblast to form the definitive endoderm.

The second wave forms intraembryonic mesoderm, while cells remaining in epiblast become ectoderm.

The notochord is derived later from axial mesoderm, not the initial migration.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fecal discharge from the umbilicus is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ileal diverticulum

A patent vitellointestinal duct associated with Meckel’s (ileal) diverticulum can present with fecal discharge from the umbilicus.

Vitellointestinal (Omphalomesenteric) duct-Connects midgut to yolk sac, normally obliterates

Urachus-Connects bladder to umbilicus, becomes median umbilical ligament

Urachal fistula causes urine discharge, while gastroschisis and omphalocele are anterior abdominal wall defects without fecal umbilical discharge.

A) Gastroschisis

Abdominal wall defect

Bowel protrudes

No fecal discharge from umbilicus

B) Urachal fistula

Persistent urachus

Causes urine discharge, not feces

C) Omphalocele

Midline abdominal wall defect

Covered by membrane

No fecal discharge

D) Ileal diverticulum

Associated with persistent vitellointestinal duct

Can form umbilical fistula

Fecal discharge

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Following fertilization, on which day does implantation of the embryo into the uterine endometrium begin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Day 6

After fertilization, the zygote undergoes cleavage to form a blastocyst by day 4–5, which reaches the uterine cavity.

Implantation begins around day 6 with attachment of the blastocyst to the endometrium.

Earlier days correspond to cleavage stages, while day 15 is well beyond the implantation window.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In fetal circulation, blood from the umbilical vein bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus. Into which vessel does it continue?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. UV-IVC

The ductus venosus is a fetal vascular shunt that allows oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein to bypass the liver and enter the inferior vena cava (IVC). This ensures that highly oxygenated blood reaches the heart and brain with minimal loss of oxygen.

Normal pathway of oxygenated fetal blood: Placenta → Umbilical vein → Ductus venosus → Inferior vena cava → Right atrium → Foramen ovale → Left atrium → Left ventricle → Aorta → Brain and coronary circulation

Key fetal shunts:

• Ductus venosus: Umbilical vein → Inferior vena cava (bypasses the liver)
• Foramen ovale: Right atrium → Left atrium (bypasses the lungs)
• Ductus arteriosus: Pulmonary artery → Descending aorta (bypasses the lungs)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Mitochondria of spermatozoa form which of the following parts?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Middle piece

Mitochondria are helical in the middle piece, supplying ATP for motility. The head contains nucleus/acrosome; tail contains axoneme; connecting piece is transitional.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Primary follicles arrest in which phase of prophase 1?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diplotene

The correct answer is Diplotene.

Primary oocytes remain arrested in the diplotene (dictyate) stage of prophase I from fetal life until puberty.

This arrest is maintained by oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI) and meiosis resumes only at ovulation.

Leptotene, zygotene, and pachytene are earlier phases of prophase I that do not show physiological arrest.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The oocyte phase in post-ovulation is:
options: Primary oocyte arrested in prophase – I
Secondary oocyte completed in prophase – II
Primary oocyte arrested in prophase – II
Secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase – II
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase – II

After ovulation, the oocyte is a secondary oocyte that has completed meiosis I and entered meiosis II.

It remains arrested in metaphase II until fertilization occurs.

Primary oocyte arrest in prophase I occurs prenatally, not post-ovulation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The primary oocyte is arrested in which of the following stages?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prophase

Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I (diplotene stage) from fetal life until puberty. Secondary oocyte arrests later in metaphase II until fertilization.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the postnatal remnant of the distal umbilical artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial umbilical ligament

The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta. After birth, the distal portions of the umbilical arteries obliterate and form the medial umbilical ligaments, which are seen as fibrous cords on the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall.

In contrast, the proximal portions remain patent and persist as the superior vesical arteries, supplying the urinary bladder.

| Fetal Structure | Postnatal Remnant

| --------------- | -----------------

| Distal umbilical artery | Medial umbilical ligament

| Proximal umbilical artery | Superior vesical artery

| Umbilical vein | Ligamentum teres hepatis

| Ductus arteriosus | Ligamentum arteriosum

| Urachus | Median umbilical ligament

| Ductus venosus | Ligamentum venosum

Why Not the Other Options?

• Ligamentum teres → Remnant of the umbilical vein.
• Superior vesical artery → Remnant of the proximal, not distal, umbilical artery.
• Ligamentum arteriosum → Remnant of the ductus arteriosus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following are correctly matched? 1. First arch – Maxillary artery 2. Second arch – Hyoid or stapedial artery 3. Third arch – Common carotid artery and distal internal carotid artery 4. Sixth arch – Arch of the aorta 5. Fourth arch – Right proximal subclavian artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 5

First arch forms the maxillary artery, second arch gives hyoid and stapedial arteries, and the right fourth arch forms the proximal right subclavian artery.

The third arch forms the common carotid and proximal internal carotid artery (not distal), while the sixth arch forms pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus, not the aortic arch.

The third arch gives the common carotid and the proximal internal carotid — not the distal ICA.

• Third aortic arch artery → common carotid artery + proximal (first part of) internal carotid artery
• Distal internal carotid artery → derived from the dorsal aorta cranial to the third arch (the persisting cranial portion of the ipsilateral dorsal aorta)

Other sources worth pairing:

• External carotid → sprouts from the third arch / common carotid, not from the 1st arch proper.
• Distal right subclavian → right 7th intersegmental artery + right dorsal aorta.
• Left subclavian → left 7th intersegmental artery entirely (no arch contribution).

Why this asymmetry matters clinically

The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks the right subclavian (4th arch) because the right 5th and 6th arches regress distally. The left RLN hooks the ligamentum arteriosum (left 6th arch), which stays put — hence the left nerve's long thoracic descent and its vulnerability in aortic arch pathology.

Aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) = failure of the right 4th arch, with the right 7th intersegmental artery persisting off the descending aorta → dysphagia lusoria and a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve (critical in thyroid surgery).

| Arch | Derivative(s)

| ---- | -------------

| 1st | Maxillary artery (mostly regresses); part of external carotid

| 2nd | Stapedial + hyoid arteries (largely regress)

| 3rd | Common carotid + proximal internal carotid

| 4th | Left: arch of aorta (between left CCA and left subclavian) Right: proximal right subclavian artery

| 5th | Never forms / regresses completely (no derivative)

| 6th | Left: left pulmonary artery + ductus arteriosus Right: right pulmonary artery (distal part regresses — no ductus)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries passes through the splenorenal ligament?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Splenic artery

The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament is a double layer of peritoneum that extends between the left kidney and the spleen. It contains the splenic artery and splenic vein, along with the tail of the pancreas. This anatomical relationship is of major surgical importance during splenectomy, as inadvertent injury to the tail of the pancreas may result in pancreatic fistula or pancreatitis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Left gastric artery: Travels within the lesser omentum (hepatogastric ligament) along the lesser curvature of the stomach.
• C. Common hepatic artery: Runs in the superior border of the pancreas and gives rise to the proper hepatic artery, which enters the hepatoduodenal ligament, not the splenorenal ligament.
• D. Superior mesenteric artery: Arises from the abdominal aorta and passes behind the neck of the pancreas into the root of the mesentery; it is not contained within any peritoneal ligament.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a remnant of embryological hindgut in the pre-rectal area?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tailgut cyst

A tailgut cyst (retrorectal cystic hamartoma) is a congenital lesion arising from persistent remnants of the embryonic hindgut (postanal gut). It is typically located in the presacral (retrorectal/pre-rectal) space and may present with pelvic pain, recurrent infection, constipation, or a palpable mass. Although usually benign, malignant transformation can occur, making complete surgical excision the treatment of choice.

Why not the other options?

• A. Chordoma: Arises from remnants of the embryonic notochord, usually in the sacrococcygeal region or clivus.
• C. Epidermoid cyst: Results from ectodermal inclusion and contains squamous epithelium without skin appendages.
• D. Dermoid cyst: A germ cell lesion containing ectodermal derivatives such as hair follicles and sebaceous glands; not derived from the hindgut.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is NCC derivative for cardiac Structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Conotruncal Septum

The correct answer is Conotruncal septum.

Neural crest cells migrate into the cardiac outflow tract to form the aorticopulmonary (conotruncal) septum and AV cushion.

Ventricular wall , septum primum, and SA node are derived from endocardial mesenchyme or cardiogenic mesoderm, not neural crest.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding embryological derivatives?
options: Stapes – 2nd Pharyngeal Pouch; External auditory meatus (EAM) – 1st Pharyngeal Pouch
Stapes – 3rd Pharyngeal Pouch; EAM – 2nd Pharyngeal Pouch
Stapes – 2nd Pharyngeal Arch; EAM – 1st Pharyngeal Cleft
Stapes – 2nd Pharyngeal Cleft; EAM – 2nd Pharyngeal Cleft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stapes – 2nd Pharyngeal Arch; EAM – 1st Pharyngeal Cleft

• The stapes develops from the cartilage of the 2nd pharyngeal (hyoid) arch (Reichert cartilage).
• The external auditory meatus (external acoustic canal) develops from the 1st pharyngeal cleft (groove).
• The 1st pharyngeal pouch forms the middle ear cavity (tympanic cavity) and auditory (Eustachian) tube, not the EAM.
• The tympanic membrane is formed by the 1st cleft + 1st pouch + intervening mesoderm.
• The malleus and incus arise from the 1st pharyngeal arch (Meckel cartilage).
• The stapes is the only auditory ossicle derived predominantly from the 2nd arch.
• 2nd, 3rd, and 4th pharyngeal clefts are normally obliterated by the overgrowth of the 2nd arch.
• Persistence of these clefts can result in branchial cysts, sinuses, or fistulas.
• Pouches form internal structures, whereas clefts form external structures.

High-yield pearl:

• EAM = 1st cleft
• Middle ear & Eustachian tube = 1st pouch
• Stapes = 2nd arch

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of these is the most common site of a branchial cyst?
options: Junction of upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle
Junction of middle and lower third of the sternomastoid muscle
Between the two heads of the sternomastoid muscle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Junction of upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle

A branchial cyst is the most common congenital lateral neck cyst and arises from persistence of the second branchial cleft. It typically presents as a painless, fluctuant swelling along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle in older children or young adults.

The most common location is at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, making Option A the correct answer.

• Painless lateral neck swelling
• Located anterior to the SCM
• May enlarge following an upper respiratory tract infection
• Usually presents in late childhood or early adulthood

Why Not the Other Options?

• B. Junction of middle and lower third of SCM

• Less common site; not the classical location of a branchial cyst.

• C. Middle of the SCM

• Branchial cysts lie along the anterior border of the muscle rather than within its midpoint.

• D. Between the two heads of the SCM

• More characteristic of lesions related to deeper cervical structures, not the typical site of a branchial cyst.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding foetal physiology?
options: Haematopoiesis is demonstrated first in the yolk sac by 14th day
Breathing movements are identified at 26 weeks
Foetal pancreas secretes insulin as early as 20 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Haematopoiesis is demonstrated first in the yolk sac by 14th day

The yolk sac is the first site of hematopoiesis, beginning around the 3rd week (day 17–18) of embryonic life. Many examination texts simplify this as around the 14th day, making this the best answer.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Meconium appears at 16 weeks: Meconium begins to accumulate by approximately 12 weeks of gestation, not 16 weeks.
• C. Breathing movements are identified at 26 weeks: Fetal breathing movements begin much earlier, around 10–12 weeks, and can be detected by ultrasound by the late first to early second trimester.
• D. Foetal pancreas secretes insulin as early as 20 weeks: Fetal insulin secretion begins by 10–12 weeks of gestation, well before 20 weeks.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A child is starting to walk and gain upright posture. Which of the following spinal curvatures develops secondarily due to the development of this function?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lumbar

Lumbar curvature develops secondarily when the child starts walking and gaining upright posture.

During embryonic life, the body appears flexed and has 2 primary spinal curvatures.These are the thoracic and the pelvic curves, which are convex dorsally.

After birth, functional muscle development leads to the early appearance of secondary spinal curvatures. These are the cervical and the lumbar curves, both of which are convex forwards (lordosis).

* The secondary cervical curvature occurs with the development of function in the muscles responsible for the head extension.

* The secondary lumbar curvature occurs with the development of function in the muscles responsible for sitting upright and walking.

Normal adult curvatures of the vertebral column are as follows:

* The cervical curve is lordosis (convex forwards)

* The thoracic curve is kyphosis (convex dorsally)

* The lumbar curve is lordosis (convex forwards)

* The pelvic curve is concave anteroinferiorly

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient developed the following deformity, after overhead (weight-lifting) exercises. Which of the following muscle is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serratus anterior

The image shows winging of the scapula which is pulled upwards and towards the spine. This is due to paralysis of the serratus anterior which is supplied by the long thoracic nerve.

When the patient is asked to push against a wall with both hands, the medial border of the scapula on the affected side becomes prominent and this is known as ‘winging of the scapula.’

Scapular winging is almost always caused by damage to one of three nerves that control muscles in your arms, back, and neck:

* The long thoracic nerve, which controls the serratus anterior muscle

* The dorsal scapular nerve, which controls the rhomboid muscles

* The spinal accessory nerve, which controls the trapezius muscle

The muscles of the back and their innervation are:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Deep inguinal ring is a defect in
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fascia transversalis

Deep inguinal ring is a defect in fascia transversalis.

* This ring lies midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, approximately 1 cm proximal to the inguinal ligament.

* It lies lateral to inferior epigastric vessels.

Pearl PF1931: Inguinal canal

It is a 4 cm long intermuscular canal directed downwards, forwards, and medially.

It extends from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial ring.

Boundaries:

Boundary

Structures forming

Anterior wall

• Skin, superficial fascia, external oblique aponeurosis (whole extent)
• Muscle fibers of internal oblique (lateral 1/3rd)

Posterior wall

• Parietal peritoneum, extraperitoneal tissues, fascia transversalis (whole extent)
• Medially reinforced by the conjoint tendon and reflected part of the inguinal ligament

Roof

• Arched fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis forming the conjoint tendon medially

Floor

• Grooved surface of the inguinal ligament
• Lacunar ligament at the medial end

Deep inguinal ring is an oval opening in the fascia transversalis situated 1.25cm above the mid-inguinal point.

Superficial inguinal ring is a triangular opening in external oblique aponeurosis situated 1cm above and lateral to pubic crest (or medial to the pubic tubercle).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the following fracture.
options: Surgical neck humerus fracture with axillary nerve injury
Humerus shaft fracture with radial nerve palsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Humerus shaft fracture with radial nerve palsy

The image shows a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus in which the radial nerve is commonly damaged.

Holstein and Lewis associated a special type of fracture of the distal humerus, a simple displaced spiral fracture, with the distal end deviating toward the radial side occurring in about 7% of all humeral shaft fractures, with an increased rate of radial nerve palsy.

Injuries of ulnar and median nerves associated with humeral shaft fractures are not as frequent as injuries of the radial nerve.

It clinically manifests as an inability to dorsiflex the wrist and digits (wrist drop and finger drop).

Numbness occurs on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the radial 3 1/2 digits.

Most cases of humerus shaft fractures can be managed conservatively using a hanging cast or U-slab for 2-3 weeks followed by functional bracing. Surgery is indicated in cases of open fractures, pathological fractures, simultaneous unstable humeral and forearm fractures (floating elbow), and in radial nerve palsy.  Surgical fixation can be performed by compression plating, interlocking intramedullary nail, semi-flexible pins or an external fixator.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The artery that is palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon is ___?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The artery that is palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon is the posterior tibial artery.

The posterior tibial artery can be felt by keeping the foot relaxed between plantar and dorsiflexion and palpating against the distal tibia behind and below the medial malleolus, approximately one-third of a line connecting the posterior border of the medial malleolus to the calcaneal tendon (Achilles tendon).

Other options:

Dorsalis pedis artery:

* Can be palpated against the underlying tarsals.

* Lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus from the midpoint between the malleoli to the proximal end of the first intermetatarsal space.

Popliteal artery:

* Most difficult of the peripheral pulses to feel because the artery lies deep in the popliteal fossa.

* Examined with the subject lying supine or prone, with the knee flexed in order to relax the tense popliteal fascia that roofs the popliteal fossa.

* Felt over the midline of the fossa by deep pressure against the popliteal surface of the femur.

Arteries of the lower limb are:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The X-ray shows an antero-posterior view of a normal elbow. What is the structure marked in the image called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Capitulum

The structure marked is called capitulum.

The lower end of the humerus forms the condyle which is expanded to form the articular part which includes:

* Capitulum ("little head"): a rounded projection that articulates with the head of the radius.

* Trochlea ("pulley"): a pulley-shaped surface that articulates with the trochlear notch of the ulna. The medial edge of the trochlea projects down 6 mm more than the lateral edge which results in the formation of carrying angle.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Secondary cartilaginous joint

Pubic Symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arises from 6th pharyngeal arch?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ductus arteriosus

Ductus arteriosus arises from the 6th pharngeal arch.

Pharyngeal arches appear in the 4th or 5th week of development and contribute to the formation of the head and neck region. They are formed as a series of 6 thickenings in the cranial most part of the foregut (the future pharynx). They are craniocaudally numbered from I to VI. The 5th pharyngeal arch disappears, so only 5 arches remain.

* The first pharyngeal arch is also known as the mandibular arch.

* The second pharyngeal arch is also known as the hyoid arch.

* The 3rd, 4th, and 6th pharyngeal arches have no special names.

Other options:

Medial pterygoids,Lateral pterygoids,Tensor veli palatini- all arise from first pharyngeal arch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following develops from the dorsal mesogastrium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Spleen

The spleen develops from the mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium.

The mesenchymal cells in the dorsal mesogastrium form small lobular masses of splenic tissue called spleniculi. Later, these lobules fuse to form a single mass of spleen. The capsule, septa, and connective tissue framework, including reticular fibers, develop from mesoderm. The mesenchymal cells also differentiate into lymphoblasts and other blood-forming cells.

When the spleen develops, the dorsal mesogastrium gets divided into an anterior segment called gastrosplenic ligament that extends from the spleen to stomach, and a posterior part called the lienorenal ligament that extends from the spleen to the left kidney.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 34-year-old male patient presents to the OPD with complaints of pain in the medial part of the elbow for the past 4-6 weeks. He gives a history that the pain worsens while lifting weights in the gym. On examination, there is tenderness over the medial epicondyle, and reverse Cozen's test is positive. Which of the following nerve is most likely to be injured in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ulnar nerve

The clinical scenario and a positive reverse cozen test is suggestive of medial epicondylitis (Golfer's/ Swimmer's elbow). In this condition, the most common nerve injured is the ulnar nerve.

Medial epicondylitis (Golfer's elbow)

Clinical features:

* Less common than tennis elbow

* It is also called Swimmer's elbow

* Pain is felt over the medial epicondyle of the humerus where pronators have their origin

* Pain is elicited on resisted forearm pronation in extension

* Well localized tenderness is seen when compared to tennis elbow

* Associated with ulnar nerve neuropathy

* The origin of pronator teres is usually affected. The other muscle that can be affected is the flexor carpi radialis.

Tests:

* Reverse Cozen: The elbow is kept in slight flexion with the hand and wrist in supination. The examiner attempts to extend the elbow, while the patient is asked to resist this movement with active flexion. If pain is elicited at the medial epicondyle, it suggests the golfer’s elbow.

Treatment:

* Conservative treatment: Activity modification and pain killers is sufficient in most cases.

* Operative treatment:  Excision of the abnormal tendons at the flexor-pronator origin

Pearl PF1180: Medial and lateral epicondylitis

Tennis elbow or Lateral epicondylitis

* Pain is felt over or below the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.

* Pain is aggravated by lifting movements.

* It is common among tennis players and in those who perform repetitive wrist extension.

* Extensor carpi radialis brevis tendon is commonly involved.

Tests:

* Cozen's test: The patient is asked to pronate the forearm and make a tight fist.  Wrist extension against resistance causes pain at the lateral epicondyle.

* Mills sign: Pain at the lateral condyle when the elbow is extended in pronation with a flexed wrist.

* Wringing test: The patient is asked to wring a towel. Pain is felt at the lateral epicondyle in tennis elbow.

* Maudsley's test: Resisted extension of the middle finger produces pain at the lateral epicondyle.

Treatment:

* Conservative treatment: Activity modification and usage of a tennis elbow clasp are sufficient in most cases. Corticosteroid and local anaesthetic injections into the tender area may reduce the pain, but is not curative.

* Operative treatment: Detachment of the common extensor muscle from the lateral epicondyle.

Golfer's elbow or Medial epicondylitis

* Pain is felt over the medial epicondyle of the humerus where pronators have their origin

* Associated with ulnar nerve neuropathy

* Less common than tennis elbow

Tests:

* Reverse Cozen: The elbow is kept in slight flexion with the hand and wrist in supination. The examiner attempts to extend the elbow, while the patient is asked to resist this movement with active flexion. If pain is elicited at the medial epicondyle, it suggests golfer’s elbow.

Treatment:

* Conservative treatment: Activity modification and pain killers is sufficient in most cases.

* Operative treatment:  Excision of the abnormal tendons at the flexor-pronator origin

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A drowsy man was brought to the casualty with minimal response. He had a progressive history of weakness of the body for 2 days. A CT scan was taken which is shown below. Which vessel is likely to be thrombosed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Middle cerebral artery

The middle cerebral artery supplies the entire motor area except for the leg area. Thus, a lesion in the middle cerebral artery causes contralateral hemiparesis, sparing the leg area.

Anterior cerebral artery:

* It is the smaller terminal branch of the internal carotid artery.

* It runs in the sagittal fissure and anastomoses with the posterior cerebral artery.

* It supplies the medial surface of the cerebral cortex and parts of lentiform, caudate nuclei, and the internal capsule.

Middle cerebral artery:

* It is the larger terminal branch of the internal carotid artery.

* It runs in the lateral sulcus.

* It supplies the entire lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere except for a narrow strip (supplied by the anterior cerebral artery) and the occipital pole and the inferolateral surface (supplied by the posterior cerebral artery).

Posterior cerebral artery:

* It is the terminal branch of the basilar artery.

* It supplies the occipital lobe, inferolateral and medial surfaces of the temporal lobe, and parts of the brainstem.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A man who was on crutches now presents with tingling and paraesthesia on the medial side of the arm, forearm, and hand. Which structure is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

A person with the use of crutches, tingling and paraesthesia along the medial side of the arm, forearm, and hand is suggestive of brachial plexus injury(shown as A), specifically lower brachial plexus injury, and is called Klumpke’s palsy.

* Klumpke’s palsy is caused by lower brachial plexus injury.

* Most lower plexus injuries are from penetrating wounds, difficult births, falling on an outstretched arm, and trauma from crutches.

* There are usually motor and sensory deficits involving C8 and T1 with or without C7 dysfunction.

* In case of an avulsing injury, Horner’s syndrome may be associated with this condition.

* There is paralysis of the flexors of the wrist and fingers.

* The sensory deficit is along the medial aspect of the arm, forearm, and hand.

Pearl PF0469: Brachial Plexus

Brachial Plexus

* C5 to T1

* Roots (from spinal cord) > Trunks (in the neck)> Divisions (passing behind clavicle) > Cords and Branches (in the axilla).

* Covered by prevertebral fascia extension called "axillary sheath"

Trunks:

* Upper trunk: C5 and C6

* Middle trunk: C7.

* Lower trunk: C8 and T1

Divisions:

* Anterior divisions - Forms lateral and medial cords supplying mainly flexors

* Posterior divisions - Forms posterior cord which suppy mainly extensors

Cords:

* Lateral cord: Formed by anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks.

* Posterior cord: Formed by all 3 posterior divisions

* Medial cord: Formed by anterior division of the lower trunk.

Branches:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient has lost sensation over the dorsum of the foot and medial 4 toes. There is associated difficulty of eversion of the foot. Which nerve injury is likely to be the reason for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superficial peroneal nerve

Loss of sensation/paresthesia/numbness in the dorsum of the foot along with loss of eversion of the foot is due to injury to the superficial peroneal nerve.

The peroneus longus (principle evertor of the foot) in the lateral compartmentof the leg, is innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve. Damage to the superficial peroneal nerve would result in loss of eversion at the sub-talar joint.

The lateral compartment of the leg is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve. It consists of peroneus longus and peroneus brevis.

Other options:

* Foot drop occurs due to common peroneal nerve injury and sensory loss would involve the front and outer half of the leg and the whole dorsum of the foot. A high stepping gait is seen in this nerve injury.

* The posterior tibial nerve will involve loss of sensation over the sole of the foot. This is also the nerve involved in tarsal tunnel syndrome.

* The deep peroneal nerve innervates all muscles of the anterior compartment which are the dorsiflexors of the foot, extensor digitorum brevis, first two dorsal interossei muscles, and skin between great and second toes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the labelled tarsal bone in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Navicular

The image shows the navicular bone which is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

There are 7 tarsal bones and they occupy the proximal half of foot.

* The proximal row is made up of the talus and calcaneum.

* The distal row from medial to lateral contains, the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiforms and the cuboid.

* Medially the navicular bone is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked as 'C' in the below image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lentiform nucleus

The structure marked in the image as 'C' is Lentiform nucleus which is made up of Globus pallidus and Putamen.

Nomenclature of basal ganglia:

* Corpus striatum: Caudate nucleus + putamen+ globus pallidus

* Lentiform nucleus: Putamen + globus pallidus

* Neostriatum: Caudate nucleus + putamen

Other options:

A - Caudate nucleus

B - Insula (portion of cerebral cortex folded deep within the floor of lateral sulcus, associated with cardiac arrhythmias)

D - Third ventricle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the tendon marked in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flexor carpi radialis

The tendon marked in the image is of Flexor carpi radialis.

Flexor carpi radialis:

* Flexor carpi radialis arises from the medial epicondyle and its fusiform muscular belly converges in the mid-forearm into a long tendon.This tendon now passes within a synovial sheath through a lateral canal, formed by the flexor retinaculum above and a groove on the trapezium below.

* It inserts on the palmar surface of the base of the second metacarpal and sends a slip to the third metacarpal.

* Blood supply is by a branch that arises from either the anterior or the posterior ulnar recurrent artery. The distal minor pedicles supplying flexor carpi radialis are six to eight branches from the radial artery that enter the muscle on the anterolateral side.

* It is innervated by the median nerve, root value is C6, C7.

* It is a wrist flexor and acts with flexor carpi ulnaris for wrist flexion, and with the radial extensors of the wrist to abduct the hand.

* Testing is by palpating its contracting fibers during flexion of the wrist against resistance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The below image is of a femur bone.Which of the following muscles is attached to "A"?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iliopsoas

The image shows the posterior surface of the right femur and the structure marked "A" is the lesser trochanter where the iliopsoas muscle is attached.

The Iliopsoas comprises of Psoas major and Iliacus. They arise from the lumbar spine and the inner surface of the ilium bone respectively, and insert on the lesser trochanter. The iliopsoas cause flexion of the hip.

The femur can be divided into the proximal femur, shaft, and distal femur.

* The proximal femur consists of the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters. The intertrochanteric line is present on the anterior surface at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur while the intertrochanteric crest is present on the posterior surface. The lesser trochanter is the posteromedial projection of the femur arising posteroinferiorly from the neck-shaft junction.

* The shaft of the femur consists of linea aspera (bony crest present on the posterior surface), gluteal tuberosity, and pectineal line.

* The distal femur consists of the medial condyle, lateral condyle, intercondylar fossa, and patellar surface.

The image below shows attachments of various muscles over the posterior surface of the right femur.
