questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure marked in the image drains into:
options: Junction of superior vena cava and left brachiocephalic veins
Junction of left jugular and left subclavian veins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Junction of left jugular and left subclavian veins

The image shows the thoracic duct which drains into the junction of the left jugular and left subclavian veins.

Thoracic duct begins in the abdomen at T-12 vertebral level as the continuation of cisterna chyli.

* It is usually beaded due to its numerous valves.

* It drains the body below the diaphragm (lower limbs, pelvis, abdomen) and left half of the body above the diaphragm (thorax, upper limb, head and neck).

* Thoracic duct passes through the aortic hiatus in the diaphragm and ascends through the posterior mediastinum between the aorta and the azygous vein.

* At T-5 level, it deviates to the left side and ascends to pass the thoracic inlet.

Tributaries of the thoracic duct:

* Bilateral (right and left) descending thoracic lymph trunks which convey lymph from lower intercostal spaces (6 – 11).

* Left upper intercostal lymph trunks, which convey lymph from the upper intercostal spaces (1-5).

* Mediastinal lymph trunks

* Left subclavian lymph trunk

* Left jugular lymph trunk

* Left bronchomediastinal lymph trunk

The lymph passes through larger lymphatics and eventually collect into two large trunks, the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct, which in turn drain into the brachiocephalic veins.

* Thoracic duct- drains both lower limbs, left upper limb, abdomen, left halves of thorax, and left side of the head and neck regions (areas shaded green in the image).

* Right lymphatic duct- drains right upper limb, and right halves of thorax, and right side of the head and neck regions (areas shaded blue in the image).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the most probable nerve to be injured based on the clinical image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Long thoracic nerve

The above image shows winging of the scapula, which is caused by injury to the long thoracic nerve.

When the patient is asked to push against a wall with both hands, medial border of the scapula on the affected side becomes prominent and this is known as ‘winging of scapula.’

Scapular winging is almost always caused by damage to one of three nerves that control muscles in your arms, back, and neck:

* The long thoracic nerve, which controls the serratus anterior muscle

* The dorsal scapular nerve, which controls the rhomboid muscles

* The spinal accessory nerve, which controls the trapezius muscle

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn presented to the NICU with respiratory distress and meconium discharge from the umbilicus. The condition occurs due to the patency of the which structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitellointestinal duct

The presence of meconium discharge at the umbilicus is suggestive of vitelline fistula, which occurs due to patent vitelline duct, which connects the primitive gut to the yolk sac.

The primitive gut is connected to the definitive yolk sac through a narrow stalk-like communication known as the vitellointestinal duct. It is also known as vitelline duct or yolk stalk or omphalomesenteric duct.

Due to the folding of the embryo in the cephalocaudal and lateral directions, the embryo gets enclosed all around by ectoderm, except in the region through which the vitellointestinal duct passes. In this region, there is a circular aperture, which is now called the umbilical opening. The vitellointestinal duct completely obliterates by the 7th week of development.

Vitelline duct abnormalities:

* Meckel's diverticulum: In about 2% of the individuals, a portion of the vitelline duct persists an outpouching of the ileum called, Meckel diverticulum. The diverticulum is usually asymptomatic unless it contains heterotopic pancreatic or gastric mucosa, which may lead to bleeding, ulceration, or perforation.

* Vitelline cyst: In some individuals, both the ends of the vitelline duct transform into fibrous cords. However, the middle portion of the duct forms a large cyst called, enterocystoma, or vitelline cyst. As the fibrous cords run across the peritoneal cavity, it may lead to intestinal obstruction, strangulation, or volvulus.

* Vitelline fistula: When the vitelline duct remains patent over its entire length, it forms a direct communication between the primitive gut and the umbilicus, a condition called an umbilical fistula or vitelline fistula. The newborn characteristically presents with meconium discharge from the umbilicus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: At what level does the spinal cord end in infants?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. L3

In infants, the spinal cord ends at the L3 level.

As the child grows, the spinal cord moves up with age. Thus in adults, the distal termination of the spinal cord is at the lower border of L1.

The nerve roots from the lower end of the spinal cord form the cauda equina which exit through the intervertebral foramina. These fibers float in the dural sac and tend to be pushed away when a needle is advanced as in spinal anesthesia.

Thus spinal anesthesia is administered in adults below the lower border of L1 and in children below the lower border of L3, to minimize the chances of injury to the spinal cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Given below is a histological section of the thyroid gland. Which of the following is secreted by the cell marked 'X' in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcitonin

The structure marked X is the C-cells or the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland and they secrete calcitonin.

The C-cells (clear cells or parafollicular cells) have a pale staining cytoplasm, they are present between the follicular cells and the basement membrane or between the follicles. They are usually found in the middle third of each lateral lobe of the thyroid and scattered in between the thyroid follicles. They are members of the APUD system of dispersed neuroendocrine cells. They secrete calcitonin which lowers blood calcium.

The thyroid gland is covered by a fibrous capsule with septae dividing it into lobules. These lobules contain follicles lined by follicular cells. The shape of the follicular cells depends on the activity of the gland. They're squamous in the inactive state, cuboidal to columnar in the active state. The cavity of the follicle contains colloid which appears pink in H and E staining.

questions.text: Identify the structure marked as 'C'.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Epiglottis

The structure marked as 'C', is the epiglottis.

The structures marked in the image are:

* Hyoid bone

* Thyroid cartilage

* Epiglottis

* Cricoid cartilage

The laryngeal skeleton is formed by a series of cartilages that are connected by ligaments and fibrous membranes:

* The thyroid, cricoid, and the greater part of the arytenoid cartilages consist of hyaline cartilage.

* The corniculate, cuneiform, tritiate, and epiglottic cartilages and the apices of the arytenoid cartilage consist of elastic cartilage.

* The hyoid bone is a 'U-shaped' bone suspended from the tips of the styloid processes by the stylohyoid ligaments.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the diagram showing the development of ovarian follicles.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antral follicle

The structure marked in the image is of a secondary follicle, also called an antral follicle.

Development of ovarian follicles:

At birth, the ovarian cortex contains numerous primordial follicles which contain primary oocytes surrounded by a single layer of flat follicular cells. Most of these follicles degenerate in the prepubertal life and are called atretic follicles. At puberty, around 20 primordial follicles get activated in each menstrual cycle. Out of these 20 primordial follicles, only one follicle is dominant which reaches maturity and releases the oocyte during ovulation.

The different stages of development of the primordial follicle are:

a) Primary follicle:

* Follicle cells change from flattened cells to cuboidal and the stromal cells surrounding the follicle differentiate into spindle-shaped cells called 'theca externa'.

* The oocyte increases in size and secretes a proteoglycan material around it which forms the layer called 'Zona Pellucida' which is seen between the plasma membrane of the oocyte and the granulosa cells.

b)Secondary follicle(Antral follicle):

* The primary follicles continue to increase in size and the granulosa cells multiply.

* Numerous cavities coalesce to form a single fluid space called antrum.

* The granulosa cells envelop the oocyte to form a structure called Cumulus oophorus.

c) Tertiary follicle (Graffian follicle):

* Numerous secondary follicles are formed but only one tertiary follicle develops while others regress and become atretic follicles.

* As the antrum draws the fhe follicle increase in size and expands to a diameter of 2 cm to become Graffian follicle.

* The oocyte and the surrounding granulosa cells called corona radiata break away from the follicular wall and float in the follicular fluid.

* The primary oocyte completes its first meiotic division to form the secondary oocyte and a polar body.

* The secondary oocyte is arrested in the metaphase of the second meiotic division until fertilization takes place.

* The follicle ruptures to release the oocyte which is captured by for the fimbriae.

d) Corpus Luteum:

* The remainder of the follicle after ovulation is called the Corpus luteum. It synthesizes a carotenoid pigment called lutein which gives it a yellowish colour.

* If the oocyte is not fertilized then corpus luteum degenerates 12-14 days after ovulation to become corpus albicans.

* If fertilization occurs then the hCG produced by the trophoblast maintains the corpus luteum. It releases progesterone, estrogen, and relaxin, and regresses at around 8 weeks when the placenta takes over.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the tarsal bone labelled in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Navicular

The image shows the navicular bone which is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

There are 7 tarsal bones and they occupy the proximal half of foot. The proximal row is made up of the talus and calcaneum. The distal row from medial to lateral contains, the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiforms and the cuboid. Medially the navicular bone is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match the auscultatory areas of the heart from image given below
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-Aortic, 2-Pulmonary, 3- Tricuspid, 4-Mitral

The image shows the auscultation areas of the heart and option B is correctly matched.

The auscultation areas correspond to the areas where the sounds and murmurs of the heart valves can be best heard.

* Aortic area- upper right sternal edge in the right 2nd intercostal space

* Tricuspid area- lower left sternal edge in the left 4th intercostal space

* Pulmonic area – upper left sternal edge in the left 2nd intercostal space

* Mitral area- located on the left 5th intercostal space, at the apex of the heart. It's in the midclavicular line.

An image showing the auscultation areas of the heart is shown below:

The routine auscultation of the heart is:

* Auscultate at the apex with the diaphragm.

* Turn the patient on to the left side and auscultate for any murmurs of MR(using diaphragm) or MS(using bell)

* Turn the patient to the supine position, recline at 45 degrees and auscultate at the tricuspid area for murmurs of TR, TS, VSD

* Auscultate at the pulmonic area (PS,PR, PDA)

* Auscultate at the aortic area (AS, HOCM)

* Sit the patient forward and auscultate again at the tricuspid area in held expiration(AR)

* Auscultate over the carotid arteries for any bruits or radiation of any murmurs.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: New A patient with leprosy presented with the deformity as shown below. Which nerve injury causes the given condition ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ulnar nerve

The given image shows extension at the metacarpophalangeal joint and flexion at interphalangeal joints of the ring and little finger, caused by ulnar nerve injury. It produces a claw hand (main en griffe). Leprosy can affect peripheral nerves and lead to their associated conditions.

In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.

The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals in the hand. The lumbricals have a combined action on metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint flexion and interphalangeal (IP) joint extension (glass holding posture). In ulnar nerve injury, since the medial lumbricals are not functional, the forearm muscles are unopposed. Hence, there is hyperextension at MCP joints and flexion at IP joints. This causes claw hand deformity. There is also numbness of the ulnar one and a half fingers.

Elbow fractures or dislocations lead to high lesions of the ulnar nerve. Here, the hand is not markedly deformed because the ulnar half of the flexor digitorum profundus is paralyzed and the fingers, therefore, appear less clawed. This is called the high ulnar paradox.

The following tests are done to test the integrity of the ulnar nerve:

* Egawa's test - In a positive test, due to the weakness of the dorsal interossei, side-to-side movements of the middle finger is weak.

* Book test or Froment's sign - The patient is asked to hold a book forcefully while the doctor tries to pull it. In a positive test, due to weakness of adductor pollicis muscle, adduction of thumb is lost. The patient tries to hold the book by using flexor pollicis longus muscle. This produces flexion at the inter-phalangeal joint while holding the book.

* Card test - In the case of weak palmar interossei, it is easy for the examiner to pull out the card when held between the fingers. This is due to the loss of adduction by palmar interossei muscles.

Other options

Option B - In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with 'wrist drop' in case of paralyzed wrist extensors, and 'finger drop' when extensor digitorum is paralyzed. When there is compression in the axilla, radial nerve palsy is called Saturday night palsy. There is paralysis of the triceps, and weakness of the wrist and hand. In high lesions, there is sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand over the anatomical stuff box.

Option C - In median nerve injury, paralysis of opponens pollicis muscle leads to 'ape thumb' deformity. In forearm or elbow injuries, there is paralysis of long flexors of the thumb, index, and middle fingers, radial wrist flexors, and forearm pronators. This leads to the characteristic 'pointing index finger'. There is sensory loss over three and a half digits on the radial side.

Option D -Posterior interosseous nerve injury, is seen in posterior interosseous syndrome. The wrist is in radial deviation and there is loss of metacarpophalangeal joint extension. However, wrist extension is preserved.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Revised The vertical plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts is known as __________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coronal plane

The coronal plane is a vertical that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts.

Four imaginary planes are used in anatomical descriptions:

* Median (mid-sagittal) plane: Vertical plane that divides the body into equal right and left halves

* Sagittal plane: Vertical plane that divides the body into unequal right and left parts; parallel to the median plane

* Coronal (frontal) plane: Vertical plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts; perpendicular to the median plane

* Transverse (horizontal) plane: Horizontal plane that divides the body into upper and lower parts; perpendicular to both the sagittal and coronal planes

Note: Axial (or trans-axial) plane is a term used in radiology for the horizontal plane.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fallopian tube is lined by ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ciliated columnar epithelium

The lining epithelium of the fallopian tube is a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium.

The ciliated epithelial cells are predominant in the distal part of the fallopian tube. There is an increase in the height and number of cilia in these cells during the estrogenic phase of the menstrual cycle.

Other cells in the fallopian tube epithelium include:

* Secretory or peg cells - maximally located in the proximal portion of the tube. These cells are active around the time of ovulation, and their secretions help in the capacitation of sperms.

* Intraepithelial lymphocytes - may present occasionally.

Pearl PF1615: Fallopian tube

Gross anatomy:

The fallopian tube is divided into the following parts:

* Intramural/Interstitial portion:

* Intrauterine

* The narrowest and shortest part

* Isthmus:

* The most common site for tubectomy

* Ampulla:

* The longest part

* The most common site for - fertilization and ectopic pregnancy

* Infundibulum:

* The widest part

Histology:

The ampulla, isthmus and infundibulum are extrauterine. They're covered by three layers:

* Mesosalpinx - It is the peritoneal layer. Also called serosa.

* Myosalpinx - It contains smooth muscle and has 2 layers:

* Inner circular

* Outer longitudinal

* Endosalpinx - It is the mucosal layer. It has the following features:

* Numerous branching folds, filling the entire lumen

* Basement membrane

* Ciliated, columnar epithelium

* Peg cells - non-ciliated epithelium. They help in the capacitation of sperms.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The image below shows the cross-section of the trachea. Identify the structure marked.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trachealis muscle

The structure marked in the image shows the trachealis muscle.

The trachea is a tube-like structure that allows air to pass between the larynx and the bronchi.

The trachealis muscle is a smooth muscle located at the posterior wall of the trachea. It connects the ends of the C-shaped tracheal cartilage rings and completes the posterior part of the tracheal wall.

The histological section of the trachea shows the following structures:

* Respiratory epithelium

* Basement membrane

* Submucosal glands (both serous and mucous parts)

* Perichondrium

* Tracheal cartilage

* Trachealis muscle (smooth muscle).

The histological image below is that of the trachea as identified by the presence of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lining, the serous and mucous glands, and hyaline cartilage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The neurovascular plane of the abdominal wall lies_______.
options: Between the internal oblique and external oblique
Between the internal oblique and rectus abdominis
Between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis

The neurovascular plane of the abdominal wall lies between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis in the anterior abdominal wall.

The plane contains:

* Lower 6 thoracic nerves (T7-12)

* Iliohypogastric nerves

* Posterior intercostal and subcostal vessels

* Anastomosis between superior and inferior epigastric arteries.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the embryological basis of the developmental defect shown in the image below?
options: Failure in closure of anterior neuropore of neural tube
Failure in closure of posterior neuropore of neural tube
Failure in closure of complete neural tube
Failure in closure of caudal neuropore of neural tube
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Failure in closure of anterior neuropore of neural tube

The image shows anencephaly.

Failure of the anterior end (cranial end) of the neural tube to close is known as exencephaly. As a result of this, the skull vault does not form. This leaves the malformed brain exposed. The exposed brain tissue degenerates, leaving a mass of necrotic tissue. This defect with the absence of a major portion of the brain, skull, and scalp is known as anencephaly. The brain stem remains intact.

In some cases, the closure defect of the neural tube extends caudally, and the spinal cord is affected. This condition is known as craniorachischisis, where there is anencephaly plus a large defect involving the spine.

Neurulation refers to the formation of the neural tube from the neural plate. The neural tube gives rise to the central nervous system.

Steps of neurulation

* The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken and form the neural plate.

* The neural plate lengthens and the lateral edges elevate to form the neural folds, and the mid-region gets depressed to form the neural groove.

* The neural folds approach each and fuse in the midline in a craniocaudal direction to form a tube-like structure called the neural tube.

* The anterior opening of the neural tube (cranial neuropore) closes by day 25 and the posterior opening (caudal neuropore) closes by day 28.

* The neural tube becomes the central nervous system.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery is being palpated in the image shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The posterior tibial artery is palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon, as shown in the image.

The posterior tibial artery can be felt by keeping the foot relaxed between plantar and dorsiflexion and palpating against the distal tibia behind and below the medial malleolus,approximately one-third of a line connecting the posterior border of the medial malleolus to the calcaneal tendon(Achilles tendon)

Other options:

Dorsalis pedis artery:

* palpated against the underlying tarsals

* lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus from the midpoint between the malleoli to the proximal end of the first intermetatarsal space.

Popliteal artery:

* most difficult of the peripheral pulses to feel because the artery lies deep in the popliteal fossa.

* examined with the subject lying supine or prone, with the knee flexed in order to relax the tense popliteal fascia that roofs the popliteal fossa.

* felt over the midline of the fossa by deep pressure against the popliteal surface of the femur.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 55-year-old man is diagnosed with left testicular carcinoma. Which of the following lymph nodes is the first to be involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Para-aortic lymph nodes

In a patient with testicular carcinoma, para-aortic lymph nodes are the first to be involved.

The lymphatic drainage of the testes is to the para-aortic lymph nodes near the origin of the gonadal vessels. The contralateral para-aortic lymph nodes are sometimes involved in tumor spread, but the inguinal lymph nodes are affected only if the scrotal skin is involved.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient is referred to a higher center with the diagnosis of fracture. On examination, the forearm pulses were not palpable. An upper arm X-ray was done which is given below. Which artery is most likely to be injured in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Brachial artery

In the above clinical scenario, the history and radiograph suggest a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus. The brachial artery is the most commonly injured artery in this condition.

The radial nerve is commonly damaged in this condition.It manifests as an inability to dorsiflex the wrist and digits (wrist drop and finger drop). Numbness occurs on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the radial 3 1/2 digits.

Management of humerus shaft fractures:

* Conservative management is by reduction of the fracture and using a hanging cast or U-slab for 2-3 weeks followed by functional bracing

* Surgical fixation by compression plating, interlocking intramedullary nail, semi-flexible pins, or an external fixator is indicated in:

* Open fractures

* Pathological fractures

* Unstable humeral and forearm fractures (floating elbow)

* Radial nerve palsy

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented to the OPD with an abnormal gait. On examination, when the patient was asked to stand on the left foot, a right-sided hip drop was observed. Which of the following muscles are paralyzed in this patient?
options: Right gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Right gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
Left gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus

The examination of the patient indicates a positive Trendelenburg's sign (Trendelenburg's gait), with sagging on the right side. It is seen in paralysis of the left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles which are supplied by the left superior gluteal nerve.

The superior gluteal nerve supplies the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus.

Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus:

* When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, on the opposite supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in the slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position.

* When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis sinks down on the unsupported (normal) side, when the patient tries to stand on the affected limb.

Inferior gluteal nerve supplies the gluteus maximus muscle.

The below GIF shows a positive Trendelenburg's sign (Trendelenburg's gait) with a left superior gluteal nerve injury.

In the GIF, when the person lifts up his right leg and tries to stand on the left leg, the right pelvis tilts down. This shows that the left side abduction mechanism is paralyzed and the right side is normal. The left superior gluteal nerve is injured in this case since it supplies the left gluteus medius and minimus.

Note: These patients can also have a characteristic lurching gait.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a cyst on the neck anterior to the sternocleidomastoid at the junction of the upper and middle third of the muscle. This cyst is due to the persistence of which of the following embryological clefts?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2nd cleft

A cyst presenting at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle at its anterior border is most likely a branchial cyst. It develops from the vestigial remnants of the second branchial cleft.

Branchial cyst is most commonly seen at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle at its anterior border. It is usually lined by squamous epithelium and contains thick, turbid fluid full of cholesterol crystals. It is fluctuant and may transilluminate to a lesser extent when it contains clear fluid.

A branchial fistula may be acquired or congenital. The congenital fistula is seen at the junction of the middle and lower third of the sternomastoid. An acquired fistula is usually seen in cases of incomplete surgery for the branchial cyst or spontaneous rupture, and it is seen at the same site as the cyst.

The below image shows a large right-sided branchial cyst.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the given histology slide:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pancreas

The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers, and containing numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. They are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum. The image given below shows the histology of the pancreas:

The islets of Langerhans contain four major and two minor cell types:

Four main types are β, α, δ, and PP (pancreatic polypeptide) cells:

* α or A cells- located peripherally and secrete glucagon

* β or B cells- located centrally and produce insulin

* δ or D cells- scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin

* PP cells- are present in islets and also in the exocrine pancreas. They secrete a pancreatic polypeptide, which exerts several gastrointestinal effects, such as stimulation of secretion of gastric and intestinal enzymes and inhibition of intestinal motility.

Minor cell types:

* D1 cells secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a hormone that induces glycogenolysis and hyperglycemia. It also stimulates gastrointestinal fluid secretion and causes secretory diarrhea.

* Enterochromaffin cells synthesize serotonin and are the source of pancreatic tumors that cause carcinoid syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs. The structure of lymph nodes consists of an outer cortex and inner medulla. The cortex contains an aggregation of B-lymphocytes (primary follicles) and quiescent secondary follicles with a pale central germinal center.

The inner medulla consists of medullary cords (lymphocytes and plasma cells) and medullary sinuses. Between the cortex and medulla, there is an ill-defined zone called the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes. The image given below shows the histology of the lymph node:

Option B: Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes. The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus:

Option C: Spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ. It contains round white pulp surrounded by red pulp. The white pulp is made up of aggregations of lymphocytes that surround a small artery or arterioles.

The red pulp is a modified lymphoid tissue infiltrated with all the cells of circulating blood. It is like a sponge permeated by spaces (splenic sinusoids) lined by reticular cells. The zone of red pulp immediately surrounding white pulp is the marginal zone. This zone has a rich network of sinusoids. The image given below shows the histology of the spleen:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the histological image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Transitional epithelium

The above image shows transitional epithelium.

The deepest layer has columnar cells, the middle layers are made up of polyhedral cells and the surface layer has cells that are large and shaped like an umbrella.

Transitional epithelium is found in the renal pelvis and calyces, the ureter, the urinary bladder, and part of the urethra. Because of this distribution, it is also called urothelium. In the urinary bladder, it is usually observed that transitional epithelium can be stretched considerably without being damaged. When stretched it appears to be thinner and the cells become flattened or rounded.

Pearl PF1699: Various Types of Epithelium, Their Location and Functions

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In the given barium swallow image, which of the following shows the left atrium impression on the esophagus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3

In the given barium swallow image, the arrow marking with the number 3 shows the left atrium impression on the esophagus.

The esophagus is a fibromuscular tube that connects the pharynx of the neck to the stomach, passing through the thorax through the superior and posterior mediastinum. It starts below the cricopharyngeus muscle, at the level of C6- the cricoid cartilage's bottom margin. The esophagus is located behind the trachea in the neck. It passes posterior to the left main bronchus, the left atrium, and the aortic arch as it descends through the mediastinum, each of which leaves an impression.

The vagus nerves accompany the esophagus as it travels through the diaphragmatic gap at T10 and finishes at the gastric cardia at T11. The left lobe of the liver is located anterior to the abdominal esophagus. Thus, the esophagus is composed of a short cervical, a long thoracic, and a short abdominal segment.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: On palpation at the site marked by the red arrow on the image a bony ridge is felt. What is the vertebral level of the marked arrow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. T4-T5 intervertebral disc

A body ridge felt when palpated a few centimeters from the suprasternal notch represents the angle of Louis/sternal angle. Recent data place the sternal angle between the T4 vertebra and the upper half of the T5 vertebra in the majority of adults.

The mediastinum is divided into superior and inferior by a line joining the sternal angle to the T4-T5 intervertebral disc.

The sternal plane is traditionally reported to pass through the intervertebral disc between the T4-T5 vertebrae posteriorly and the manubriosternal joint (sternal angle or angle of Louis) at the level of the second costal cartilage anteriorly. It can be used as an anatomical landmark for structures of the mediastinum.

Pearl PF0473: Angle of Louis

The angle of Loius (sternal angle) is formed by the manubriosternal joint at the level of 2nd costal cartilage anteriorly.

A plane joining the angle of Louis to the intervertebral disc between T4 and T5, called the sternal plane marks the following anatomical landmarks:

* Separates superior mediastinum form inferior mediastinum.

* Marks the position superior limit of pericardium.

* Bifurcation of pulmonary trunk

* Bifurcation of trachea (newer studies shows its lower)

* Origin of arch of aorta.

* Site where superior venacava pierces the pericardium.

questions.text: The following condition seen in the image results from failure of fusion of :
options: Lateral nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Lateral nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Medial nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence

Cleft lip is due to failure of fusion between the medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence.

Various defects of fusion of prominences in the face region are as follows:

* Cleft lip is due to the failure of the fusion of maxillary prominence with medial nasal prominence. It can be unilateral or bilateral. It can vary in severity from a small notch in the upper lip to a double cleft extending into both the nostrils. There is also associated underdevelopment of the part of the maxilla that bears the incisors.

* Median (midline) cleft lip is a rare defect occurring due to failure of fusion of the two medial nasal prominences in the midline.

* Oblique facial cleft is caused by the failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the lateral nasal prominence along the line of the nasolacrimal groove. The nasolacrimal duct is exposed to the surface in these cases.

Orthodontic management

*

Excision of maxillary arch, Rhinoplasty - 16+ years

questions.text: Which of the following structures passes through the foramen marked by the arrow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thoracic duct

The marked arrow indicates the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm. Out of the given options, the thoracic duct passes through it.

The diaphragm has several openings through which structures can pass between the thorax and abdomen. There are three large openings and several smaller openings. The large openings are the aortic hiatus, the esophageal hiatus, and the caval hiatus.

The aortic opening is the most posteroinferior large diaphragmatic opening. It is found at the level of the lower border of the twelfth thoracic vertebra and the corresponding intervertebral disc. It is bounded by the diaphragmatic crura laterally, vertebral column posteriorly, and the median arcuate ligament anteriorly.

Structures passing through the aortic opening are:

* Azygous vein

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient is brought to the ER due to a suspected stroke. The patient has difficulty forming words but can make noises and give expressions as if he understands the questions asked. Which type of aphasia is most likely present in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Broca’s aphasia

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Broca's aphasia.

In Broca's aphasia/ Motor aphasia / Non-fluent aphasia, areas 44 and 45 in the prefrontal and premotor facial regions of the cerebral cortex are affected. The affected individuals will have difficulty forming verbal or written words. The comprehension aspect of speech is preserved but the person cannot repeat or name the words and lacks fluency.

Other options:

Option A: Wernicke's aphasia is a type of fluent aphasia in which comprehension is impaired. The speech is easy and fluent but it is full of jargon and neologisms(non-existent words) that make little sense. Damage to the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus(area 22) or blockade of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery causes Wernicke's aphasia.

Option C: Global aphasia- In this, both understanding and speaking are impaired. It is also non-fluent aphasia.

Option D: Conduction aphasia is seen in lesions of the arcuate fasciculus, the bundle of nerve fibres connecting the Wernicke and Broca's areas. Repetition of words is impaired and paraphasias are observed, though not as much as in Wernicke aphasia.

questions.text: Identify the tendon marked in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flexor carpi radialis

The tendon marked in the image is of flexor carpi radialis.

Flexor carpi radialis:

* Flexor carpi radialis arises from the medial epicondyle and its fusiform muscular belly converges in the mid-forearm into a long tendon. This tendon now passes within a synovial sheath through a lateral canal, formed by the flexor retinaculum above and a groove on the trapezium below.

* It inserts on the palmar surface of the base of the second metacarpal and sends a slip to the third metacarpal.

* Blood supply is by a branch that arises from either the anterior or the posterior ulnar recurrent artery. The distal minor pedicles supplying flexor carpi radialis are six to eight branches from the radial artery that enter the muscle on the anterolateral side.

* It is innervated by the median nerve, root value is C6, C7.

* It is a wrist flexor and acts with flexor carpi ulnaris for wrist flexion, and with the radial extensors of the wrist to abduct the hand.

* Testing is by palpating its contracting fibers during flexion of the wrist against resistance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The below image is of a femur bone. Which of the following muscles is attached to "A"?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iliopsoas

The image shows the posterior surface of the right femur and the structure marked "A" is the lesser trochanter where the iliopsoas muscle is attached.

The Iliopsoas comprises of Psoas major and Iliacus. They arise from the lumbar spine and the inner surface of the ilium bone respectively, and insert on the lesser trochanter. The iliopsoas cause flexion of the hip.

The femur can be divided into the proximal femur, shaft, and distal femur.

* The proximal femur consists of the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters. The intertrochanteric line is present on the anterior surface at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur while the intertrochanteric crest is present on the posterior surface. The lesser trochanter is the posteromedial projection of the femur arising posteroinferiorly from the neck-shaft junction.

* The shaft of the femur consists of linea aspera (bony crest present on the posterior surface), gluteal tuberosity, and pectineal line.

* The distal femur consists of the medial condyle, lateral condyle, intercondylar fossa, and patellar surface.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The common carotid artery pulse is assessed at the level of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cricoid cartilage

The common carotid artery pulse is taken at the level of the cricoid cartilage.

The common carotid artery pulse is assessed at the level of the neck, typically just lateral to the trachea, where the artery can be palpated against the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Position the fingers between the larynx and the front edge of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at the level of the cricoid cartilage. When palpating the pulse, adjust the pressure on the artery until the strongest pulsation is felt.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the embryological origin of the labelled structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. First pharyngeal arch

The bony structure depicted in the image is the malleus, which can be identified from its hammer shape. It is derived embryologically from the first pharyngeal arch.

The ear ossicles - malleus, incus, and stapes, as shown in the image below, are the three bones of the middle ear which conduct sound energy from the tympanic membrane to the oval window and the inner ear fluid.

The malleus is the largest of the three and is hammer-shaped. The handle of the malleus is attached to the upper half of the tympanic membrane and the head is attached to the incus.

The incus is the middle bone, as described above. Incus is shaped like an anvil. It has a body, a short process, and a long process. It has a saddle-shaped articular facet on its anterior surface that articulates with the malleus. The long process descends vertically and ends as a rounded lenticular process. It is also derived embryologically from the first pharyngeal arch.

The stapes is the smallest and medial most ossicle, which is stirrup-shaped, with two distinct limbs and a footplate attached to the oval window. It has a head, neck, footplate, and anterior and posterior crura. The annular ligament holds the footplate of the stapes in the oval window. It develops mainly from the second pharyngeal arch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the vertebral level of the abdominal plane labelled 2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upper border of L3

The plane marked 2 in the given image is the subcostal plane. It is at the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

The subcostal plane is an anatomical reference plane used in clinical and surgical practice. It is defined as a horizontal plane passing through the lower border of the 10th costal cartilage bilaterally. The 10th costal cartilage corresponds approximately to the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

The costal cartilages are extensions of the ribs that articulate with the sternum anteriorly. The 10th costal cartilage is the cartilage of the 10th rib.

In the given image, structure 2 represents the subcostal plane, which corresponds to the level of the lower border of the 10th costal cartilage. Since the 10th costal cartilage is at the level of the upper border of L3, it indicates that the subcostal plane is also at the level of the upper border of L3.

Pearl PF0627: Abdominal planes and their landmarks

Planes that divide the abdomen into 9 regions

* Horizontal planes

* L3 - Subcostal plane (between 10th costal cartilages). Corresponds to the 3rd part of the duodenum

* L5 - Transtubercular plane (between tubercles of iliac crests). Corresponds to the origin of Inferior vena cava.

* Vertical planes (Paramedian or lateral planes)

* Mid-clavicular point to mid-inguinal point on both sides

The nine regions of the abdomen include:

* Left hypochondriac, Epigastric, Right hypochondriac

* Left lumbar, Umbilical (Central), Right lumbar

* Left iliac, Hypogastric (Suprapubic), Right iliac

Other planes and angles in the abdomen

* Transpyloric (Addison's) plane passes midway between the suprasternal notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

* The supracristal plane passing through the highest point of the iliac crest on both sides. Posteriorly, it corresponds to the level of the L4 body or L4/5 disc and its spinous process. It is an important landmark when performing a lumbar puncture or spinal injection. The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta lies approximately in this plane.

* The plane of the pubic crest passes through the upper border of the pubic symphysis. When supine, this plane intersects the tip of the coccyx and the femoral head.

* Renal angle is the angle between the 12th rib and the outer border of Erector spinae muscle. The lower border of normal kidneys may occasionally be felt here.

* Lumbar triangle (of Petit) is marked below by the iliac crest, anteriorly by external oblique and posteriorly by latissimus dorsi. Lumbar herniation can occur here.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 1-month-old baby is diagnosed with ventricular septal defect (VSD) and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). The VSD is caused by _________?
options: Improper fusion of both the membranous and muscular portions of the interventricular septum
Improper fusion of the membranous portion of the interventricular septum
Improper development of the muscular portion of the interventricular septum
Improper fusion of the endocardial cushions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Improper fusion of both the membranous and muscular portions of the interventricular septum

A ventricular septal defect (VSD) arises due to incomplete formation or fusion of the membranous and muscular portions of the interventricular septum during embryonic development.

The muscular septum develops from the ventricular floor and grows upward, while the membranous septum forms from the endocardial cushions and conotruncal ridges. Fusion of these components is critical for separating the right and left ventricles. Failure in the growth, alignment, or fusion of these structures can result in a defect, leading to an abnormal connection between the ventricles.

The embryological formation of the interventricular septum begins around the 4th week of gestation. The muscular septum grows upward toward the endocardial cushions, while the neural crest-derived conotruncal ridges spiral and fuse to form the aorticopulmonary septum. The membranous portion is formed by the fusion of the conotruncal septum with the endocardial cushions and the muscular septum.

Defects in the membranous portion are the most common cause of VSD, but malformations in the muscular septum or misalignment of the conotruncal ridges can also contribute. These defects result in abnormal blood flow between the ventricles, which can lead to complications such as heart failure or pulmonary hypertension if left untreated.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A child presents with the findings shown in the image below. Which structure is most likely involved in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cranial nerve 7

The given clinical findings are suggestive of Bell's palsy which is a paralysis of the facial nerve.

Facial nerve paralysis can be central or peripheral. Peripheral is more common and is usually idiopathic.

Bell's palsy is an acute onset idiopathic, peripheral facial paralysis. It is a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve and involves the ipsilateral side of the upper and lower halves of the face.

It presents an inability to close the eye, and if the patient attempts to close it, it turns up and out. This is known as the Bell's phenomenon. Other features include drooling of saliva and facial asymmetry. There may be noise intolerance and a loss of taste sensation.

Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion. Investigations should rule out all other possible causes of facial paralysis.

Treatment of Bell's palsy involves prednisone 60-80 mg daily during the first 5 days and then tapered over the next 5 days. Tape to depress the upper eyelid during sleep and artificial tears can be used to prevent corneal drying. Most patients recover within a few weeks or months.

Other options:

Option B: In oculomotor nerve (CN 3) palsy, there is ptosis, a dilated pupil, and the eye appears to be down and out due to the unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique action.

Option C: Orbicularis oculi palsy refers to weakness or paralysis of the muscle responsible for closing the eyelids. This condition can lead to incomplete eyelid closure, resulting in exposure keratitis and difficulty blinking.

Option D: Erb's palsy is a paralysis of the arm caused by injury to the upper brachial plexus (C5-C6 nerves), often during birth. It results in weakness or loss of movement in the shoulder and arm, commonly presenting as a "waiter's tip" deformity as shown in the image below.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A clinician touched the eyes of a patient with a piece of cotton, and rapid blinking of the eyes occurred in response. What is the structure responsible for carrying the above sensation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trigeminal nerve

The response of blinking when the clinician touches the patient's eye with a piece of cotton is known as the corneal reflex. The sensation is transmitted by the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V), while the motor response is controlled by the facial nerve (CN VII).

The corneal reflex is an involuntary, protective response that causes blinking when the cornea is stimulated, such as by a light touch. It serves as a defence mechanism to prevent foreign objects from entering the eye and causing damage. The reflex involves two main components: sensory input and motor output. The sensation of touch or irritation on the cornea is detected by the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V), specifically its nasociliary branch, which sends the signal to the brainstem.

The motor response, which is the blinking of the eyelids, is mediated by the facial nerve (Option B). The facial nerve innervates the orbicularis oculi muscle, which is responsible for closing the eyelids. This reflex is important for protecting the eye from potential damage, and any disruption to the trigeminal or facial nerves can impair the corneal reflex, leading to difficulty in protecting the eye from injury.

Other options:

Option B: The Facial Nerve (CN VII) is a major nerve responsible for controlling the muscles of facial expression including orbicularis oculi, which is responsible for forced closing of the eyelid. Although orbicularis oculi and facial nerve is a part of corneal reflex, its is not responsible for carrying the sensation and hence cannot be the answer.

Option C: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) plays a key role in several eye reflexes, particularly in the pupillary light reflex and the accommodation reflex. The pupillary light reflex mediates pupil constriction in response to light exposure by controlling the sphincter pupillae muscle. In the accommodation reflex, it coordinates the convergence of the eyes and the constriction of the pupils when focusing on a near object.

Option D: The optic nerve (CN II) plays a crucial role in sensory input for several reflexes. In the pupillary light reflex, it detects light entering the eye and sends the signal to the brain, triggering pupil constriction via the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Additionally, the optic nerve is involved in the accommodation reflex, where it helps detect the visual stimulus, prompting changes in eye focus and pupil constriction

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear with loss of sensation. Neck examination reveals a thickened structure, as shown in the image below. What is this structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Greater auricular nerve

In the given clinical scenario, the patient presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear accompanied by loss of sensation, and neck examination reveals a thickened structure suggestive of leprosy, and the thickened structure is the greater auricular nerve.

Great auricular nerve:

It is the largest ascending branch of the cervical plexus and arises from the second and third cervical spinal nerves. It winds over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and ascends upwards. On reaching the parotid gland it divides into the anterior and posterior branches:

* The anterior branch supplies the facial skin over the parotid gland and joins the facial nerve in the gland.

* The posterior branch supplies the skin over the mastoid process, the lower part of the back of the auricle, lobule and concha.

Clinical considerations:

* The nerve can be thickened in conditions like leprosy and can be palpated over the upper part of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (as seen in the above image). Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial, ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most frequently involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

* Cross-inervation between the somatic sensory supply (great auricular nerve) and the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland is considered an anatomical basis for the phenomenon of Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A primigravida woman gives birth to a baby with the following defect. Identify the anomaly.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Open neural tube defect

The above clinical scenario, along with the image showing anencephaly and a contiguous bony defect of the spine, is suggestive of craniorachischisis which is an open neural tube defect that occurs due to failure of complete closure of the neural tube.

Craniorachischisis is a severe neural tube defect characterized by the failure of neural tube closure, resulting in the exposure of both the brain (anencephaly) and spinal cord (rachischisis). This condition leads to a completely open brain and spinal column, making it incompatible with life. The exposed neural tissues often become necrotic. It occurs due to defects in primary neurulation during early embryonic development.

The image given below shows craniorachischisis.

Other options:

Spina bifida is a general term used for neural tube defects affecting the spinal region and associated with splitting of the vertebral arches. It is characterized by gaps in the vertebral arches and may or may not involve the underlying neural tissue.

The illustration shown below shows spina bifida.

The 3 main types of spina bifida:

* Spina bifida occulta (Option C) is the mildest form of spina bifida. The skin covers the defect in the vertebral arches. The splits in the vertebrae are so small that the spinal cord does not protrude. The skin at the site of the lesion may be normal, or it may have some hair growing from it.

* Meningocele - The defect in the vertebra allows the meninges to protrude through the defect.

* Meningomyelocele (Option A) - A defect in the vertebral column allows the spinal cord with the meningeal coverings to protrude.

The image given below shows the different types of spina bifida.

Option D: Encephalocele is caused due to defects in the skull through which the meninges and/or neural tissue herniate. The squamous part of the occipital bone is the most frequently affected bone.

The image shows a newborn with encephalocele.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: After a roller coaster ride, a person experiences a brief sense of imbalance before standing upright. Which tract helps maintain balance in this situation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vestibulospinal Tract

After a roller coaster ride, a person feels a slight imbalance and takes a minute to stand upright. The tract responsible for maintaining balance in this situation is the vestibulospinal tract.

Vestibular nuclei are situated in the pons and medulla oblongata beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle. The vestibular nuclei receive afferent fibres from the inner ear through the vestibular nerve and from the cerebellum. Neurons of the lateral vestibular nucleus give rise to the axons that form the vestibulospinal tract. The tract descends uncrossed through the medulla and through the length of the spinal cord in the anterior white column. The fibres terminate by synapsing with internuncial neurons of the anterior grey column of the spinal cord.

The inner ear and the cerebellum, using this tract, facilitate the activity of the extensor muscles and inhibit the activity of the flexor muscles in association with the maintenance of balance.

Other options:

Option A: The tectospinal tract is a neural pathway that originates in the superior colliculus of the midbrain and plays a role in coordinating head and neck movements in response to visual and auditory stimuli. It helps orient the body toward visual or auditory sources of stimuli, contributing to reflexive head-turning.

Option B: The rubrospinal tract is a motor pathway that originates in the red nucleus of the midbrain and helps regulate voluntary movement, particularly in the upper limbs. It plays a role in facilitating flexor muscles and inhibiting extensor muscles, contributing to fine motor control.

Option D: The pyramidal tract, also known as the corticospinal tract, is a major pathway for voluntary motor control that originates in the cerebral cortex and travels through the brainstem. It is responsible for precise, skilled movements, particularly in the limbs and hands.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cystic artery

In the given image the marked structure is the cystic artery.

The image below mentions the boundaries of Calot's triangle and cystic artery.

Calot's triangle is an important surgical landmark as the cystic artery usually can be found within its boundaries. The cystic artery should be identified while performing a cholecystectomy to avoid damage to the extrahepatic biliary system.

The boundaries of Calot’s triangle are: 3C's

* Medially – Common hepatic duct.

* Inferiorly – Cystic duct.

* Superior – Cystic artery.

The cystic artery is the main source of blood supply to the biliary system. After originating from the right hepatic artery, it passes posterior to the common hepatic duct and superior to the cystic duct at the hepatobiliary triangle. On reaching the superior aspect of the neck of the gallbladder, it divides into a superficial branch and a deep branch.

The image given below shows the cystic artery arising from the right hepatic artery within the Calot’s triangle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lymph nodes located at the site indicated by the arrow are classified under which level?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Level 2

The lymph nodes at the arrow-marked position are classified as level 2. The upper jugular group of lymph nodes corresponds to level 2 neck lymph nodes.

The cervical lymph nodes of the neck are a group of lymphatic structures responsible for filtering lymph and playing a key role in immune defence. They are categorized into superficial and deep groups based on their location relative to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The superficial cervical lymph nodes lie along the external jugular vein, while the deep cervical lymph nodes are situated along the internal jugular vein. These nodes drain lymph from the head, face, and neck, including areas like the scalp, nasal cavity, and oral cavity, and help combat infections in these regions.

The deep cervical lymph nodes are further divided into levels I through VII for clinical purposes, which aids in diagnosing and managing head and neck conditions. For instance, level I includes the submental and submandibular nodes, while level II encompasses nodes along the upper internal jugular vein. Enlargement of these lymph nodes may indicate infections, malignancies, or systemic diseases, and their evaluation is critical in conditions such as lymphoma, metastatic cancer, or tuberculosis.

The diagrammatic presentation of the levels of lymph nodes in the neck is given in the image below.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 39 year old patient presents to the OPD with complaints of pain over his ear lobule. He also complains of difficulty in eating food and the inability to close his eyes completely. On examination, there is a swelling below his ear. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be involved in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Facial nerve

The clinical scenario of pain over the ear lobule, inability to close eyes, and difficulty in eating point toward an injury to the facial nerve. The swelling could possibly be a parotid swelling injuring the facial nerve. The course of facial nerve is given below

Nerve supply of external ear

* Lesser occipital nerve - upper part of medial surface.

* Auriculotemporal nerve - tragus, crus of helix and adjacent part of helix.

* Auricular branch of vagus (Arnold's nerve or Alderman's nerve) - concha on the lateral surface and post auricular groove medially.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A female patient presents with complaints of pain over the anterolateral aspect of thigh after normal vaginal delivery. Which is the nerve injured in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lateral cutaneous nerve

The given clinical scenario of a patient with symptoms of pain over the anterolateral aspect of the thigh is suggestive of meralgia paresthetica. It is due to compression neuropathy or neuroma of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve of the thigh.

The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh arises from the posterior divisions of the ventral rami of L2 and L3, and it supplies the skin of the anterior and lateral surfaces of the thigh up to the knee.

It is prone to injury especially as it leaves the pelvis deep to the inguinal ligament just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. The angulation of the nerve as it crosses the iliac crest makes it vulnerable to compression during hip extension which may increase angulation and tension on the nerve. This leads to impaired sensation, pain and paraesthesia on the anterolateral aspect of thigh, in the distal end of the cutaneous distribution of this nerve. The symptoms don't cross the midline, nor extend below knee or behind hamstrings laterally

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A man is brought to the emergency department after falling from a height with his hand outstretched. X-ray shows a clavicular fracture. Which part of the clavicle is most likely to be fractured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd

The junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd (middle third) of the clavicle is most likely to be fractured.

The middle third of the clavicle is the narrowest and has the least amount of surrounding soft tissue structures. Therefore, most fractures (~80%) are seen in the middle third.

Fall on the shoulder (direct impact) and fall on the outstretched hand are the most common causes of clavicle fracture.

The patient will be presented with the flexed elbow as the arm will be held to the chest to prevent movement. It is divided into three based on the location of the fractures:

* Group I – middle-third fractures

* Group II – lateral-third fractures

* Group III – medial-third fractures

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient had his molar teeth extracted following which, he developed loss of general sensation in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Which of the following nerves is likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lingual nerve

General sensation from the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue is carried by lingual nerve, which is likely to be inujured in this case.

In the anterior two-thirds of the tongue,

* General sensation is carried by the lingual nerve.

* Taste sensation is carried by chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve.

In the posterior one-third of the tongue,

* Both general and taste sensations are carried by the glossopharyngealnerve.

Valleculae is supplied by the internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient sustained an injury to the head and now presents with blood collected around his eyes. Attachment of which of the following structure leads to this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aponeurosis

The clinical picture of blood collection around eye is called black eye or raccoon eye. It occurs due to the extravasation of blood to periorbital connective tissue. The attachment of aponeurosis in such a manner that the sub-aponeurotic tissue is continuous with the periorbital connective tissue.

The scalp is a soft tissue that covers the calvaria of the skull. It consists of five layers (Mnemonic- SCALP):

* Skin

* Connective tissue (superficial fascia) with blood vessels and nerves

* Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) with occipitofrontalis muscle

* Loose areolar (sub-aponeurotic) tissue

* Pericranium

The sub-aponeurotic tissue loose areolar tissue of the scalp is referred to as the dangerous area of the scalp. Infection from this layer can pass into the cranial cavity through small emissary veins, which pass through parietal foramina in the calvaria. It can reach intracranial structures causing meningitis and intracranial abscesses. It is also continuous with submuscular connective tissue of the eyelid. Hence pus or effusions that can occur at the scalp can drain down to this level

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A schoolboy presented with the following finding. He has a history of trauma to his upper arm in the past. Which nerve is most likely to be injured in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radial nerve

The image shows wrist drop and the radial nerve is commonly damaged in this condition.

It occurs because the radial nerve supplies the dorsiflexors of the wrist and digits and an injury to it lends them paralyzed. Other findings include numbness on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand , the dorsal aspect of the radial 3 1/2 digits and  over the anatomical stuff box. When there is compression in the axilla, radial nerve palsy is called Saturday night palsy. There is paralysis of the triceps, and weakness of the wrist and hand.

Shaft of humerus fracture is one of the most common causes of radial nerve injury because of how its closely related to the nerve. Given below is the course of radial nerve

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: At what time during the intrauterine life does talus ossification center appear?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6 months

The talus bone ossification center appears in the 6th month of intrauterine life.

Nearly all secondary centers commence ossification after birth, although a few develop in the last few weeks of intrauterine life. Secondary ossification centers that are already present when an infant is born include:

* Distal femur - 7th week

* Proximal tibia - 7th week

* Humerus - 8th week

* Calcaneus - 3 to 4th month

* Talus - 6th month

* Cuboid - 9th month

Forensic medicine textbooks like Knight's Forensic Pathology (4th edition page 456), The essentials of Forensic medicine and Toxicology
Dr. K.S. Narayan Reddy (34th edition page 75) states that the talus ossification begins at 7 months instead of 6th.

The answer is as per Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice (42nd Edition page 1436)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the maneuver shown.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pringle's manoeuver

The given image depicts Pringle's maneuvre.

It is a technique where the free margin of the lesser omentum is compressed to obtain rapid control of the hepatic artery and portal vein in liver trauma and surgery.

The hepatoduodenal ligament is encircled with a vessel loop or vascular clamp to occlude hepatic blood flow from the hepatic artery and portal vein. This maneuver helps distinguish hepatic arterial and portal venous bleeding from hepatic vein bleeding, which will persist with the hepatoduodenal ligament clamped. In many cases, the liver laceration can then be explored and any actively bleeding vessels controlled with suture ligation.

4 P's in the management of liver injuries are:

* Push : compression of the edges of the laceration

* Pringle : applying pressure on the portal triad

* Plug: the defects with silicon tubes

* Pack : apply packs in and around the liver to arrest bleeding

Other options:

Option A: Mattox maneuver refers to left medial visceral mobilisation done to visualise and repair the vascular injury in case of retroperitoneal bleeds near the kidney.

Option C: Cattell braash maneuver refers to mobilisation of right viscera, namely the colon, to visualise the superior mesenteric artery and repair bleed in infrarenal region.

Option D: Liver hanging maneuver (LHM) is a method of liver resection by passing a tape between the inferior vena cava and liver to have adequate vascular control.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the given histopathology slide.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Brunner's gland

The slide shows section of the duodenum and marked structures glands located on the duodenum called Brunner's glands

Brunner's glands (or duodenal glands) are compound tubular submucosal glands present in the upper duodenum (above the sphincter of Oddi).

The alveoli of duodenal glands are lined mostly by mucous secreting columnar cells. Their ducts pass through the muscularis mucosae and empty into the intestinal crypts (of Lieberkuhn).

The duodenum can be easily differentiated from the jejunum or ileum by the presence of these submucosal glands. The jejunum and ileum do not have glands in their submucosa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the type of joint shown in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Syndesmosis

The type of joint shown in the given image is syndesmosis.

The radius and ulna are united with each other by three joints:

* Proximal (superior) radioulnar joint

* Middle radioulnar joint

* Distal (inferior) radioulnar joint

Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot joints (synovial) and are involved in pronation and supination movements of the forearm.

The middle radioulnar joint is a fibrous joint (syndesmosis). The radius and ulna, in the middle, are connected by two syndesmoses namely:

* The oblique cord - extends from the lateral side of the ulnar tuberosity to the radius, distal to the radial tuberosity.

* Interosseous membrane - a broad, thin collagenous structure, which runs perpendicular to the oblique cord. It extends distomedially between the interosseous borders of the radius and ulna.

Based on the structure, joints are classified into three types:

* Fibrous joints

* Sutures

* Syndesmosis

* Gomphosis

* Cartilaginous joints

* Primary cartilaginous joints or synchondrosis

* Secondary cartilaginous joints or symphysis

* Synovial joints

* Ball-and-socket or spheroidal joints

* Sellar or saddle joints

* Condylar or bicondylar joints

* Ellipsoid joints

* Hinge joints

* Pivot or trochoid joints

* Plane joints

The illustration below depicts types of fibrous joints.

The illustration below depicts the types of synovial joints.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the condition shown in this picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rupture of biceps tendon

The image shows Popeye sign and it is seen in rupture of proximal tendon of biceps.  Proximal tendon of biceps refers to both long head and short head of biceps.

Popeye sign: On flexing the elbow there is an extremely prominent bulge of the muscle belly as its unrestrained fibers contract.

The proximal biceps tendon makes up 90-97% of all biceps tendon ruptures. In isolation, it has little effect on the upper limb function

The 4 most common areas of tendon rupture include:

* Quadriceps

* Achilles

* Rotator cuff (most commonly, the supraspinatus)

* Biceps.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the vertebral level of the plane between the highest points of the iliac crests?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. L4-L5

The plane passing through the highest point of the iliac crest is called the supracristal plane.

Posteriorly, it corresponds to the level of the L4 body or L4/5 disc and its spinous process

Pearl PF0627: Abdominal planes and their landmarks

Planes that divide the abdomen into 9 regions

* Horizontal planes

* L3 - Subcostal plane (between 10th costal cartilages). Corresponds to the 3rd part of the duodenum

* L5 - Transtubercular plane (between tubercles of iliac crests). Corresponds to the origin of Inferior vena cava.

* Vertical planes (Paramedian or lateral planes)

* Mid-clavicular point to mid-inguinal point on both sides

The nine regions of the abdomen include:

* Left hypochondriac, Epigastric, Right hypochondriac

* Left lumbar, Umbilical (Central), Right lumbar

* Left iliac, Hypogastric (Suprapubic), Right iliac

Other planes and angles in the abdomen

* Transpyloric (Addison's) plane passes midway between the suprasternal notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

* The supracristal plane passing through the highest point of the iliac crest on both sides. Posteriorly, it corresponds to the level of the L4 body or L4/5 disc and its spinous process. It is an important landmark when performing a lumbar puncture or spinal injection. The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta lies approximately in this plane.

* The plane of the pubic crest passes through the upper border of the pubic symphysis. When supine, this plane intersects the tip of the coccyx and the femoral head.

* Renal angle is the angle between the 12th rib and the outer border of Erector spinae muscle. The lower border of normal kidneys may occasionally be felt here.

* Lumbar triangle (of Petit) is marked below by the iliac crest, anteriorly by external oblique and posteriorly by latissimus dorsi. Lumbar herniation can occur here.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries is palpated in the image shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The posterior tibial artery is palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon, as shown in the image.

The posterior tibial artery can be felt by keeping the foot relaxed between plantar and dorsiflexion and palpating against the distal tibia behind and below the medial malleolus, approximately one-third of a line connecting the posterior border of the medial malleolus to the calcaneal tendon(Achilles tendon)

Other options:

Option A: The anterior tibial artery is palpated on the dorsum of the foot, lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. This pulse point is important for assessing peripheral circulation in the lower limb.

Option C: Dorsalis pedis artery is palpated against the underlying tarsals, lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus from the midpoint between the malleoli to the proximal end of the first intermetatarsal space.

Option D: The popliteal artery is the most difficult of the peripheral pulses to feel because the artery lies deep in the popliteal fossa. It is examined with the subject lying supine or prone, with the knee flexed to relax the tense popliteal fascia that roofs the popliteal fossa. It is felt over the midline of the fossa by deep pressure against the popliteal surface of the femur.
