questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following layers is absent in esophagus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serosa

The serosa is absent in the esophagus except in the intra-abdominal part.

The oesophagus consists of the following layers:

* Mucosa:Inner-most layer is the mucous membrane with the following sub-layers:

* Lining epithelium: non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium

* Lamina propria: connective tissue supporting the lining epithelium

* Muscularis mucosae: thin layer of smooth muscle

*  Submucosa: A special feature of the submucosa is the presence of compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands

*  Muscularis externa with the inner layer of circular muscle fibres and an outer layer of longitudinal muscle fibres

* Upper 1/3rd: Only skeletal muscle fibres are present

* Middle 1/3rd: Both skeletal and smooth muscle fibres are present

* Lower 1/3rd: Only smooth muscle fibres are present

The stomach has 3 layers in the muscularis externa, with an extra oblique layer.

In the colon, the outer longitudinal fibers join to form prominent bundles called the taenia coli.

* Adventitia: Most of the esophagus has a dense fibrous tissue covering called the adventitia. Only a short length of the esophagus in the lower part(Intra-abdominal) has a peritoneal covering (serosa).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 20-year-old male patient presents to the emergency department with swelling at the base of the thumb after falling on an outstretched hand while playing football. Which of the following is most likely to be to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scaphoid

The history of falls on the outstretched hand and swelling at the base of the thumb suggests the diagnosis of a scaphoid fracture.

The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Mechanism of injury is:

* Axial compression directly on the bone

* Hyperextending the wrist joint

Such mechanisms are commonly seen when a person falls onto an outstretched hand.

Clinical features:

* Pain is typically felt along the radial side of the wrist. Proximal to the metacarpal of the thumb.

* An important feature is focal tenderness, which is usually detected at specific points:

* Just below Lister’s tubercle

* Over the volar prominence near the distal wrist crease

* Swelling is not specific. It may or may not be present.

The most common complications include nonunion, avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the proximal fracture segment, and osteoarthritis.

Diagnostic sign- precisely localized tenderness in the anatomical snuff box.

X-ray of the wrist is taken but it has a high false-negative rate. Hence empiric splinting or MRI is recommended as the next step in such cases where clinical suspicion exists but X-ray findings are normal. Undisplaced fractures are managed by immobilization in a scaphoid cast applied in a glass-holding position. Reduction with compression screw is preferred for displaced fractures.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a history of repeated pain over the medial canthus and chronic use of nasal decongestants presents to the OPD with high-grade fever, chills, headache, and bilateral proptosis. On eliciting further history, it was confirmed that proptosis began in the right eye, and a few days later, the left eye was also affected. Fundoscopy reveals papilloedema. On examination, damage to the abducens nerve was noted. Which of the following ocular movements will be impaired?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lateral

The given clinical scenario, with recurrent episodes of headache and pain over the medial canthus and repeated use of nasal decongestants, suggests that the patient was suffering from sinusitis, which has most likely resulted in cavernous sinus thrombosis, and the injury of the abducens nerve will affect the lateral ocular movement as it supplies the lateral rectus muscle of the eye.

Cavernous sinus syndrome (CSS) is a rare condition characterized by ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, ocular and conjunctival congestion, trigeminal sensory loss, and Horner’s syndrome. These signs and symptoms result from the involvement of the cranial nerves passing through the cavernous sinus. The cavernous sinus syndrome affects III, IV, V, and VI cranial nerves.

In cavernous sinus thrombosis, proptosis is initially unilateral but soon becomes bilateral due to the spread of infection to the contralateral sinus through the intercavernous communication. Also, cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with high-grade fever with chills, rigor, and headache.
On the other hand, orbital cellulitis and panophthalmitis are unilateral conditions

The cavernous sinuses are two large venous plexuses that lie on either side of the body of the sphenoid bone, extending from the superior orbital fissure to the apex of the petrous temporal bone.

Structures related to the lateral wall of the cavernous sinuses are the oculomotor nerve, trochlear nerve and the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Within the cavernous sinus are the abducens nerve and the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery.

Image showing cavernous sinus and the structures related to it.

Orbital apex syndrome is a condition similar to cavernous sinus syndrome with retro-orbital pain and involvement of 2,3,4,5 and 6 cranial nerves. The differentiating feature is the optic nerve involvement leading to early visual loss and afferent pupillary defect.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient came to the clinic, and the following test was performed, as shown in the image below. Which of the following is being tested here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abduction

The test being performed here is the Trendelenburg test, which is done to check the action of the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, which are powerful abductors of the hip supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

A positive Trendelenburg test on the right side indicates a right superior gluteal nerve injury, and vice versa.
When the patient stands on his left foot, there is drooping of the right; this is a positive Trendelenburg test on the left side.

Normally, when the leg is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus on the opposite (unsupported) side exert traction on the hip bone. This results in a slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in an upright position.

If the gluteus medius and minimus are paralysed, the pelvis drops on the contralateral side. This is known as a positive Trendelenburg sign. It is positive in the paralysis of the hip abductors and in developmental dysplasia of the hip. A characteristic lurching gait is seen.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with a fracture of the structure marked below following a road traffic accident. Which of the following symptoms will be seen in this is patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anosmia

The structure marked in the given image is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid and fracture to the cribriform plate will lead to anosmia as the olfactory nerve fibres pierce through it.

Olfactory nerves transmit olfactory information from the sensory receptors in the nasal mucosa to the brain. Damage to these fibres can disrupt this pathway, resulting in a loss of smell. A cribriform plate fracture may also lead to a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak, manifesting as clear, watery nasal discharge.

The olfactory bulbs are located just above the cribriform plate, as the first relay station for olfactory information. Trauma can cause displacement or direct injury to these bulbs, further disrupting the transmission of olfactory signals. Following trauma, inflammation or swelling can occur in the region, potentially leading to additional damage or pressure on the olfactory nerve fibres and bulbs, exacerbating the loss of smell.

Olfactory nerve fibres pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid and can lead to the spread of infection to the intracranial space and trauma can lead to CSF rhinorrhea.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with an inability to shrug his shoulders after a fall from the stairs. On examination, an injury to the posterior triangle of his neck is noted. Which of the following structures is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spinal accessory nerve

In the given scenario, the patient is unable to shrug his shoulders due to an injury to the spinal accessory nerve, which is present in the posterior triangle of the neck and supplies the trapezius muscle.

The spinal accessory nerve innervates the sternocleidomastoid just before entering the posterior triangle.

* If the nerve is injured before it enters the posterior triangle, actions of the sternocleidomastoid will be affected.

* If the nerve is injured within the posterior triangle, the sternocleidomastoid will be spared.

The trapezius is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI). It causes:

* Retraction of scapula

* Shrugging of the shoulder

* Overhead abduction (along with serratus anterior)

Paralysis of the trapezius causes drooping of the shoulder and slight winging of the scapula (the superior angle of the scapula becomes more prominent).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During surgery for patent ductus arteriosus, which anatomical structure is most susceptible to injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left recurrent laryngeal nerve

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is most susceptible to injury during surgery for patent ductus arteriosus.

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the 6th arch artery while the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the 4th arch artery. This occurs because the distal portion of the 6th arch disappears on the right side along with the 5th arch artery. Thus the nerve on the right side loops under the 4th arch artery.

The patent ductus arteriosus is due to a defect in the 6th aortic arch, also known as the pulmonary arch, as it gives off a branch to the growing lung bud. On the right side, this arch forms the right pulmonary artery proximally and disappears distally. On the left side, the distal part remains patent to form the ductus arteriosus that shunts blood from the right ventricle to the dorsal aorta. This is obliterated after birth forming the ligamentum arteriosum. If the ductus arteriosus remains patent after birth, it is referred to as patent ductus arteriosus.

Pearl PF0428: Derivatives of Various Aortic Arches

The aortic arches or pharyngeal arch arteries are a series of six paired embryological vascular structures which give rise to the great arteries of the neck and head. They are ventral to the dorsal aorta and arise from the aortic sac.

questions.text: During surgical intervention on the great saphenous vein situated 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus, which structure should be protected from damage during the application of ligatures around the vein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Saphenous nerve

During surgery on the great saphenous vein located 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus, care must be taken to protect the nearby saphenous nerve from damage during ligature placement around the vein.

The Saphenous nerve accompanies the Great Saphenous Vein medially from the ankle to the level of the knee and supplies cutaneous sensation to the medial leg and ankle. Thus it is more prone to injury during stripping of GSV.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the labelled structure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Internal capsule

The labelled structure is the Internal capsule.

The internal capsule is a component of the white matter of the brain. They contain projection fibers. It can be divided into the following parts:

* anterior limb

* genu

* posterior limb

* retrolenticular/ retrolentiform portion

* sublenticular/ sublentiform portion

The anterior limb of the internal capsule carries the fronto-pontine fibers, while the genu carries the corticonuclear tract.

The posterior limb of the internal capsule carries cortico-spinal motor fibers in the anterior part. The posterior part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule carries sensory fibers.

The retrolenticular part contains the parietopontine, occipitopontine and occipitotectal fibres and the sublenticular part contains temporopontine and some parietopontine fibres.

The basal ganglia constitutes accessory motor system that functions in close association with the cerebral cortex and corticospinal motor control system. On each side of the brain, these ganglia consist of the caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, and subthalamic nucleus.

Nomenclature of basal ganglia:

* Corpus striatum: Caudate nucleus + putamen+ globus pallidus

* Lentiform nucleus: Putamen + globus pallidus

* Neostriatum: Caudate nucleus + putamen

The internal capsule separates the thalamus and the caudate nucleus from the lentiform nucleus. The caudate nucleus is a C-shaped mass of grey matter. It is divided into a head, body, and tail. Degeneration of the caudate nucleus is seen in Huntington's disease.

Both the Putamen and external capsule lie lateral to globus pallidus. It receives fibers from the striatum and subthalamic nuclei. It acts as the main output of the basal ganglia to the thalamus and superior colliculus. The substantia nigra is seen in each cerebral peduncle of the midbrain located deep to the crus cerebri. The levels of dopamine in the substantia nigra and striata are reduced in parkinsonism disease.

questions.text: Identify the liver segment marked in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. VIII

The highlighted liver segment is segment VIII.

A horizontal plane known as the portal plane divides the liver where the portal vein bifurcates and becomes horizontal. This divides each section of the liver into superior and inferior segments:

* Left lateral section: segment II above and segment III below the portal plane

* Left medial section: segment IVa above and segment IVb below the portal plane

* Right anterior (or medial) section: segment VIII above and segment V below the portal plane

* Right posterior (or lateral) section: segment VII above and segment VI below the portal

Couinaud classification is the commonly used classification of the liver. It divides the liver is divided into eight segments. Each segment has its own vascular supply, biliary drainage, and lymphatic drainage. Segment I corresponds to the caudate lobe of the liver and segment IV corresponds to the quadrate lobe of the liver.

The Couinaud's liver segments are as follows:

Pearl PF0481: Couinaud's Liver Segments

The Couinaud classification is currently the most widely used system to describe functional liver anatomy.

* Based on the distribution of hepatic portal venous branches in the parenchyma

* Each segment has its own dual vascular inflow, biliary drainage and lymphatic drainage

Segment I corresponds to the gross anatomical caudate lobe and is considered as posterior segment.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the epithelial lining of the trachea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium

The trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.

The trachea is a tube-like structure that allows air to pass between the larynx and the bronchi.

The trachealis muscle is a smooth muscle located at the posterior wall of the trachea. It connects the ends of the C-shaped tracheal cartilage rings and completes the posterior part of the tracheal wall.

The histological image below is that of the trachea as identified by the presence of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lining, the serous and mucous glands, and hyaline cartilage.

The histological section of the trachea shows the following structures:

* Respiratory epithelium

* Basement membrane

* Submucosal glands (both serous and mucous parts)

* Perichondrium

* Tracheal cartilage

* Trachealis muscle (smooth muscle).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What joint is present between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Synchondrosis

The joint present between the epiphysis and diaphysis of a long bone is called synchondrosis.

Synchondrosis refers to the primary cartilaginous joints in which the advancing areas of ossification are separated by hyaline cartilage. They are temporary joints and are associated with growth. Hyaline cartilage has the ability to ossify with age, thus making these joints undergo synostosis (fusion) once the growth is complete. An example of this type of joint is the epiphyseal plate between the epiphysis and diaphysis of long bones

Structurally, joints are classified as fibrous joints, cartilaginous joints, and synovial joints (see the table). Sutures, syndesmosis, and gomphosis are fibrous joints. Symphysis and synchondrosis are types of cartilaginous joints.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: When does the anterior fontanelle close?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 12-24 months

The anterior fontanelle ideally closes between 18-24 months. However, the closest answer in the given options is 12–24 months of age.

Fontanelle of the skull:

* The anterior fontanelle is present between the two frontal and two parietal bones. It closes at around 18-24 months. The junction is marked by bregma where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet.

* The posterior fontanelle is present between the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid suture and closes at around 2-3 months of birth.

* The sphenoid fontanelle corresponds to the pterion and also closes at around 2-3 months of birth.

* The mastoid fontanelle closes around at the end of the first year.

Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The given image shows the physician's fingertips between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon, and the artery being palpated here is the posterior tibial artery.

questions.text: Which of the following structures will be present in the area marked below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pterygopalatine ganglion

The pterygopalatine ganglion will be present in the area marked in the image above which is the pterygopalatine fossa.

The pterygopalatine ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion located in the pterygopalatine fossa, a small, cone-shaped depression situated deep in the skull. This fossa is located posterior to the maxilla (upper jaw) and adjacent to the nasal cavity.

It is responsible for parasympathetic innervation to the lacrimal gland, nasal glands, and palatine glands. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers originate from the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) and travel through the greater petrosal nerve. These fibres join with the deep petrosal nerve to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal before synapsing in the ganglion.

Boundaries of the Pterygopalatine Fossa:

* Anteriorly: Posterior wall of the maxillary sinus.

* Posteriorly: Pterygoid process of the sphenoid bone.

* Medially: Perpendicular plate of the palatine bone.

* Laterally: Pterygomaxillary fissure, which opens into the infratemporal fossa.

* Superiorly: Inferior surface of the sphenoid bone.

* Inferiorly: Palatine bone.

Structures surrounding the Pterygopalatine Ganglion:

* Maxillary Nerve (V2): A branch of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) that passes through the fossa, giving off branches to the ganglion.

* Greater and Lesser Palatine Nerves: Emerge from the ganglion to innervate the hard and soft palate.

* Nasal Nerves: Branches that innervate the nasal cavity, including the nasopalatine nerve.

* Pharyngeal Nerve: Provides innervation to parts of the nasopharynx.

* Arterial Supply: The maxillary artery's branches, including the sphenopalatine artery, which supplies the nasal cavity, are present in the fossa.
Foramina and fissures:

* Foramen rotundum: Transmits the maxillary nerve (V2) into the fossa.

* Pterygoid Canal: Contains the nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve), which carries both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers.

* Sphenopalatine Foramen: Connects the fossa to the nasal cavity.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: While performing an endoscopy, a constriction is felt at the oesophageal junction, 25 cm from the upper incisors. Which of the following structures is responsible for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arch of aorta

The constriction is felt due to the arch of aorta and left bronchus crossing the esophagus at 25 cm from the upper incisor teeth.

Normally, the esophagus shows 3 constrictions at the following levels measured from upper incisors:

* Junction of the esophagus with cricopharynx (15 cm from the incisor teeth)

* Crossed by arch of aorta and left bronchus (25 cm from the incisor teeth)

* It pierces the diaphragm (40 cm from the incisor teeth)

questions.text: A 20-year-old man reports to the emergency room after falling from a ladder. Physical examination reveals an inability to abduct the arm and flex the elbow, as shown in the image below. There is sensory loss from the shoulder to the lateral arm. Which nerve roots are affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. C5 and C6

The image shows a typical presentation of a policeman's tip, waiter's tip or porter's tip deformity seen in Erb’s palsy, and the nerves affected are the C5 and C6 roots.

The Erb’s point in the brachial plexus is in the upper trunk, where the six nerves meet. The nerves are the C5 and C6 roots, the suprascapular nerve, the nerve to subclavius, and the anterior and posterior divisions of the upper trunk.

Given below is a diagram depicting the location of the Erb's point:

Anatomically, the brachial plexus consists of roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and branches.

The common causes of Erb's palsy are the undue separation of head and neck, i.e., falling on the shoulder, and birth injuries. The resulting muscle weakness results in the depicted deformity, which includes the following features:

* The arm is adducted and medially rotated at the shoulder joint

* The elbow joint is extended

* The radioulnar joint is pronated

* Sensory loss along the outer aspect of the arm

Aeroplane splint is used in the treatment of brachial plexus injury (Erb’s palsy). Here, the shoulder is maintained in abduction and external rotation, the elbow in flexion, the forearm in supination, and the wrist in extension.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 3-year-old male is brought into the OPD by his mother. She complains that his left eyelid is constantly drooping. Physical examination reveals that the eyeball is abducted and depressed in its primary position. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3rd nerve palsy

The clinical scenario is suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy (3rd nerve palsy).

In primary gaze, the patient's left eye has deviated down and out. There is also profound ptosis due to the weakness of the levator muscle. Due to the involvement of the superior rectus and medial rectus, elevation and adduction will be impaired. Abduction and depression in the primary position (down and out) due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles. All of these findings indicate left oculomotor nerve palsy.

The signs of left oculomotor nerve palsy are summarised in the image attached below.

In trochlear nerve palsy (4th nerve palsy), the superior oblique is affected, causing:

* The weakness of depression: Mainly seen when the eye is adducted (depression during abducted position is a function of the Inferior rectus)

* Weakness of abduction

* Failure of intorsion: cause of diplopia.

In abducens nerve palsy (6th nerve palsy), the lateral rectus is affected. Due to the involvement of only the lateral rectus, abduction will be impaired.

In facial nerve palsy (7th nerve palsy), there is facial weakness.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presented with choking episodes after ingestion of a fish bone. The fishbone was impacted at the T4 level in the oesophagus. Which is the most likely site of obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arch of aorta

The most likely site of obstruction in the case of a fishbone impacted at the T4 level is the arch of the aorta.

Normally, the oesophagus shows 3 constrictions at the following levels measured from upper incisors:

* At the pharyngo-oesophageal junction (C6)—15 cm from the upper incisors.

* At the crossing of the arch of the aorta (T4)—25 cm from the upper incisors.

* Where it pierces the diaphragm (T10)—40 cm from the upper incisors.

Foreign bodies in the oesophagus can be held up at these constrictions.

Acute dysphagia is common with foreign body obstruction. They might also experience odynophagia, regurgitation of food, neck pain, or chest pain. Esophageal obstruction can cause complications such as esophageal perforation and lung aspiration.

When impaction of a foreign body occurs in an adult esophagus, it usually occurs in the presence of underlying structural abnormalities (such as a web or stricture), functional abnormalities resulting from abnormal esophageal peristalsis, or when the swallowed object is too large to navigate the anatomic constrictions of the normal esophagus. The two most common causes are eosinophilic oesophagitis and Schatzki rings. Esophageal webs, tracheo-oesophageal fistula/esophageal atresia (TOF/OA), and peptic strictures are conditions that predispose to food bolus obstructions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 60-year-old male presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear with loss of sensation. Physical examination reveals paraesthesias with associated numbness in extremities and a raised jugular venous pressure. A thickened nerve is observed as shown in the image below. Identify the structure marked by the arrow in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Greater auricular nerve

In the given clinical scenario, the patient presents with a hypopigmented patch behind the ear accompanied by loss of sensation, and neck examination reveals a thickened structure suggestive of leprosy, and the thickened structure is the greater auricular nerve.

Great auricular nerve:

It is the largest ascending branch of the cervical plexus and arises from the second and third cervical spinal nerves. It winds over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and ascends upwards. On reaching the parotid gland, it divides into the anterior and posterior branches:

* The anterior branch supplies the facial skin over the parotid gland and joins the facial nerve in the gland.

* The posterior branch supplies the skin over the mastoid process and the lower part of the back of the auricle, lobule, and concha.

Clinical considerations:

* The nerve can be thickened in conditions like leprosy and can be palpated over the upper part of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (as seen in the above image). Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerve is the posterior tibial nerve, followed by the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most frequently involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

* Cross-inervation between the somatic sensory supply (great auricular nerve) and the parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland is considered an anatomical basis for the phenomenon of Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

questions.text: A man suffered damage to his right knee's lateral side. He complains of having trouble walking two days later because his toes continue to drag on the floor. Additionally, he observes numbness over the dorsum of the foot and upper lateral aspect of the leg. What is the most likely injured nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Common peroneal nerve

The clinical scenario, combined with a high-stepping gait (foot drop), indicates common peroneal nerve injury. This is associated with loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot and the first interdigital space.

The nerves supplying the marked areas are shown below.

The common peroneal nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st and 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves.

The first interdigital space is supplied by the deep fibular nerve, while the dorsum of the foot (except the lateral and medial borders) is supplied by the superficial fibular nerve.

Superficial fibular nerve
Deep fibular nerve

Motor innervation

• Peroneus longus
• Peroneus Brevis

• Extensor digitorum longus
• Extensor hallucis longus
• Tibialis anterior
• Peroneus tertius

Sensory innervation

• Lateral aspect of the lower leg
• Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital webspace

• The first interdigital space

Injury to the common peroneal nerve at the level of the neck of the fibula causes foot drop. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion of the foot are lost, while the inversion and plantar flexion are usually preserved. Sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot, including the first web space, is lost. The ankle reflex is usually preserved.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What remnant is derived from the structure marked in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nucleus pulposus

The nucleus pulposus is derived from the notochord (marked by the arrow).

The nucleus pulposus is a mucoid, gel-like substance that lies between the centre of the intervertebral disc and its posterior surface. At birth, it is almost completely gelatinous and liquid, but as the individual ages, it becomes less differentiated from the remainder of the intervertebral disc, becoming less hydrated and increasingly fibrous.

The notochord is derived from the epiblast cells. Epiblast cells from the primitive knot region of the primitive streak multiply and pass cranially in the midline between the ectoderm and endoderm. They undergo several stages of rearrangement to form the notochord. During the initial stages of neurulation, the notochord induces overlying ectoderm to thicken and form the neural plate.

During vertebral column development, the notochord gradually regresses, with its cells persisting as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.

Rarely, these notochordal remnants may give rise to slow-growing tumors known as chordomas. These malignant bone tumors arise from residual embryonic notochordal tissue and are usually located along the axial midline. It is the most common primary malignancy of the sacrum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following receives venous drainage from the left atrium and both ventricles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Great cardiac vein

The great cardiac vein receives venous drainage from the left atrium and both ventricles.

The great cardiac vein begins at the apex of the heart. It ascends in the anterior interventricular sulcus. At the coronary sulcus, the great cardiac vein turns to the left and lies at the base of the heart. Here, it is associated with the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery. In the coronary sulcus, the great cardiac vein enlarges to form the coronary sinus.

The middle cardiac vein begins near the apex of the heart and ascends in the posterior interventricular sulcus. It is associated with the posterior interventricular branch of the right or the left coronary artery.

The small cardiac vein begins in the anterior section of the coronary sulcus between the right atrium and the right ventricle. It continues in this groove onto the base of the heart and then enters the coronary sinus. It accompanies the right coronary artery in its course and may receive the right marginal vein.

The posterior cardiac vein lies on the posterior surface of the left ventricle just to the left of the middle cardiac vein. Anterior veins of the right ventricle drain the anterior portion of the right ventricle and enter the right atrium directly.

Venae cordis minimae, or veins of Thebasius, drain directly into the cardiac chambers and are mainly associated with the right atrium and right ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A man was brought to the emergency department after he fell into a manhole and injured his perineum. He was unable to pass urine and blood was seen at the tip of the urethra. A diagnosis of bulbar urethral injury was made. Where do you least expect the urine to get collected in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial portion of thigh

In bulbar urethral injury, the medial portion of the thigh is the least likely site for the collection of urine.

The rupture of the urethra below the urogenital diaphragm will result in extravasation of urine into the superficial perineal pouch, penis and scrotum in males and labia majora in females, and the anterior abdominal wall.

The superficial fascia of the abdomen is divided below the umbilicus into a superficial fatty layer (fascia of Camper) and a deep membranous layer (fascia of Scarpa). Scarpa's fascia is continuous with the membranous layer of the superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia).

Colles' fascia is attached to fascia lata (the deep fascia of the thigh) along the Holden's line that extends from the pubic tubercle laterally for 8 cm. Extravasated fluid cannot pass into the medial thigh below Holden's line due to the firm attachment of Colles' fascia to the fascia lata.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Killian's dehiscence is seen between___?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cricopharyngeus and Thyropharyngeus

Killian's dehiscence is seen between the cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus muscles.

The inferior constrictor muscle is made up of 2 parts: The upper thyropharyngeus made of oblique fibres and the lower cricopharyngeus made of transverse fibres. Between the two muscles, there is a potential gap which is called as the pharyngeal dimple or Killian's dehiscence.

This is the site of weakness in the pharyngeal wall and therefore is the potential site for the development of the diverticula- Zenker's diverticula.

Another site of weakness in the pharyngeal wall is the Laimer's triangle, which is present between the cricopharyngeus and the circular muscle of the oesophagus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the structure marked in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Genioglossus

The structure marked 'A' in the image is the Genioglossus muscle.

Genioglossus is one of the extrinsic muscles of the tongue which brings about the forward traction of the tongue to protrude its apex from the mouth. Hence, it is also called the safety muscle of the tongue.

Acting bilaterally, the two muscles depress the central part of the tongue, making it concave from side to side. Acting unilaterally, the tongue diverges to the opposite side.

Other options:

Hyoglossus: Depresses and retracts the tongue, pulling it downward and backward.

Styloglossus: Elevates and retracts the tongue, drawing it upward and backward.

Palatoglossus: Elevates the posterior portion of the tongue and narrows the fauces during swallowing.

Note:

* All the muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus (cranial accessory nerve through pharyngeal plexus) are supplied by hypoglossal nerve.

* All the muscles of pharynx except stylopharyngeus (glossopharyngeal nerve) are supplied by pharyngeal plexus.

* All muscles of soft palate except tensor veli palatini (nerve to medial pterygoid from mandibular nerve) are supplied by pharyngeal plexus.

* All muscles of larynx except cricothyroid (external laryngeal nerve) are supplied by recurrent laryngeal nerve.

All intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of tongue are derived from occipital myotomes, hence innervated by hypoglossal nerve, except palatoglossus which is derived from the pharyngeal arch and is supplied by vago-accessory nerve.

Aryepiglotticus, Interarytenoids

Posterior cricoarytenoid

Adductor of vocal cords

Lateral cricoarytenoid

Safety muscle of larynx: Posterior cricoarytenoid

Safety muscle of tongue: Genioglossus

Vocalis is known as the modulator of larynx because, the anterior part of the vocalis muscle can tense the vocal cord, and its posterior part can relax the vocal cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about thoracolumbar fascia?
options: In the lumbar region it is in 4 layers
In the thoraic region it is attatched medially to the vertebrae
The posterior and middle layers join with the anterior layer to form the aponeurotic origin of transversus abdominis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. In the lumbar region it is in 4 layers

In the lumbar region, the fascia consists of 3 layers - anterior, middle and posterior.

The thoracolumbar fascia is a complex arrangement of multiple fascial layers in the thoracolumbar region. This fascia encloses the paraspinal, quadratus lumborum, and lattismus dorsi muscles.

a) Thoraic region: The thoracolumbar fascia provides a thin fibrous covering for the extensor muscles of the vertebral column.

Relations:

* Medially attached to the spines of the thoracic vertebrae

* Laterally to the angles of the ribs

b)Lumbar region: It is in three layers:

* Anterior

* Medially - anterior surface of the lumbar transverse processes.

* Laterally - blends with the middle layer at the lateral border of the quadratus lumborum.

* Superiorly - lateral arcuate ligament and tip of Transverse process L1 to 12th rib.

* Inferiorly - inner lip of iliac crest and the ilio-lumbar ligament.

* Middle

* Medially - tips of the lumbar transverse processes and inter-transverse ligaments.

* Laterally - blends with the anterior layer at the lateral border of the quadratus lumborum.

* Superiorly - lower border of the 12th rib and lumbocostal ligament.

* Inferiorly - intermediate area of the iliac crest.

* Posterior

* Medially - lumbar and sacral spines and interspinous ligaments.

* Laterally - blends with the middle layer at the lateral border of the erector spinae.

* Superiorly - back of thorax - lumbar vertebral spines.

* Inferiorly - outer lip of the iliac crest

The posterior and middle layers unite to form a tough raphe at the lateral margin of erector spinae, and at the lateral border of quadratus lumborum they are joined by the anterior layer to form the aponeurotic origin of transversus abdominis.

Function:

* The attachments have a role in lifting and load transfer ,although controversial.

* They contain nociceptive nerve endings that may be responsible for back pain due to injury to the area and also impaired proprioceptive signalling.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn had hypoplasia of the mandibles and zygomatic bones, malformed external ears, and slanted palpebral fissures. Abnormality in the development of which of the following pharyngeal arches will most likely lead to the given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pharyngeal arch 1

Treacher Collins syndrome that results from abnormal development of the 1st pharyngeal arch (mandibular arch).

First arch syndromes are congenital defects caused due to the failure of the neural crest cells to migrate into the 1st pharyngeal arch.

* Treacher-Collins syndrome (mandibulo-facial dysostosis) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder seen in 1/50,000 live births. It is characterized by

* Craniofacial bone defects involving the mandible (causing micrognathia), maxilla, and zygomatic arches

* Ear defects involving the external ear, atresia of auditory canals, and abnormalities of the middle ear ossicles, leading to bilateral conductive hearing loss

* Eye defects such as down-slanting palpebral fissures and lower eyelid colobomas

* Pierre Robin sequence (or Robin sequence) is a deformity seen in 1/8500 births. It may be caused due to genetic defects or due to environmental factors. It can also be seen in oligohydramnios, when the chin gets compressed against the chest in utero.

* It is characterized by a triad of micrognathia, glossoptosis (posteriorly placed tongue), and cleft palate.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient underwent a left submandibular gland excision during which the hypoglossal nerve was injured. Which of the following deficits would be seen in this case?
options: Deviated tongue to the contralateral side
Deviated tongue to the same side
Loss of taste in posterior 1/3rd of the tongue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Deviated tongue to the same side

A hypoglossal nerve injury would damage all muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus resulting in deviation of the tongue to the same side. Since, the left hypoglossal nerve is injured in the above scenario, the tongue will deviate to the left side.

Hypoglossal nerve injury:

* Ipsilateral tongue atrophy

* Paralysis of all muscles except palatoglossus resulting in ipsilateral deviation of the tongue on protrusion

* Paralysis of geniohyoid and thyrohyoid resulting in deviation of larynx to the contralateral side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A woman presented with sudden onset of dysphagia, dysarthria and gait ataxia. MRI revealed an acute infarct in the right dorsolateral medulla. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wallenberg syndrome

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Wallenberg syndrome. The symptoms of dysphagia and dysarthria are due to the involvement of nucleus ambiguus. Ataxia is a feature of inferior cerebellar peduncle involvement.

Option A: Medial medullary syndrome is also known as Dejerine's anterior bulbar syndrome.

Option B: Lateral medullary syndrome is also known as Wallenberg syndrome.

Option C: Medullary tegmental paralysis is also known as Babinski-Nageotte syndrome.

Option D: Midbrain stroke syndrome is also known as Weber syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the anatomical structure marked in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Extensor pollicis longus

The marked structure in the given image is extensor pollicis longus.

The name "snuffbox" originates from the use of this surface for placing and then sniffing powdered tobacco, or "snuff."

Anatomical snuffbox boundaries:

Lateral wall:

* Abductor pollicis longus (APL),

* Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)

Medial wall:

* Extensor pollicis longus (EPL).

Roof:

* Cephalic vein

* Sup. Br of radial nerve

Floor:

* Radial styloid, Scaphoid, Trapezium and 1st Metacarpal.

Only content: Radial artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pons

The structure marked in the given image is pons.

Pons houses the motor nucleus of the facial nerve, and also the vestibulocochlear nuclei and abducens nuclei.

The pneumotaxic center is located in the upper pons.

Neural regulation of respiration:

It involves set of neurons located in pons and medulla:

* Pons: Pneumotaxic centre and apneustic centre (mnemonic PAP: Pons Pneumotaxic center Apneustic center)

* Medulla: Pre-Botzinger complex

* Dorsal respiratory group

* Ventral respiratory group

5th nerve nuclei: the motor nucleus is situated medially and sensory nucleus laterally in the pons. The spinal trigeminal nucleus is a caudal continuation of the main sensory nucleus, extending from the mid pons through the medulla to the cervical spinal cord.

The 6th nerve nucleus is found near the midline in the floor of the fourth ventricle just lateral to the medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Infer the extent of the thyroid gland from the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A to D

The thyroid gland extends from vertebral levels C5 to T1. This corresponds to A to D in the given image.

Levels with respect to the tracheal rings and vertebra

Lobes of the thyroid gland

Thyroid cartilage to 4th tracheal ring

Vertebral level- C5-T1

Isthmus of the thyroid gland

Opposite 2nd and 3rd tracheal rings

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: State the action of the muscle marked in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Abduction of shoulder joint

The muscle marked in the given image is supraspinatus and the action of the muscle is abduction of the shoulder joint. It steadies the head of the humerus during movements, and abducts the shoulder joint from 0-15°

Supraspinatus is a part of the rotator interval, an area between the superior edge of the subscapularis and the anterior edge of supraspinatus with the coracoid as the medial boundary of the interval.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The image shows the cross-section of the abdominal cavity. Identify the structure marked 'A'.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Descending aorta

In the given image, the structure marked 'A' corresponds to the descending aorta.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the vertebral level of the abdominal plane labeled 2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Upper border of L3

The structure marked '2' in the given image is the subcostal plane. It is at the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

The subcostal plane is an anatomical reference plane used in clinical and surgical practice. It is defined as a horizontal plane passing through the lower border of the 10th costal cartilage bilaterally. The 10th costal cartilage corresponds approximately to the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

The costal cartilages are extensions of the ribs that articulate with the sternum anteriorly. The 10th costal cartilage is the cartilage of the 10th rib.

In the given image, structure 2 represents the subcostal plane, which corresponds to the level of the lower border of the 10th costal cartilage. Since the 10th costal cartilage is at the level of the upper border of L3, it indicates that the subcostal plane is also at the level of the upper border of L3.

Other options: As mentioned earlier, the subcostal plane is positioned at the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3), not L1 or L2 or L4.

Pearl PF0627: Abdominal planes and their landmarks

Planes that divide the abdomen into 9 regions

* Horizontal planes

* L3 - Subcostal plane (between 10th costal cartilages). Corresponds to the 3rd part of the duodenum

* L5 - Transtubercular plane (between tubercles of iliac crests). Corresponds to the origin of Inferior vena cava.

* Vertical planes (Paramedian or lateral planes)

* Mid-clavicular point to mid-inguinal point on both sides

The nine regions of the abdomen include:

* Left hypochondriac, Epigastric, Right hypochondriac

* Left lumbar, Umbilical (Central), Right lumbar

* Left iliac, Hypogastric (Suprapubic), Right iliac

Other planes and angles in the abdomen

* Transpyloric (Addison's) plane passes midway between the suprasternal notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

* The supracristal plane passing through the highest point of the iliac crest on both sides. Posteriorly, it corresponds to the level of the L4 body or L4/5 disc and its spinous process. It is an important landmark when performing a lumbar puncture or spinal injection. The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta lies approximately in this plane.

* The plane of the pubic crest passes through the upper border of the pubic symphysis. When supine, this plane intersects the tip of the coccyx and the femoral head.

* Renal angle is the angle between the 12th rib and the outer border of Erector spinae muscle. The lower border of normal kidneys may occasionally be felt here.

* Lumbar triangle (of Petit) is marked below by the iliac crest, anteriorly by external oblique and posteriorly by latissimus dorsi. Lumbar herniation can occur here.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which among the following aids in supination and pronation of the forearm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pivot joint

Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot joints (synovial) and are involved in pronation and supination movements of the forearm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following dural venous sinuses receives the great cerebral vein of Galen as its tributary?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B

The venous sinus marked with 'B' in the given image is the straight sinus. The great cerebral vein of Galen drains into the straight sinus.

The straight sinus is a continuation of the inferior sagittal sinus. It lies in the junction of the falx cerebri with tentorium cerebelli. The straight sinus further drains into one of the transverse sinuses (mostly the left).

Other options

A - Superior sagittal sinus

C - Superior petrosal sinus

D - Sigmoid sinus

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient not able to chew the food and food stuck between cheeks and teeth. Which muscle weakness is associated with this clinical condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Buccinator

The correct answer is Buccinator.

Buccinator compresses the cheek against the teeth, preventing food from accumulating in the vestibule during mastication.

Weakness leads to food getting trapped between cheek and teeth, a classic sign seen in facial nerve palsy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with complaints of numbness over the mandibular region. Injury to which of the following nerves best explains this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inferior alveolar nerve

The inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve, provides sensory innervation to the mandibular teeth and, through its terminal mental nerve, supplies sensation to the chin, lower lip, and skin over the mandibular region. Injury to this nerve causes numbness of the lower lip, chin, and mandibular area.

Why not the other options?

• A. Auriculotemporal nerve: Supplies sensation to the temporal region, external ear, and TMJ.
• B. Masseteric nerve: A motor nerve supplying the masseter muscle.
• D. Lingual nerve: Provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and floor of the mouth, not the skin over the mandible.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with numbness over the chin and lower lip. Which nerve is most likely involved in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mental nerve

The mental nerve is the terminal sensory branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). It exits the skull through the mental foramen and provides cutaneous sensation to the chin, lower lip, and labial mucosa. Injury to the mental nerve results in numbness of the chin and lower lip without affecting the mandibular teeth.

Why not the other options?

• A. Great auricular nerve: Supplies the skin over the parotid region, angle of the mandible, and ear.
• C. Inferior alveolar nerve: Supplies the mandibular teeth and gives rise to the mental nerve; a lesion proximal to the mental foramen also causes dental sensory loss.
• D. Lingual nerve: Provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and floor of the mouth.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling below the left earlobe and is experiencing pain. What is the most likely cause of this pain?
options: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Greater auricular nerve

Swelling below the earlobe commonly involves the parotid region, where pain sensation is carried by the greater auricular nerve (C2–C3).

This nerve supplies the skin over the parotid gland, angle of mandible, and lower auricle.

Facial nerve is motor, auriculotemporal nerve carries secretomotor fibers and sensory supply to temple, and fascia itself is not a pain-transmitting structure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A student got his jaw locked while yawning. Identify the muscle attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lateral pterygoid

The lateral pterygoid muscle inserts into the neck of mandible and the articular disc of the TMJ, controlling disc movement during mouth opening.

Excessive contraction during yawning can displace the disc, leading to jaw locking.

Temporalis, medial pterygoid, and masseter attach to the mandible but do not insert into the articular disc.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A woman develops choking, hoarseness of voice, and a foreign body sensation in the throat while eating fish. Examination reveals a fish bone lodged in the pyriform fossa. Which nerve is primarily responsible for mediating this irritation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Internal branch of SLN

The correct answer is Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN).

The pyriform fossa mucosa is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve, which carries sensory fibres above the vocal cords.

Irritation here causes foreign body sensation, choking, and cough reflex.

Glossopharyngeal nerve supplies oropharynx, while RLN and external SLN are motor and do not mediate this sensory irritation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: After parotidectomy, lower lip paralysis was seen in a patient. Which of the following part of facial nerve was involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cervical branch of facial nerve

The cervical branch of the facial nerve is responsible for innervating the platysma muscle, which is crucial for controlling lower lip movements. During a parotidectomy, if this branch is damaged, it can lead to paralysis of the lower lip.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ansa cervicalis supplies all of the following muscles, except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thyrohyoid

The ansa cervicalis (C1–C3) is a loop of the cervical plexus that supplies most of the infrahyoid (strap) muscles, including the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and both bellies of the omohyoid.

The thyrohyoid is the exception, as it is supplied by C1 fibers traveling with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), not by the ansa cervicalis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sternothyroid: Supplied by the ansa cervicalis.
• B. Omohyoid: Supplied by the ansa cervicalis.
• C. Sternohyoid: Supplied by the ansa cervicalis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During resection of the submandibular gland along with its duct, which of the following structure lying below the duct is most likely to be injured during the procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypoglossal nerve

During submandibular gland resection with removal of the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct), the nerve most at risk below the duct is the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

During submandibular gland surgery, the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) runs below and deep to the submandibular duct (on the hyoglossus muscle) and is at risk of injury during deep dissection. The lingual nerve has a characteristic lateral-below-medial (LBM) relationship with the duct and is also at risk. Injury to the hypoglossal nerve results in ipsilateral tongue paralysis with deviation toward the side of the lesion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury to which nerve results in absent gag reflex?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IX & X

The afferent limb of the gag reflex is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) from the posterior pharynx.

The efferent limb is carried by the vagus nerve (CN X) supplying the pharyngeal muscles.

Injury to either nerve can abolish the gag reflex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Paralysis of which muscle causes ptosis in Horner syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Superior tarsal muscle

Ptosis in Horner syndrome is due to paralysis of the superior tarsal (Müller’s) muscle, which is a sympathetically innervated smooth muscle.

This causes mild ptosis, unlike complete ptosis from levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) palsy.

Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelid, and orbitalis has no role in eyelid elevation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A chronic tobacco consumer went to the dental clinic with bleeding lesions on the tongue and was diagnosed with carcinoma of the tongue. Which of the papillae does not have taste buds?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Filiform

Filiform papillae are most numerous and have a mechanical role, lacking taste buds and often keratinized.

Circumvallate, foliate, and fungiform papillae contain taste buds and are involved in gustation, making them clinically relevant in tongue carcinomas affecting taste.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Longitudinal growth of the bone is affected from fracture at:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Growth plate

Longitudinal growth of long bones occurs at the epiphyseal (growth) plate, where cartilage proliferation and ossification take place.

Fracture or damage to this plate in growing children can cause growth arrest or limb length discrepancy.

Epiphysis, metaphysis, and diaphysis do not directly mediate longitudinal growth.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match the following part of GIT with their histologic findings: GIT: 1. Oesophagus 2. Transverse colon 3. Duodenum 4. Terminal ileum Histology: a. Taenia coli and haustrations b. Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium c. Peyer’s patches and mucus-secreting goblet cells d. Villi and submucosal glands
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c

Each segment of the gastrointestinal tract has characteristic histological features that reflect its specialized function. Recognizing these hallmark findings is essential for identifying GIT sections in histology.

Correct Match:

• 1. Oesophagus → b. non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium
• 2. Transverse colon → a. Taenia coli and haustrations
• 3. Duodenum → d. Villi and submucosal (Brunner’s) glands
• 4. Terminal ileum → c. Peyer’s patches and mucus-secreting goblet cells

Why not the other options?

• Oesophagus does not have villi or Brunner’s glands.
• Colon lacks villi and Peyer’s patches; it is identified by taenia coli, haustra, and abundant goblet cells.
• Duodenum is distinguished by Brunner’s glands in the submucosa.
• Terminal ileum contains Peyer’s patches, which are aggregated lymphoid follicles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which secondary ossification center of the femur is the first to fuse with the shaft?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lesser trochanter

The lesser trochanter is the first secondary ossification center of the femur to fuse with the shaft, typically fusing around 16–17 years of age. Knowledge of the appearance and fusion of femoral ossification centers is important in pediatric radiology, forensic age estimation, and orthopedics.

Order of Fusion of Femoral Secondary Ossification Centers

1. Lesser trochanter → first to fuse
2. Greater trochanter
3. Femoral head
4. Distal femoral epiphysis → last to fuse

Why Not the Other Options?

• Greater trochanter: Fuses later than the lesser trochanter.
• Femoral head: Fusion occurs after the trochanters.
• Distal end of femur: Although it is the first ossification center to appear (near birth), it is among the last epiphyses to fuse with the shaft.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 12-year-old presented with fever and difficulty swallowing. He had swelling in the marked region and was advised to undergo surgery. Post-surgery the gauze continued to soak with blood. Which of the following vessels must have been injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paratonsillar vein

The given image is a cadaveric specimen with the arrow pointing towards, the tonsillar fossa, and the given clinical vignette is suggestive of tonsillitis. Post tonsillectomy hemorrhage is commonly venous in origin, from the paratonsillar/ external palatine vein.

Torrential hemorrhage can be due to injury to an aberrantly large or aberrantly placed tonsillar arterial branch of the facial artery.

Blood supply of the tonsils:

Arterial supply:

• The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the main supply.
• Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery.
• Ascending pharyngeal branch of the external carotid artery.
• Dorsal lingual branches of the lingual artery.
• Descending palatine branches of the maxillary artery.

Venous supply:

• Veins from the tonsils drain into paratonsillar vein which joins the common facial vein and pharyngeal venous plexus.

Types of Hemorrhage seen during/post tonsillectomy:

• Primary hemorrhage:

• Occurs during surgery due to injury to blood vessels.
• Can be controlled by pressure, ligation, or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels.

• Reactionary hemorrhage:

• It occurs within 24 hours of surgery.
• It may be due to dislodgement of the clot, slippage of ligature, or return of blood pressure to normal.
• It is managed by removal of clot and application of pressure or vasoconstrictor.
• If not controlled the patient is anesthetized and hemorrhage is managed by re-exploration.

• Secondary hemorrhage:

• It occurs between 24 hours to 10 days (most common between 5th to 8th postoperative days).
• It is due to sepsis and premature separation of the membrane.
• The patient is started on IV antibiotics and if not controlled, general anesthesia is given and the bleeding vessel is electrocoagulated or ligated.

The images below summarize the blood supply to the tonsils and the relations of the tonsillar bed respectively.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presented with symptoms of inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits. He was also not able to hold a piece of paper between his fingers. What is the likely site of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C

The given clinical situation with a positive card test and an inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits, suggests an ulnar nerve injury. The most likely site of injury would thus be medial epicondyle: site C

Injury at the medial epicondyle damages the ulnar nerve, leading to paralysis of flexor carpi ulnaris (loss of ulnar deviation) and medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (loss of distal interphalangeal joint flexion). It leads to hypothenar paralysis (lead to atrophy) and sensory loss. Also, flexor digitorum superficialis (supplied by median nerve) and extensor digitorum (supplied by the radial nerve) are still functional. Hence complete paralysis of the 3rd and 4th digits is not seen.  The positive card test is due to the weakness of palmar interossei leading to loss of adduction.

Ulnar nerve branches and supply:

Superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis, skin on the palmar surface of medial 1½ fingers. The deep branch runs within the concavity of deep palmar arch and supplies all intrinsic muscles of the hand (except first 2 lumbricals and thenar muscles).

Injury to the Ulnar nerve:

High lesion
(Elbow)
Low lesion
(Wrist)

Site of injury

Fracture/dislocation of the medial epicondyle

Cubital tunnel syndrome

Compression between the two heads of FCU

Tardy ulnar nerve palsy (Valgus deformity)

Wrist laceration/ slashing

Motor loss

Claw-hand deformity

Hypothenar & interosseous wasting

Loss of:

• Abduction & adduction of fingers
(Card test - Positive)
• Adduction of thumb
(Froment sign- Positive)
• Flexion of MCP joints

Weakness of wrist flexion (radial deviation)

Claw-hand deformity
(more pronounced)

Hypothenar & interosseous wasting
