Other options :

Option A - Diagonal artery supplies the left ventricle.

Option B - Right marginal artery supplies the right ventricle and the apex of the heart.

Option D - Left circumflex artery supplies the left atrium and the left ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The cranial component of the neural crest cells leads to the formation of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Conotruncal septum

The cranial component of neural crest cells (NCC) leads to the formation of Conotruncal septum.

The conotruncal septum is also known as the aortopulmonary septum. The formation of the aortopulmonary septum in the truncus arteriosus divides the outflow channel of the heart into the ventral aorta and the pulmonary trunk. Persistent truncus arteriosus results when the conotruncal ridges fail to form.

The development of the heart begins in the third week of embryogenesis with the formation of the cardiogenic mesoderm. The heart tube forms through fusion of paired endocardial tubes, which then undergo looping and septation to establish the four chambers. By the end of the eighth week, the heart achieves its definitive structure, with separate atria, ventricles, and major vessels.

The heart develops from mesodermal origins, with different parts deriving from specific embryonic structures:

• First Heart Field (Primary Heart Field): Forms the left ventricle and part of the atria.
• Second Heart Field: Contributes to the right ventricle, outflow tract (conus arteriosus and truncus arteriosus), and part of the atria.
• Neural Crest Cells: Contribute to the septation of the outflow tract and the formation of the aorticopulmonary septum.
• Proepicardium (Epicardial Cells): Forms the epicardium and contributes to coronary vessels.
• Sinus Venosus: Forms part of the right atrium (sinus venarum) and the coronary sinus.
• Endocardial Cushions: Form the atrioventricular valves and contribute to septation.

Other options:

Option A: SA node is derived from the primary heart field - sinus venosus.

Option B: AV cushions are derived from adjacent endocardial cells. The endocardial cells along with the epicardium and mesenchyme, form the AV cushions.

Option D: Chordae tendineae are formed from mesenchymal tissue within the heart.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The marked structure serves as a surface landmark for which anatomical structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stem of the lateral sulcus

The marked structure indicates the pterion and it serves as a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus.

The frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet at the pterion. It is a landmark for the stem of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), the most prominent sulcus of the cerebral hemisphere. It separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe. Deep to the lateral sulcus lies the insular cortex.

Pterion marks as a surface landmark for the following structures:

• Middle meningeal artery and vein: fractures in this area can rupture the middle meningeal artery, leading to an epidural hematoma.
• Broca’s area: Located in the dominant hemisphere (usually left) in the inferior frontal gyrus, it lies in proximity to the pterion
• The insular cortex and parts of the basal ganglia, such as the putamen, are located deep to the pterion, beneath the lateral sulcus.
• Stem of the lateral sulcus, also called the Sylvian fissure. It houses the middle cerebral artery and its branches, playing a crucial role in brain vascularization and cortical organization.

During surgeries, the pterion is a common site for trephining (making a hole in the skull).

Other Options:

Option A: The pineal gland is located in the posterior aspect of the cranial fossa in the brain. It is located deep in the brain, near the midline.

Option B: Wenicke's area is in the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant cerebral hemisphere. It is found in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus.

Option D: The internal carotid artery siphon is a part of the internal carotid artery's course. Characterized by its S-shaped curvature as it traverses the cavernous sinus and enters the cranial cavity. This configuration helps dissipate pulsatile energy, reducing stress on cerebral vessels, and allows adaptability to cranial movements while maintaining cerebral perfusion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve related to the area marked in the picture has its root value from?
options: Dorsal root ganglia of T1 and T2
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ventral horn of C4

The above is an image of the left lung with the arrow pointing at the nerve passing anterior to the left hilum. The phrenic nerve passes in front of the left hilum and has its root value from the ventral horn of C4.

In the given image, the left lung is identified by the vertical sequence of structures at the left hilum - pulmonary artery, principal (hyparterial) bronchus, and inferior pulmonary vein. The image also shows an oblique fissure dividing the lung into superior and inferior lobes.

The phrenic nerve, originating from the cervical nerves C3–C5, is a mixed nerve that carries motor fibres to the diaphragm and sensory fibres from the mediastinal pleura, pericardium, and a portion of the peritoneum.

The course of the left phrenic nerve:

Cervical region - both phrenic nerves pass, Anterior to scalenus anterior muscle
Posterior to sternocleidomastoid and inferior belly of omohyoid
Posterior to internal jugular vein, transverse cervical artery, and suprascapular artery
Posterior to the thoracic duct on the left

Root of the neck - It lies medial to the trunks of the brachial plexus in the neck. At the root of the neck, it runs anterior to the second part of the subclavian artery and posterior to the subclavian vein.

Thorax - The phrenic nerve enters the thorax by crossing medially in front of the internal thoracic artery. Within the thorax, the phrenic nerve descends anterior to the pulmonary hilum between the fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura, accompanied by the pericardiacophrenic vessels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The spinal sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve has 2nd order neurons to carry which sensation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pain

The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensory input from the face, as well as motor functions such as chewing. Its sensory pathway involves three branches: the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions. The first-order neurons for each division originate from different sensory ganglia:

1.Ophthalmic Division (V1):
First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion (also called the semilunar or Gasserian ganglion).

2. Maxillary Division (V2):
First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

3. Mandibular Division (V3):
First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

These first-order neurons carry sensory information from the face to the brainstem. Upon entering the brainstem, the fibers synapse with second-order neurons in specific nuclei:

1. Principal Sensory Nucleus (Main Sensory Nucleus):
a.Receives input from all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve.
b.Located in the pons.
c.Second-order neurons here carry discriminative touch and proprioceptive information.

2. Spinal Trigeminal Nucleus (Spinal Nucleus of Trigeminal):
a.Receives input mainly from the maxillary and mandibular divisions.
b.Located in the medulla.
c.Second-order neurons here carry pain and temperature sensations.

After synapsing in these nuclei, the sensory information is further relayed to higher brain centers for processing and perception.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure marked as 'X' in image A has a direct connection with which of the following structures marked in image B?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1

Image A shows a section of the cerebellum and image B shows a section of the midbrain. The structure labeled as 'X' represents the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum, which has a direct connection with the structure marked as '1', which is the red nucleus.

The dentate nucleus is the largest of the cerebellar nuclei. It has the shape of a crumpled bag with the opening facing medially. The interior of the bag is filled with white matter made up of efferent fibers that leave the nucleus through the opening to form a large part of the superior cerebellar peduncle.

The efferent pathways from the dentate nucleus connect to the thalamus and the red nucleus, via the dentato- rubro -thalamic pathway.

Other structures in the image B :

2 - Represents superior colliculus, which receives afferents from the retina and the occipital cortex.

3 - Represents substantia nigra, which receives afferents mainly from the caudate nucleus

4 - Represents the crus cerebri, which contains fibers from the cerebral cortex.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What are the structures passing between the muscles marked as 1 and 2?
options: Recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior thyroid vessels
Internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glossopharyngeal nerve and stylopharyngeus muscle

The structures passing in between the superior constrictor muscle ( structure 1 ) and middle constrictor muscle ( structure 2) are glossopharyngeal nerve and stylopharyngeus muscle.

The structures passing in between pharyngeal muscles are as follows:

1. Sinus of Morgagni - It is a semilunar space that exists between the upper concave border of the superior constrictor and the skull base. It is closed off by the upper sturdy portion of the pharyngobasilar fascia. Structures passing through this space include:
a. The auditory tube
b. The levator veli palatini muscle (Option C)
c. The ascending palatine artery
d. Palatine branch of the ascending pharyngeal artery.

2. Between the superior and middle constrictors -  the stylopharyngeus muscle and the glossopharyngeal nerve.

3. Between the middle and inferior constrictors -the internal laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal vessels penetrate the thyrohyoid membrane (Option B).

4.  Between the lower border of the inferior constrictor and the esophagus - The recurrent laryngeal nerve and the inferior laryngeal vessels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What level of the vertebral column does the given cross-sectional image correspond to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. T10

The above cross-sectional picture is denoted to be T10 because ,

At the level of the T10 vertebra, we observe:

• The esophagus enters the abdomen through the diaphragm (at the level of T10), connecting shortly afterward to the stomach at the cardiac orifice. In this image, the esophagus is positioned slightly left to the midline and is surrounded by the crura of the diaphragm.
• Adipose tissue around the stomach representing greater omentum
• Nearby structures include the spleen posteriorly, and the right and anterior left lobes of the liver.
• The inferior vena cava (IVC), slightly right of midline, is mostly surrounded by the liver.
• The descending aorta, azygos vein, and thoracic duct are within the thorax.
• A small portion of the left and right lung are still visible.
• Small cross-sectional area of the sternum and the costal cartilages of the 7th ribs. The 7th ribs are the last true ribs with costal cartilages articulating with the sternum
• Predominance of thoracic and upper limb musculature.
• Diaphragm encircling the abdominal cavity, still positioned deep to the thoracic wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not a derivative of neural crest cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinal pigment epithelium

Retinal pigment epithelium is not a derivative of neural crest cells.

Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is derived from the neuroectoderm. The RPE develops from the outer layer of the optic cup, a structure that arises from the neural tube (neuroectodermal origin), not from neural crest cells.

Neural crest cells are a group of cells that migrate during embryonic development and give rise to various structures, including parts of the nervous system, face, and heart.

Neural crest cells (NCC) are present adjacent to the neural tube and are sometimes referred to as the fourth germ layer. It contributes to the formation of many organs and tissues:

In the trunk region, they form:

• Melanocytes (Option D)
• Sensory ganglia
• Sympathetic and enteric neurons
• Schwann cells
• Adrenal medulla cells

In the cranial region, they contribute to the:

• Craniofacial skeleton
• Neurons for cranial ganglia-Ciliary ganglion  (Option C)
• Ciliary muscles  (Option A)
• Satellite glial cells
• Melanocytes

Some of the other neural crest derivatives are:

• C cells of the thyroid gland
• Conotruncal septum in the heart
• Odontoblasts
• Smooth muscle cells to blood vessels to the face and forebrain.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tail of caudate nucleus

The tail of the caudate nucleus is not seen on the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. It is present on the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.

The inferior horn is the largest compartment of the lateral ventricle and extends up to 2.5 cm from the temporal pole. The relations are:

Roof - Tapetum of corpus callosum laterally and tail of caudate nucleus medially.

Floor (lateral to medial) - Collateral eminence produced by collateral fissure, hippocampus.

The floor of the temporal horn consists of the hippocampus medially and the collateral eminence, formed by the infolding of the collateral sulcus, laterally. The inferior part of the choroidal fissure, located between the fimbria of the fornix and the inferolateral aspect of the thalamus, lies in the medial wall.

The lateral ventricle is divided into the body and 3 horns. The locations of the parts are:

• Body - parietal lobe
• Anterior horn - frontal lobe
• Posterior horn - occipital lobe
• Inferior horn - temporal lobe.

The anterior horn extends from the genu of the corpus callosum up to the interventricular foramen. The relations of the anterior horn are:

• Anteriorly - Genu and rostrum of the corpus callosum
• Roof - Anterior part of the body of the corpus callosum
• Floor and lateral wall - Caudate nucleus
• Medial wall - Septum pellucidum and anterior column of fornix

The body or central part extends from the interventricular foramen to the splenium of the corpus callosum. The relations of the body are:

• Roof - Body of the corpus callosum
• Medial wall - Septum pellucidum
• Floor (from lateral to medial) - Caudate nucleus, stria terminalis, thalamostriate vein, thalamus, choroid plexus, and body of the fornix

The posterior horn extends from the splenium to the occipital pole. The relations are:

• Roof and lateral wall - Tapetum of corpus callosum
• Medial wall - Forceps major and calcar avis (calcarine sulcus

Note: There is no lateral wall for the lateral ventricle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endoderm

Endoderm is the first to be formed by the migration of the epiblast along the primitive streak.

Gastrulation is when the single-layered blastula reorganizes into a multi-layered structure called the gastrula. This process establishes the three primary germ layers that give rise to all tissues and organs of the body. During gastrulation, epiblast cells migrate through the primitive streak to form the three germ layers: endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm.

Cells from the epiblast migrate inward (invagination) through the primitive streak.

The first group of migrating epiblast cells replaces the hypoblast to form the definitive endoderm. The endoderm gives rise to structures like the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and lungs.

Subsequent migrating cells spread between the epiblast and the newly formed endoderm to create the mesoderm, which forms structures like muscles, bones, and the cardiovascular system.

Remaining epiblast cells that do not migrate through the primitive streak form the ectoderm, which gives rise to the epidermis and the nervous system.

Other Options:

Option B: Cardiac Mesoderm: The mesoderm forms after the endoderm and differentiates later into subtypes, including the cardiac mesoderm.

Option C: Epidermis: The epidermis arises from the ectoderm, which forms after both the endoderm and mesoderm.

Option D: Neural Groove: The neural groove is part of the ectoderm and forms during neurulation, which occurs much later than the formation of the endoderm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following joints is not formed by the structure shown in the picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Synchondrosis

The provided image depicts a thoracic vertebra, which does not participate in forming a synchondrosis-type joint. The example for a synchondrosis is the costochondral joint formed between the ribs and the costal cartilage.

A vertebral bone participates in the following joints :

1. Intervertebral joint - secondary cartilaginous joint ( symphysis type )
2. Costovertebral joint - plane synovial joint
3. costotransverse  joint - plane synovial joint
4. Facet joints or zygapophysial joints - synovial joint

A syndesmosis is a type of complex fibrous joint between two bones connected by ligaments and a strong membrane[1] with slight movement allowed.The vertebra is connected by a anterior and posterior ligament where some degree of syndesmosis type of joint is seen.

Structurally, joints are classified as fibrous joints, cartilaginous joints, and synovial joints.

Type
Subtypes

Fibrous joints

• Sutures
• Syndesmosis
• Gomphosis

Cartilaginous joints

• Primary cartilaginous (synchondrosis)
• Secondary cartilaginous (symphysis)

Synovial joints

• Ball-and-socket or spheroidal joints
• Sellar or saddle joints
• Condylar or bicondylar joints
• Ellipsoid joints
• Hinge joints
• Pivot or trochoid joints
• Plane joints

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following marked areas in the histopathological specimen shows calcification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given specimen is that of an epiphyseal cartilage, where zone 3 corresponds to the zone of calcification.

Epiphyseal cartilage is divided into five zones :

• The resting zone consists of hyaline cartilage without morphological changes in the cells (option 1)
• In the proliferative zone, chondrocytes divide rapidly and form columns of stacked cells parallel to the long axis of the bone (option 2)
• The hypertrophic cartilage zone contains large chondrocytes whose cytoplasm has accumulated glycogen. The resorbed matrix is reduced to thin septa between the chondrocytes.
• Simultaneous with the death of chondrocytes in the calcified cartilage zone, the thin septa of cartilage matrix become calcified by the deposit of hydroxyapatite.
• In the ossification zone, endochondral bone tissue appears (option 4). Blood capillaries and osteoprogenitor cells formed by mitosis of cells originating from the periosteum invade the cavities left by the chondrocytes. The osteoprogenitor cells form osteoblasts, which are distributed in a discontinuous layer over the septa of the calcified cartilage matrix. Ultimately, the osteoblasts deposit bone matrix over the three-dimensional calcified cartilage matrix.

The epiphyseal cartilage is responsible for the growth in the length of bone and it disappears in adults, which is why bone growth ceases in adulthood.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true concerning the anatomy of the breast?
options: Inner quadrants contain most breast tissue
Ligaments of cooper are found only in lower quadrants
Tail of Spence extends across anterior axillary fold
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tail of Spence extends across anterior axillary fold

The tail of Spence extends across the anterior axillary fold and is a small extension of the upper lateral quadrant of the breast.

The breast lies in the superficial fascia of the pectoral region. It is divided into four quadrants, i.e. upper medial, upper lateral, lower medial and lower lateral.

Vertically, it extends from the second to the sixth ribs. Horizontally, it extends from the lateral border of the sternum to the midaxillary line. A small extension of the upper lateral quadrant, called the axillary tail of Spence, passes through an opening in the deep fascia and lies in the axilla. The opening is called the foramen of Langer.

The breast lies on the deep pectoral fascia covering the pectoralis major and serratus anterior superiorly, the external abdominal oblique and its aponeurosis inferiorly, and the clavipectoral fascia laterally. Fibrous strands or sheets consisting of condensations of connective tissue extend between the posterior lamina of the superficial fascia and the dermis. These suspensory ligaments (retinacula or Cooper’s ligaments) are often well-developed in the superior parts of the breast and support the breast tissue, helping to minimize drooping.

The breasts normally comprise up to 20 discrete lobes that contain ductal-glandular tissue consisting of branching ducts and terminal secretory lobules in a connective tissue stroma. Each lobe is derived by branching from one central lactiferous duct in the nipple. The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU or lobule) is the functional milk secretory component of the breast.

The upper outer quadrant of the breast contains a greater volume of tissue than the other quadrants. This is the reason for the majority of the carcinomas arising in the upper outer quadrant.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 32-year-old man sustains a fracture of the neck of the fibula following a road traffic accident. A few days later, he develops foot drop with weakness of dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot. Sensory examination reveals loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot and the lateral aspect of the leg. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Common peroneal nerve

The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds superficially around the neck of the fibula, making it the most commonly injured nerve in fibular neck fractures. Injury results in paralysis of both the deep and superficial peroneal nerves. The patient has the classical features of common peroneal nerve injury:

• Fracture of the neck of the fibula (common site of injury)
• Foot drop due to paralysis of the anterior compartment (loss of dorsiflexion)
• Weak eversion due to paralysis of the lateral compartment
• Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral aspect of the leg

Why not the other options?

• A. Tibial nerve: Injury causes loss of plantar flexion, inability to stand on tiptoes, and sensory loss over the sole of the foot, not foot drop.
• B. Superficial peroneal nerve: Causes weak eversion and sensory loss over most of the dorsum of the foot, but dorsiflexion is preserved.
• C. Deep peroneal nerve: Causes foot drop due to loss of dorsiflexion and sensory loss limited to the first dorsal web space, while eversion is largely preserved.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman undergoes a minor pelvic surgery involving dissection along the lateral pelvic wall. During the procedure, a nerve that passes through a canal is inadvertently injured. Postoperatively, she has difficulty in adduction of thigh while walking, along with loss of sensation over the medial aspect of the thigh. Which nerve was most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Obturator nerve

The obturator nerve (L2–L4) arises from the lumbar plexus and exits the pelvis through the obturator canal to supply the adductor muscles of the thigh and provide sensory innervation to the medial aspect of the thigh. It is at risk of injury during pelvic lymph node dissection, gynecologic surgery, and surgery along the lateral pelvic wall.

Why not the other options?

• A. Femoral nerve: Supplies the quadriceps (knee extension) and sensation over the anterior thigh and medial leg; injury causes difficulty climbing stairs and reduced patellar reflex, not isolated loss of thigh adduction.
• B. Sciatic nerve: Supplies the posterior thigh and most muscles below the knee; injury causes foot drop and weakness of knee flexion, not medial thigh sensory loss.
• D. Superior gluteal nerve: Supplies gluteus medius and minimus; injury causes a Trendelenburg gait due to hip abductor weakness.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient is unable to flex the hip and knee following trauma to the anterior thigh. Injury to which of the following muscles is most likely responsible for this combined deficit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sartorius

The sartorius is the only muscle that produces both hip flexion and knee flexion, as it crosses both the hip and knee joints. It originates from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and inserts into the pes anserinus on the medial surface of the proximal tibia. It is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2–L3).

Injury to the sartorius results in weakness of hip flexion, abduction, and lateral rotation, along with knee flexion, producing difficulty assuming the cross-legged (“tailor’s”) position.

Why not the other options?

• B. Rectus femoris: Flexes the hip but extends the knee; injury causes weakness of hip flexion and knee extension, not knee flexion.
• C. Tensor fasciae latae: Flexes, abducts, and medially rotates the hip and stabilizes the knee via the iliotibial tract, but does not flex the knee.
• D. Gracilis: Adducts the thigh and assists in knee flexion, but does not flex the hip.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with an ankle injury following excessive eversion of the foot. Which of the following ligaments is most commonly injured in this type of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Deltoid ligament

The correct answer is Deltoid ligament.

Excessive eversion stresses the medial collateral (deltoid) ligament, making it the ligament most commonly injured in eversion ankle trauma.

ATFL, PTFL, and calcaneofibular ligaments are lateral ligaments typically injured in inversion injuries, not eversion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with loss of sensation on the lateral aspect of the sole. Which of the following nerve roots is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. S1

The lateral aspect of the sole corresponds to the S1 dermatome, supplied via branches of the tibial nerve.

S1 root involvement is classically associated with sensory loss over the lateral foot and sole, often seen in L5–S1 disc pathology.

L4 and L5 supply medial leg and dorsum of foot, while S2 mainly supplies the posterior thigh and perineal region.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with pain along the lateral aspect of the thigh. What is the root value of this nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. L2-L3

Pain along the lateral aspect of the thigh with sensory symptoms indicates involvement of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

This nerve arises from L2–L3 roots, passes under the inguinal ligament near ASIS, and is commonly compressed causing meralgia paresthetica.

It is a purely sensory nerve, with no motor deficit, helping distinguish it from femoral or obturator nerve lesions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient sustains an injury on the lateral aspect of the knee. After a few days, he develops difficulty in walking due to dragging of foot, along with numbness over the upper lateral side of the leg and dorsum of the foot. Which of the following nerves is most commonly injured in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Common peroneal nerve

The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula on the lateral side of the knee, making it highly vulnerable to injury.

Damage causes foot drop due to loss of dorsiflexion (deep peroneal nerve) and sensory loss over the upper lateral leg and dorsum of the foot (superficial peroneal nerve).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient undergoes a surgery involving the lateral part of the pelvis and postoperatively has difficulty in adduction of the thighs. Which of the following nerves is responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obturator nerve

• The obturator nerve (L2–L4) is the primary motor supply to the adductor compartment of the thigh — it innervates adductor longus, adductor brevis, adductor magnus (adductor part), gracilis, and obturator externus. Injury therefore produces weakness of thigh adduction and a characteristic abduction/circumduction gait, along with sensory loss over a small patch of the medial thigh.
• Anatomically, the nerve runs along the lateral wall of the pelvis and exits through the obturator canal, making it vulnerable during pelvic surgery, difficult forceps delivery, or lateral pelvic wall/nodal dissection — matching the "lateral part of pelvis" clue.

Other options:

• B. Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory to the anterolateral thigh (meralgia paresthetica) — no motor deficit.
• C. Femoral nerve supplies the anterior compartment → quadriceps → controls knee extension/hip flexion, not adduction.
• D. Deep peroneal nerve is a leg/foot nerve → foot dorsiflexion; injury causes foot drop, unrelated to thigh adduction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient underwent surgery for the varicose vein. He now complains of sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Saphenous nerve

The saphenous nerve is a pure sensory branch of the femoral nerve supplying the medial aspect of the leg and foot.

It runs alongside the great saphenous vein, making it vulnerable during varicose vein surgery.

Sural nerve supplies the lateral foot, while superficial and deep peroneal nerves supply the dorsum of foot and first web space, respectively.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During examination of a patient with an intern, the professor asks the patient to invert his foot and he points at the prominent tendon behind the medial malleolus. Which is the tendon being pointed at here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tibialis posterior

The tibialis posterior tendon passes behind the medial malleolus and is the chief inverter of the foot.

It also supports the medial longitudinal arch, making its tendon prominent during inversion.

Tibialis anterior and extensor tendons lie anterior to the ankle joint, not behind the medial malleolus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery is used for AV shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis and is present behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendon calcaneus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Posterior tibial artery

The posterior tibial artery runs behind the medial malleolus, approximately 2.5 cm anterior to the tendon calcaneus, making it easily accessible.

It is commonly used for arteriovenous shunting with the great saphenous vein in haemodialysis.

Peroneal artery lies deep, anterior tibial continues as dorsalis pedis on the dorsum of foot, and dorsalis pedis is not located behind the medial malleolus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve supplies the hybrid muscle partially spared in a patient who presented with sciatica and tender hamstrings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Obturator nerve

The hybrid muscle referred to is the adductor magnus, which has a dual nerve supply—the hamstring (ischiocondylar) part by tibial nerve and the adductor part by obturator nerve.

In sciatica, tibial nerve fibers are affected, but the obturator nerve supply partially spares the muscle.

Thus, residual function of adductor magnus points to obturator nerve involvement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles are supplied by superficial peroneal nerve? 1. Peroneus brevis 2. Peroneus longus 3. Peroneus tertius 4. Extensor hallucis longus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2

The leg is divided into three compartments, each with its specific nerve supply. The lateral compartment of the leg contains only two muscles: peroneus longus and peroneus brevis. Both of these muscles are innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve? Options: 1. Abductor hallucis 2. Flexor digitorum accessorius 3. Flexor hallucis brevis 4. First lumbrical 5. First interossei
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 and 5

The correct answer is 2 and 5.

The lateral plantar nerve supplies most intrinsic sole muscles, including flexor digitorum accessorius (quadratus plantae) and the interossei (via its deep branch).

Abductor hallucis and the first lumbrical are supplied by the medial plantar nerve, while flexor hallucis brevis has dual supply but its medial head is medial plantar—hence excluded here.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which segment of the vertebrae is involved in a patient presenting with pain in the back of the thigh and the leg after lifting heavy weight?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. S1

Pain radiating along the back of the thigh and posterior leg corresponds to the S1 dermatome, classically seen in sciatica.

S1 root involvement commonly occurs with L5–S1 disc herniation, affecting the Achilles reflex.

L4 and L5 involve anterior/anterolateral leg regions, while S2 pain is more perineal/posterior thigh only.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: While walking, the suspended leg is supported by which muscle on other side?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gluteus medius

The correct answer is Gluteus medius.

During walking, gluteus medius of the stance limb stabilizes the pelvis and prevents dropping of the pelvis on the suspended side.

Paralysis causes a positive Trendelenburg sign with pelvic tilt toward the unsupported limb.

Gluteus maximus extends the hip, tensor fascia lata assists abduction, and quadriceps stabilizes the knee, not pelvic support.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Broca’s area is situated in the __________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inferior frontal gyrus

Broca’s area is situated in the inferior frontal gyrus.

Broca’s motor speech area (44,45) is located in the inferior frontal gyrus.

Wernicke’s area (22) is located in the superior temporal gyrus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the thickened nerve marked in the arrow in the image shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Great auricular nerve

The thickened nerve marked with the arrow in the above image is the great auricular nerve and the thickened nerve visible below the great auricular nerve is the transverse cervical nerve.

Nerve thickening in this case is likely to be due to leprosy.

Great auricular nerve:

It is the largest ascending branch of cervical plexus and arises from the second and the third cervical spinal nerves.

It winds over the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and ascends upwards. On reaching the parotid gland it divides into the anterior and posterior branches:

• Anterior branch - supplies the facial skin over the parotid gland and joins the facial nerve in the gland.
• Posterior branch - supplies the skin over the mastoid process, posteroinferior part of the auricle, lobule, and concha.

Clinical considerations:

• Leprosy - Nerve thickening is present. The nerve is palpable over the upper part of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (as seen in the above image)
• Frey's syndrome - An aberrant connection between the auriculotemporal nerve and great auricular nerve causes gustatory sweating.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The hard palate contains ________
options: Keratinised epithelium, submucosa, minor salivary glands
Keratinised epithelium, absent submucosa, no salivary glands
Non-keratinised epithelium, submucosa, minor salivary glands
Non-keratinised epithelium , absent submucosa, minor salivary glands
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratinised epithelium, submucosa, minor salivary glands

The hard palate contains keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, has a submucosa, and contains minor salivary gland. This keratinised stratified squamous epithelium has regional variations and may be orthokeratinised or parakeratinised(found in hard palate and gingiva).

The bony structure of the hard palate is covered by a firmly attached mucosa in the central part. In the lateral parts, the hard palate also has a submucosal layer containing blood vessels. There are minor mucous type salivary glands in the submucosa in the posterior part of the hard palate.

(Note: In the orthokeratinized epithelium the cell nuclei disappear in the keratinized layer, whereas in the parakeratinized epithelium flattened, highly condensed nuclei remain in the cell cytoplasm of the keratinized layer until exfoliation)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The heart starts to beat in the ______week of development.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 4th week

The heart starts to beat in the 4th week of development.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The joint between the attachment of the 8th and 9th rib to the 7th rib is a:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Synovial joint

The interchondral joint between the attachment of the 8th and 9th rib with the 7th rib is a synovial joint.

Joints in the thoracic cavity are of the following types:

• Synarthrosis - structures are connected by a fibrous band of tissue. E.g, 1st sternocostal joint
• Synchondrosis - primary cartilaginous joints. E.g., costochondral joints
• Symphysis - secondary cartilaginous joints. E.g. manubriosternal and xiphisternal joints
• Synovial joints - the presence of these help the thoracic cavity expand during inspiration. E.g.:

• Interchondral joint
• Sternocostal joint
• Costovertebral joint
• Costotransverse joint

Note:

The interchondral joint between the 9th and 10th cartilages is never synovial and sometimes absent.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The nerve of the second branchial arch is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Facial nerve

The facial nerve is the nerve of the 2nd pharyngeal arch.

Each pharyngeal arch is characterized by its own muscular components. The muscular components of each arch have their own cranial nerve. Wherever the muscle cells migrate, they carry their nerve component with them.

The neurons of the 5th, 7th, 9th, and 10th cranial sensory ganglia that supply the pharyngeal arch structures are derived from ectodermal placodes (epipharyngeal placodes) and from the neural crest cells.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure not passing through the aortic opening of the diaphragm is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vagal trunk

The vagal trunk does not pass through the aortic opening of the diaphragm.

It passes through the esophageal opening at the level of T10 vertebra.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ureteric bud develops from:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mesonephric duct

Ureteric bud develops from Mesonephric duct.

• Intermediate mesoderm is a type of mesoderm that is located between the paraxial mesoderm and lateral plate.
• It develops into a part of the urogenital system as well as the reproductive system.
• Intermediate mesoderm develops into Genital ridge and Nephrogenic cord.
• Nephrogenic cord further develops into Pronephros, Mesonephros and Metanephros.
• Ureteric bud develops from mesonephros which later fuses with Mesonephric duct.
• Metanephros proliferates around the ureteric bud which forms metanephric blastema (definitive kidneys).

Structures arising from metanephric blastema and ureteric bud are as follows -

Metanephric blastema

Ureteric bud

Bowmans capsule

Collecting tubules

Proximal convoluted tubule

Renal papillae

Loop of Henle

Calyces

Distal convoluted tubule

Renal pelvis

Ureter

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the function of the muscle marked as A in the image below, at the metacarpophalangeal joint?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flexion

The muscle marked 'A' is lumbricals and they cause flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints.

Lumbricals are intrinsic muscles of the hand that flex the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCP) and extend the interphalangeal joints (PIP & DIP).

They originate from flexor digitorum profundus.

• The lateral two are unipennate, supplied by the median nerve.
• The medial two are bipinnate, supplied by the ulnar nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which among the following is a tensor of vocal cords?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cricothyroid

Cricothyroid is a tensor of vocal cords.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which is the last fontanelle to close?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior

The anterior fontanelle is the last fontanelle to close. It closes at around 18-24 months of age.

Fontanelles of the skull:

Fontanelle
Location
Closes at

Anterior

Between frontal and parietal bones

Junction marked by bregma

18-24 months

Posterior
Sagittal and lambdoid sutures
2-3 months

Sphenoid
Pterion
2-3 months

Mastoid/Posterolateral
Intersection of temporal, parietal, and occipital bones.
6-18 months (average 12 months)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following cranial nerve nuclei is not a part of the special visceral afferent (SVA) column?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trochlear nerve

The trochlear nerve nucleus is a part of the general somatic efferent (GSE) column, not the special visceral afferent column.

The trochlear nerve is a motor nerve that innervates superior oblique muscle in the orbit.

The neurons of the general somatic efferent (GSE) column innervate the extrinsic ocular muscles and muscles of the tongue (III, IV, VI, and XII cranial nerves).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 1st pharyngeal arch gives rise to all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Levator veli palatini

Levator veli palatini is not derived from first pharyngeal arch.

All soft palate muscles including levator veli palatini are derived from the 4th pharyngeal arch and are supplied by vagal plexus.

First pharyngeal arch gives rise to:

• Muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, lateral and medial pterygoids)
• Mylohyoid
• Anterior belly of digastric
• Tensor tympani
• Tensor veli palatini and
• Anterior 2⁄3 of tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following are true about the right coronary artery except _____
options: It's diameter is less than left coronary artery
It arises from the anterior aortic sinus
It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch
Right conal artery is it's first branch
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch

The right coronary artery does not give rise to the circumflex coronary artery.

The right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus (right coronary sinus) of the ascending aorta. It passes anteriorly and descends vertically in the coronary sulcus between the right atrium and the right ventricle. On reaching the inferior margin, it turns posteriorly and continues in the sulcus onto the diaphragmatic surface and the base of the heart.

The diameter of the right coronary artery is less than that of the left coronary artery.

The right conal artery is, usually the first branch of the right coronary artery.

The circumflex coronary artery is a branch of the left coronary artery and is the exclusive supplier to the right bundle branch.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following structures are derived from the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Linea semilunaris

Linea semilunaris is derived from the aponeurosis of the internal oblique muscle.

Pectineal ligament, inguinal ligament and lacunar ligament are derived from the external oblique aponeurosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Area marked in the given image is supplied by dermatome number?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. T10

The marked dermatome which includes the umbilicus is supplied by T10.

The dermatomal distribution of the abdominal region is as follows:

• T7, T8, T9 - supplies skin from the xiphoid process to just above the umbilicus.
• T10 - supplies skin around the umbilicus.
• T11, T12 - supplies skin below the umbilicus upto the suprapubic region.
• L1 - supplies skin around the genitalia and upper medial thigh.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Boundaries of Calot triangle are formed by all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gall bladder

The gall bladder does not form a boundary of the Calot’s triangle.

Calot's triangle is bounded by 3C's:

• Medially – Common hepatic duct
• Inferiorly – Cystic duct
• Superior – Cystic artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cholecysto-vena caval line separates which of the following?
options: Porta hepatis and inferior vena cava
Right and left lobe of liver
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right and left lobe of liver

Cholecysto-vena caval line (Cantlie line) separates right and left lobe of the liver.

Cantlie line is an imaginary line that that divides the liver into 2 planes. It extends from the midpoint of the gallbladder fossa at the inferior margin of the liver back to the midpoint of the inferior vena cava (IVC) and contains the middle hepatic vein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Foot drop is caused by damage to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Common peroneal nerve

Foot drop is caused by damage to the common peroneal nerve.

The common peroneal nerve is a component of the sciatic nerve. In the posterior thigh, it supplies the short head of the biceps femoris. It curves around the neck of the fibula deep to peroneus longus and divides into superficial and deep peroneal nerves.

• The superficial peroneal nerve innervates peroneus longus and peroneus brevis which are the evertors of the foot and to the skin over the dorsal area of the foot except for the first webspace and lateral side of the little toe.
• The deep peroneal nerve innervates all muscles of the anterior compartment which are the dorsiflexors of the foot, extensor digitorum brevis, first two dorsal interossei muscles, and skin between great and second toes.

Hence, injury to the common peroneal nerve will lead to:

• Weakness of dorsiflexion of foot or foot drop
• Loss of eversion
• Loss of extension of toes
• Sensory loss

• Anterior and lateral side of the leg
• Dorsum of the foot including the medial side of the great toe

Th image given below shows the course of common peroneal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked B in the image given below :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fornix

The image given shows a midsagittal section of the brain. The structure marked B is the Fornix.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Nerve supply of the area marked by arrow in the image is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Radial nerve

The area marked in the image is supplied by radial nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The arrow in the image denotes which of the following muscles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extensor carpi radialis longus

The arrow shows extensor carpi radialis longus.

It originates from the distal third of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts at the second metacarpal (radial side). It is innervated by the radial nerve, C6, and C7.

The vascular supply is by radial recurrent artery and it is responsible for the extension and abduction of the wrist joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The movements at the ____________ joint permit a person to look to the right and left.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atlanto-axial

The movements at the atlanto-axial joint allow a person to look left and right.

The atlanto-axial joints include 3 synovial joints:

• Median atlanto-axial joint- The central pivot joint between the dens of the axis and a ring formed by the anterior arch and transverse atlantal ligament
• Lateral atlanto-axial joints- Plain synovial joints between lateral masses of atlas and upper facets of the body of axis

Movements at the atlanto-axial joint almost exclusively is rotation around the axis, which help side-to-side rotation of the head. The normal range of atlanto-axial rotation is about 40°.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the basis for the formation of omphalocele?
options: Physiological hernia failing to go back
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Physiological hernia failing to go back

Omphalocele is protrusion of abdominal contents through the umbilical ring. It is due to failure of physiological hernia to reduce into the abdominal cavity, which results in non-closure of the umbilical ring. .

An omphalocele may contain stomach, liver, and intestines. And these contents are enclosed in a sac.

Omphalocele is usually associated with other congenital anomalies (e.g., trisomy 13, trisomy 18, or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome) and with increased levels of α-fetoprotein.

Note: In gastroschisis, there is an absence of a membranous sac and is paraumbilical.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the nerve supply of the structure marked in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Median nerve

The marked structure is second lumbrical which is supplied by the median nerve.

The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve and the medial two are supplied by the ulnar nerve. Function of these muscles is flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints and extension at both the interphalangeal joints.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which fibre is marked by the arrow in the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Projection

The marked structure is the internal capsule, which is a form of projection fiber.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve passes through the foramen marked in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inferior alveolar nerve

The marked structure is mandibular foramen and inferior alveolar nerve passes through it.

The inferior alveolar nerve (IAN), a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3), it descends behind the lateral pterygoid, at the lower border of the muscle, the nerve passes between the sphenomandibular ligament and the mandibular ramus and enters the mandibular canal via the mandibular foramen
The mandibular foramen is located above the mandibular angle, the opening through which the IAN and the vessels of the mandible pass.
The IAN continues its course through the mandibular canal and then branches off to supply the lower teeth, gums, and lower lip.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is false about skin?
options: Skin accounts for 15% of total body weight
Dermis is made up of type 1 and type 3 collagen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dermis is derived from ectoderm

Dermis is derived from mesoderm and epidermis is derived from ectoderm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding De Quervain’s tenosynovitis?
options: Fingers are held in mild extension
Most common involvement is index finger
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It affects APL and EPB

De Quervain's disease is a stenosing tenosynovitis of the extensor tendons of the first dorsal compartment, namely extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) and abductor pollicis longus (APL).

It is prominent among females, especially pregnant women. Most commonly thumb is involved.

Finkelstein's test: On grasping the patient’s thumb and quickly abducting the hand ulnar ward, the pain over the radial styloid tip is excruciating. It’s the most pathognomonic objective sign but is also seen in other conditions like radial nerve entrapment and arthritis.

Treatment:

• Majority of the patients are treated medically
• Only few require the release of the 1st dorsal compartment which houses the APL and EPB tendons.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following lobes of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Median

The median lobe of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae.

Uvula vesicae is an elevation in the mucous membrane of the urinary bladder, behind the internal urethral orifice. It is often enlarged in benign prostatic hypertrophy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with an enlarged inguinal lymph node. The most likely primary cause is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anal cancer

The most likely primary cause of an enlarged inguinal lymph node is anal cancer.

Lymphatics from the anal canal distal to the dentate line (anal margin) drains into the inguinal lymph nodes. Hence, anal cancer arising distal to dentate line can cause enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. Lymphatics proximal to the dentate line (anal canal) drains into internal iliac lymph nodes through superior rectal lymphatics.

Option A: In testicular cancer, lymphatic spread occurs to the paraaortic lymph nodes.

Option C: In sigmoid colon cancer, lymphatic spread occurs to the regional lymph node and then to the central lymph node.

Option D: In prostate cancer, lymphatic spread occurs to the:

• Lymph nodes beside the internal iliac vein and in the hollow of the sacrum
• External iliac lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with clinical features of ataxia and incoordination. This is due to thrombosis of which artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Superior cerebellar

Thrombosis of the superior cerebellar artery causes cerebellar lesion which presents with ataxia and incoordination.

Blood supply of cerebellum:

• Superior cerebellar artery
• Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
• Anterior inferior cerebellar artery

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with the extension of MCP joint and flexion of IP joints. Which muscle is affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Interossei and lumbricals

The lumbricals and interossei muscles are affected.

The lumbricals and interossei muscles through their attachments to the dorsal digital expansions, cause:

• Flexion of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints
• Extension of the interphalangeal (IP) joints

In cases of ulnar nerve injury, these muscles may get atrophied leading to the extension of MCP joints and flexion of IP joints.

Note: The ulnar nerve innervates all the intrinsic muscles of the hand, except for

• First and second lumbrical
• Abductor pollicis brevis
• Opponens pollicis
• Part of flexor pollicis brevis

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with weakness of the right side of the face with the loss of pain and temperature. Pain and temperature sensation of the left leg is also lost. The lesion is most likely located at?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lateral pons

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of lateral pontine syndrome which occurs due to a lesion located at lateral pons.

Lateral pontine syndrome occurs due to the involvement of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery.

• Ipsilateral manifestations include:

• CN VII: Facial paralysis
• CN V: loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face.
• Vestibular nerve or nucleus: Horizontal and vertical nystagmus, vertigo, nausea, vomiting, oscillopsia.
• Auditory nerve or cochlear nucleus: Deafness, tinnitus.
• Middle cerebellar peduncle: Ataxia of limb and gait.

• Contralateral manifestations include:

• Spinothalamic tract: Loss of pain and temperature sensation over the body.

Medial pontine syndrome occurs due to the involvement of the paramedian branch of the basilar artery.

• Ipsilateral manifestation

• CN VI: Diplopia(lateral rectus muscle paralysis - the affected eye looks downwards and inwards)
• Vestibular nucleus: Nystagmus.
• Middle cerebellar peduncle: Ataxia of limb and gait.

• Contralateral manifestation

• Corticobulbar and corticospinal tract: Paralysis of face, arm, and leg.
• Medial lemniscus: loss of touch and proprioception from the body.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A tumor of the uncinate process of the pancreas affects which of the following vessels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superior mesenteric artery

A tumor of the uncinate process of pancreas affects the superior mesenteric artery.

The superior mesenteric artery arises from the abdominal aorta. It lies first behind the body of the pancreas and then in front of the uncinate process.

Relations of the other parts of pancreas:

Head of pancreas:

• Anterior:

• 1st part of the duodenum
• Origin of the transverse mesocolon

• Posterior:

• Right renal vein
• Right renal artery
• Inferior vena cava
• Common bile duct (which is embedded in the head)
• Right crus of the diaphragm
• Termination of the right gonadal vein

Neck of the pancreas:

• Anterior:

• Lesser sac
• pylorus
• The anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal branch of the gastroduodenal artery

• Posterior:

• Portal vein
• Superior mesenteric vein
• Inferior mesenteric vein (in 1/3rd individuals)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Purkinje cells

The cells marked in the above histological image are Purkinje cells.

Characteristics of Purkinje cells:

• Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum.
• The cells are evenly spaced and are arranged in a single layer.
• A dendrite arises from the neck of each flask-shaped cell, which passes upward to enter the molecular layer, which then branches extensively to form a dendritic tree.
• The axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer to enter the white matter.
• Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex.
• The initial segment of the axon receives synaptic contacts from basket cell axons.
• The main axon terminates in one of the cerebellar or vestibular nuclei.
• Purkinje cells are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter.

Pathological significance:

• Negri bodies in rabies, are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells.
• Loss of Purkinje cells and granule cells is seen in ataxia-telangiectasia.
• In patients with subacute cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells. Some patients show circulating PCA1 antibody (antiYo) against Purkinje cells.
• Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia, and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the sign shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Popeye sign

The sign shown in the above image is the popeye sign, which occurs due to the rupture of the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii.

On flexing the elbow, the characteristic deformity appears due to the bulging of the muscle belly caused by the contraction of the unrestrained muscles.

Option B: Hill-Sachs sign refers to a defect in the postero-lateral surface of the humeral head due to repeated impact against anterior glenoid rim. It is a common complication of Anterior shoulder dislocation.

Option C: Griesinger sign refers to oedema of the postauricular soft tissues overlying the mastoid process as a result of thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein. It is a complication of acute mastoiditis.

Option D: Rising sun sign , also known as Schwartze sign, is the otoscopic sign of active otospongiosis characterised by reddish discolouration of the cochlear promontory.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the type of cartilage shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Elastic cartilage

The above image shows an elastic cartilage.

The elastic cartilage, like the hyaline cartilage, contains individual or small groups of chondrocytes that are surrounded by type II collagen fibrils. However, it differs from hyaline cartilage in that, much of the interterritorial matrix consists of fine yellow elastic fibres containing elastin protein.

On microscopy, elastic cartilage consists of:

• Chondrocytes within lacunae
• Elastic fibres in the matrix
• Perichondrium with outer fibrous layer and the inner cellular layer

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Ligation of common hepatic artery will impair blood supply in:
options: Right gastric and right gastroepiploic artery
Right gastric and left gastric artery
Right gastroepiploic and short gastric vessels
Right gastric and short gastric vessels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right gastric and right gastroepiploic artery

Ligation of the common hepatic artery will cause impairment in the blood supply through its branches i.e right gastric artery and right gastroepiploic artery.

Blood supply of the stomach:

The arterial supply of the stomach is contributed exclusively by the branches of the celiac trunk. They are:

• Left gastric artery - Supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach
• Splenic artery- This further divides into:

• Short gastric arteries- Supplies the fundus of the stomach
• Left gastroepiploic artery- Supplies the greater curvature of the stomach

• Common hepatic artery, which gives the following branches

• Right gastric artery- Supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach
• Gastroduodenal artery- Right gastroepiploic artery arises from this and supplies the greater curvature of the stomach.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Meiosis occurs in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adult ovary

Meiosis occurs in the adult ovary.

Meiosis takes place only in germ cells and results in the formation of haploid gametes. Meiosis requires two cell divisions, meiosis I and meiosis II, to reduce the number of chromosomes to the haploid number of 23.

Option C: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty. Primordial germ cells (PGCs) remain dormant in the testis until puberty. At puberty, PGCs differentiate into spermatogonial stem cells. These spermatogonial stem cells then give rise to spermatogonia which marks the beginning of spermatogenesis.

Options A and D: These are somatic cells that only undergo mitosis and not meiosis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The false statement about fetal circulation is:
options: Anatomical closure of foramen ovale is by 3 to 5 days
Anatomical closure of ductus venosus is by 3 to 7 days
Anatomical closure of ductus arteriosus is by 2 to 3 weeks
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anatomical closure of foramen ovale is by 3 to 5 days

The anatomical closure of the foramen ovale takes 1 month to a year.
