questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling under the left ear lobule and complains of pain. Which of the following structures is the likely cause of the pain?
options: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Greater auricular nerve

The cause of the pain in this patient complaining of pain in the parotid region is likely to be the greater auricular nerve.

The greater auricular nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin overlying the parotid gland and the ear lobule. Pain associated with swelling and inflammation in the parotid region could be transmitted through the greater auricular nerve. The parotid gland is covered by a parotid capsule that is derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Any acute inflammation of the gland such as acute sialadenitis results in pain in the preauricular region. The pain is mainly due to stretching of the capsule resulting in stimulation of the greater auricular nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The facial nerve is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling. The Hitzelberger sign(numbness in the posterosuperior meatal wall of the external auditory canal), associated with facial nerve involvement, is seen in acoustic neuroma and is not the cause of pain in this scenario.

Option D: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia is not the correct answer because the investing layer of deep cervical fascia itself does not transmit pain sensation. The investing layer of deep cervical fascia is a layer of connective tissue that envelops the neck and extends to cover the parotid gland, forming the parotid capsule. While inflammation or swelling in the parotid gland can stretch the capsule and cause pain, the actual transmission of pain sensation is mediated by sensory nerves, such as the greater auricular nerve, which innervates the skin over the parotid gland and the ear lobule.

The greater auricular nerve (Option B) is a more appropriate answer in this context, as it is responsible for carrying the pain sensation from the area of swelling and inflammation in the parotid region.

Option C: The auriculotemporal nerve can cause referred pain due to caries tooth, ulcerative lesions of the oral cavity, temporomandibular joint disorders, and sphenopalatine neuralgia. However, it is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A student had his jaw locked while yawning. Which of the following muscles is attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lateral pterygoid

The muscle that is attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint is the lateral pterygoid.

Lateral pterygoid muscle:

• Origin - Upper head arises from the infratemporal surface and infratemporal crest of the greater wing of the sphenoid bone. The lower head arises from the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate.
• Insertion - It is inserted into the pterygoid fovea, the capsule of the temporomandibular joint, and the articular disc.

The action of lateral pterygoid muscle is depression, protrusion, and side-to-side movement of the jaw.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure(s) in the following histological image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glomerulus

The above histology image shows the glomerulus.

Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries lined by fenestrated endothelium. Blood enters the tuft through an afferent arteriole and leaves it through an efferent arteriole. It is supported by the mesangium containing mesangial cells and a non-cellular mesangial matrix.

The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes.

The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus.

Option A: Leydig cells, also known as interstitial cells of Leydig, are present in the interstitial connective between seminiferous tubules.

The testis contains numerous seminiferous tubules separated by connective tissue in between. Seminiferous tubules are lined by several spermatogonia cells, which produce spermatozoa, and Sertoli (sustentacular) cells, which have a supportive function.

The connective tissue in between the tubules is made up of Leydig cells, collagen fibers, fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, blood vessels, and lymphatics. Leydig cells are large, round, or polyhedral cells with eccentric nuclei. They are lightly stained and often have a foamy appearance. They secrete testosterone upon stimulation by luteinizing hormone from the anterior pituitary.

The image below shows seminiferous tubules and Leydig cells.

Option B: Islets of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers and contain numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. The islet cells are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum.

The islet of Langerhans is mainly composed of three types of cells:

• α or A cells - located peripherally and secrete glucagon
• β or B cells - located centrally and produce insulin
• δ or D cells - scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin

The image given below shows the islets of Langerhans.

Option C: Hassall's corpuscles are small rounded structures present in the medulla of the thymus. Each corpuscle has a central core of degenerated epithelial cells and macrophages surrounded by concentrically arranged epithelial cells. The degenerated cells ultimately give pink staining hyaline mass. The function of the corpuscles of Hassall is still not known.

The image given below shows Hassall's corpuscle.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury at which of the following marked sites causes failure of dorsiflexion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3

The site marked as '3' in the x-ray given above is the neck of the fibula. Injury at this site causes failure of dorsiflexion (foot drop) due to injury to the common fibular nerve (also know as common peroneal nerve)

The common fibular nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st and 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves.

Superficial fibular nerve
Deep fibular nerve

Motor innervation

• Peroneus longus
• Peroneus brevis

• Extensor digitorum longus
• Extensor hallucis longus
• Tibialis anterior
• Peroneus tertius

Sensory innervation

• Lateral aspect of the lower leg
• Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital web-space

• The first interdigital space

Injury to the common peroneal nerve (common fibular nerve) at the level of the neck of the fibula causes foot drop. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion of the foot are lost, while the inversion and plantar flexion are usually preserved. Sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot, including the first web space, is lost. The ankle reflex is usually preserved.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures develops from the structure marked A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Median umbilical ligament

The structure marked A is the allantois. Its distal portion forms the urachus, which in turn gives rise to the median umbilical ligament.

The given image shows an embryo at the end of the third week.

Meckel's diverticulum is a congenital diverticulum arising from anti-mesenteric border of ileum. It is a remnant of the proximal part of the vitelline duct, which is made up of pluripotent cell lining. Meckel's diverticulum may harbor abnormal tissues, containing embryonic remnants of other tissue types, mostly gastric mucosa.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A chronic tobacco consumer went to the dental clinic with bleeding lesions on his tongue and was diagnosed with carcinoma of the tongue. Which of the following papillae, which do not have taste buds, is least likely to be involved in such a cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Filiform

Among the different types of papillae on the tongue, the one that does not have taste buds is the filiform papillae.

Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections that are mainly present on the dorsal part of the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue. The filiform papillae do not contain taste buds. They are covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

Other papillae of the tongue are:

Circumvallate papillae are 8-12 in number which are large cylindrical structures. They form a V-shaped row just in front of the sulcus terminalis. Usually, the entire papillae are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Taste buds are present in the lateral wall of these papillae which surrounds the papillae circumferentially.

Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, and red and are mainly present on the lingual margins and also on the dorsal surface of the tongue. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. They are supplied by the facial nerve.

Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges that are present bilaterally in two zones at the sides of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

A diagrammatic representation of the various papillae of the tongue is given below:

Below is the image showing the various parts of the tongue.

The given image depicts the histology image of filiform papillae:

The given image depicts the histology image of circumvallate papillae:

The given image depicts the histology image of foliate papillae:

The given image depicts the histology image of fungiform papillae:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with sciatica and tenderness in the hamstring muscles. Which nerve supplies the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Obturator nerve

The adductor magnus is the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition.

In sciatica, the sciatic nerve is typically affected, which branches into the tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve. The adductor magnus muscle is an example of a hybrid muscle with dual innervation:

• The adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve.
• The hamstring part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the tibial nerve.

During sciatica, the tibial nerve is often affected, which would impact the hamstring part of the adductor magnus. However, because the adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve, it remains functional and is likely to be spared.

The obturator nerve arises from the anterior division of the ventral rami of L2-L4. Near the obturator foramen, it divides into anterior and posterior branches.

• Anterior division supplies pectineus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, and gracilis
• Posterior division supplies adductor magnus, obturator externus. It also supplies adductor brevis if the muscle is not supplied by the anterior division

The image given below shows the course of the obturator nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The common peroneal nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and can also be affected in sciatica. It is responsible for innervating muscles in the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg.

Option B: The tibial nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and is often affected in sciatica. It supplies the hamstring part of the adductor magnus, which would be impacted during sciatica.

Option C: The femoral nerve is not involved in sciatica. It supplies the quadriceps and other muscles in the anterior compartment of the thigh, and does not innervate the adductor magnus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An absent gag reflex can result from injury to which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ⅸ and Ⅹ

An absent gag reflex can result from injury to the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) and the vagus nerve (X).

The afferent nerve for the gag reflex is the glossopharyngeal nerve, while the efferent nerve consists of both the glossopharyngeal (to the stylopharyngeus muscle) and vagus. Both these nerves pass through the jugular foramen and damage to them may be the cause for loss of gag reflex.

Pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve form the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. These plexes mainly supply the pharynx. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion.

Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve are:

• All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve)
• All the muscles of the pharynx(except the stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve).

The glossopharyngeal nerve is rarely damaged alone. Lesions will result in loss of sensation of the posterior third of the tongue, reduced gag reflex, loss of sensation over the ipsilateral soft palate, etc. Motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland are also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. Sensory supply includes uvula, posterior one-third of the tongue, tympanic cavity etc.

The main functions of IX and X can be tested together by assessing swallowing, phonation/articulation and sensation from the pharynx/larynx.

Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve examinations include:

• Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula at rest and with phonation (“aah”).
• By assessing the strength of the cough

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An elderly woman reports difficulty in buttoning her shirt and increased clumsiness during daily activities. On examination, she is unable to make an 'O' shape by opposing her thumb and index finger. Which of the following muscles is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Abductor pollicis brevis

The difficulty in buttoning the shirt and the inability to make the "O" shape with fingers suggest the involvement of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle.

This is a case of anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome. The AIN is a purely motor branch of the median nerve that affects specific muscles in the forearm, the flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus leading to difficulty in performing tasks requiring fine motor control, such as the "OK" sign. Among the options provided, the abductor pollicis brevis is uniquely and consistently innervated by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve, making it susceptible to dysfunction in conditions affecting the median nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The opponens pollicis is innervated primarily by the lateral terminal branch of the median nerve, with some contributions from a branch of the deep terminal branch of the ulnar nerve. While it plays a role in thumb opposition, it is not consistently affected in anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome, which primarily impacts deeper flexor muscles like the flexor pollicis longus. Therefore, it is less likely to be the cause of the patient’s inability to perform the "OK" sign.

Option B: The palmar interossei muscles are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Because they do not receive any innervation from the median nerve, they are not implicated in AIN syndrome. Their primary function involves the adduction of the fingers.

Option C: The flexor pollicis brevis has dual innervation: the superficial head is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, while the deep head is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. This dual supply makes it less likely to be solely affected in AIN syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During the examination of a patient, a professor asks the patient to invert his foot and points to a prominent tendon located behind the medial malleolus. Which tendon is being highlighted?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tibialis posterior

The tendon being highlighted here is of the tibialis posterior.

It passes behind the medial malleolus and is a key muscle responsible for foot inversion. The tendon of this muscle becomes prominent in this area during foot inversion. Dysfunction of this tendon can lead to flatfoot deformity.

The given image shows the tarsal tunnel and position of the tendon of tibialis posterior:

Other options:

Option A: Tibialis anterior lies anterior to the medial malleolus and aids in dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot but is not located behind the medial malleolus.

Option B: Extensor digitorum is involved in extending the toes and runs anteriorly to the foot, not behind the medial malleolus.

Option D: Extensor hallucis longus extends the big toe and runs along the anterior portion of the foot, also not behind the medial malleolus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the marked structure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medial pectoral nerve

The marked structure in the image is the medial pectoral nerve.

The given image shows the medial pectoral nerve arising from the medial cord of the brachial plexus. It also shows the axillary artery traversing inferior to the median pectoral nerve and the thoracoacromial artery. The medial pectoral nerve and the thoracoacromial artery both contribute to the neurovascular supply of the pectoral muscles.

After originating from the medial cord, the medial pectoral nerve passes anterior to the axillary artery. This nerve is specifically known for its anatomical path of piercing the pectoralis minor muscle before branching out to supply both the pectoralis minor and the pectoralis major muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: If a tumor compresses the structures passing through the opening marked in the given image, which of the following sensations would be affected?
options: Sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose

The marked foramen is the superior orbital fissure. If a tumour compresses the structures passing through this foramen, it would impair sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose, as this would affect the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve.

The superior orbital fissure is an important anatomical opening in the skull that allows several critical structures to pass through. Among these structures, the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve are branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the first division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), which is responsible for sensory innervation to parts of the face.

The frontal nerve provides sensation to the forehead, the anterior scalp, and the dorsum of the nose, while the nasociliary nerve supplies sensation to parts of the nasal cavity. Therefore, if a tumour or lesion compresses the structures passing through the superior orbital fissure, it would likely affect the sensation in the anterior scalp and dorsum of the nose because these areas are innervated by the branches of the trigeminal nerve that pass through this fissure.

Other options:

Option A: Sensation of the nasopharynx is innervated by other branches of the trigeminal and glossopharyngeal nerve, not by structures passing through the superior orbital fissure.

Option B: While some sensation from the nasal cavity comes from the trigeminal nerve, the specific branches affected by a lesion in the superior orbital fissure are more focused on the anterior areas of the face.

Option D: Sensation of the chin is primarily innervated by the mandibular branch (CN V3) of the trigeminal nerve, which passes through the foramen ovale, not the superior orbital fissure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the outer covering of the condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amnion

The diagnosis based on the given image is omphalocele and is covered by the amnion.

Omphalocele is a midline abdominal wall defect where the bowel and other solid viscera protrude through the umbilicus. In this condition, the herniated organs are covered by both peritoneum and an amnion. The umbilical cord inserts directly into this sac, which helps in identifying the condition. The defect occurs due to the failure of the physiological hernia to return to the body cavity by the 11th week of gestation.

The size of an omphalocele can vary significantly. It may be relatively small, containing only the gut, or it can be classified as a giant omphalocele if it measures 4 cm or more in diameter, encompassing the gut, liver, and other abdominal organs. The condition is often associated with other congenital anomalies such as trisomies 13, 15, 18, or 21, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, exstrophy of the bladder or cloaca, and pentalogy of Cantrell.

Treatment for omphalocele involves covering the exposed organs to prevent fluid loss and protect them from infection. Prophylactic antibiotics may be administered in case of rupture. Surgical correction is usually performed once the baby is stable. In omphalocele, since the umbilicus is covered by a reflection of the amnion, this membrane also covers the omphalocele itself, differentiating it from other types of abdominal wall defects.

Note : Gastroschisis is a condition where the intestinal loops herniate through the defect in the abdominal wall. The defect usually lies on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly). The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion. It is associated with elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Where will you find the epithelium shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ureter

The epithelium shown in the above image can be found in the ureter.

The ureter is lined by transitional epithelium (also called urothelium), similar to the urinary bladder. This specialized epithelium allows stretching, which is crucial as the urine passes through. The presence of transitional epithelium is characteristic of structures in the urinary system, such as the ureters, bladder, and part of the urethra.

Given below is a cross-section of the ureter showing the transitional epithelium and the layer of smooth muscle.

Other options:

Option A: Gall bladder: The gall bladder is lined by simple columnar epithelium, which facilitates the absorption of water and electrolytes from bile.

Option B: Trachea: The trachea is lined by pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells, which helps trap and remove particles from the respiratory tract.

Option D: Duodenum: The duodenum is lined by simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells, aiding in digestion and nutrient absorption.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery is used for arteriovenous shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis, and is located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The posterior tibial artery, located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, that is used for arteriovenous (AV) shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis.

The posterior tibial artery is situated behind the medial malleolus and approximately 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, making it a suitable site for creating an AV fistula with the great saphenous vein. This location allows for optimal access and ensures that the shunt can handle the necessary blood flow for effective dialysis with the great saphenous vein. However, they are not commonly used for AV shunting in common practices.

Arteries used for AV shunting include the radial artery and the brachial artery in the upper arm, which are frequently employed for hemodialysis access. In the lower leg, the anterior tibial artery and the peroneal (fibular) artery are less commonly used for this procedure.

Other options:

Option A: In comparison, the anterior tibial artery is located on the anterior aspect of the leg and runs down the front of the tibia, not behind the medial malleolus.

Option C: The peroneal (fibular) artery is situated on the lateral side of the leg, travelling alongside the fibula, and is also not located behind the medial malleolus.

Option D: The fibular circumflex artery is a small artery and is not commonly used for hemodialysis access. It is not a standard choice and does not fit the anatomical location described, as it is a branch of the anterior tibial artery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 55-year-old man sustains a head injury involving the left temporal region following a road traffic accident. After regaining consciousness, he speaks fluently, but his speech is irrelevant and meaningless, and he is unable to comprehend spoken language. Which cortical area is most likely affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wernicke's area

Wernicke’s area, located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere (Brodmann area 22), is responsible for language comprehension. Lesions produce Wernicke (receptive/fluent) aphasia, characterized by fluent but meaningless speech, impaired comprehension, impaired repetition, and poor awareness of the language deficit.

FMGE/NEET PG Pearl

• Broca’s area (BA 44, 45) → Non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension.
• Wernicke’s area (BA 22) → Fluent but nonsensical speech with impaired comprehension.
• Arcuate fasciculus → Conduction aphasia with impaired repetition but relatively preserved fluency and comprehension.
• Primary auditory cortex (BA 41, 42) → Receives auditory input; lesions cause cortical hearing deficits rather than aphasia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient cannot identify objects but she can see the colour, texture, shape. What is the site of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inferior temporal lobe

The scenario points toward visual agnosia, with the most probable lesion located in the inferior temporal lobe. Agnosia is defined as the inability to recognize objects visually despite intact vision,also termed optic aphasia.

Since the patient can still perceive colors, the occipital lobe is intact, making the inferior temporal lobe the most likely site of pathology.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents to the OPD with the right eye positioned downwards and rotated outwards. Which of the following cranial nerves is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. III

The correct answer is Oculomotor nerve (CN III).

Injury to CN III causes unopposed action of lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV), resulting in the eye being positioned downward and outward.

Associated features include ptosis and dilated pupil due to loss of levator palpebrae and parasympathetic fibers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a drooping of the eyelid, miosis and anhidrosis. A diagnosis of Horner syndrome is made. Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Sympathetic plexus around the internal carotid artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cervical sympathetic chain

Horner syndrome results from interruption of the sympathetic pathway supplying the eye, commonly at the cervical sympathetic chain.

Lesion causes ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis due to loss of postganglionic sympathetic fibres.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia. The condition is diagnosed as Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome. Which of the following cranial nerves are most likely compressed in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. III, IV, V1, VI

Superior orbital fissure syndrome involves compression of structures passing through the fissure, including oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic division of trigeminal (V1), and abducens (VI) nerves.

This explains ptosis and ophthalmoplegia due to involvement of extraocular muscle nerves.

The optic nerve (II) passes through the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient sustains a deep laceration over the scalp. Separation of the wound margins occurs due to injury to which of the following layers of the scalp?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica)

The galea aponeurotica (epicranial aponeurosis) is the third layer of the scalp and connects the frontalis and occipitalis muscles. When this layer is lacerated, the opposing pull of these muscles causes wide separation (gaping) of the wound margins, especially in wounds that run transversely across the scalp. Therefore, scalp lacerations involving the galea require meticulous repair to restore the continuity of the aponeurosis.

• The patient has a deep scalp laceration with separation of wound margins.
• This occurs because the galea aponeurotica is divided, allowing:

• Frontalis muscle to pull the anterior flap forward.
• Occipitalis muscle to pull the posterior flap backward.

• The resulting tension causes the wound to gap widely

| Layer Injured | Clinical Finding

| ------------- | ----------------

| Skin | Superficial abrasion/laceration

| Dense connective tissue | Profuse bleeding

| Galea aponeurotica | Gaping scalp wound

| Loose areolar tissue | Spread of infection; “black eye” after scalp injury

| Pericranium | Limited subperiosteal hematoma (cephalohematoma)

Why not the other options?

• A. Skin: Provides the external covering of the scalp but does not cause wound gaping when injured.
• B. Dense connective tissue: Contains blood vessels and nerves anchored by fibrous septa. Injury causes profuse bleeding but not wound separation.
• D. Loose areolar tissue: Known as the “danger area of the scalp” because infection can spread through emissary veins to the intracranial venous sinuses. Injury to this layer does not cause gaping of the wound.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A woman has a difficulty opening her mouth but no problem in closing it. Which of the following is true about the muscle affected in the condition? 1. The muscle attaches close to the temporal mandibular joint. 2. The muscle depresses the mandible. 3. It is attached to the medial pterygoid plate. 4. The muscle is supplied by the mandibular nerve.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, and 4

Difficulty in opening the mouth indicates paralysis of a mandible depressor, mainly the lateral pterygoid muscle.

Lateral pterygoid attaches near the TMJ (neck of mandible and articular disc) and is responsible for depression and protrusion of mandible.

It is supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3), but it is not attached to the medial pterygoid plate (that is medial pterygoid), Lateral pterygoid arises from- greater wing of sphenoid & Lateral pterygoid plate.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cranial nerve X carries multiple functional components. Which nucleus or functional group does not contribute fibers to the vagus nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GSE

The correct answer is GSE (General Somatic Efferent).

The vagus nerve (CN X) carries GVE (parasympathetic) fibres from the dorsal motor nucleus, GVA fibres from thoracoabdominal viscera, and GSA fibres from the external auditory canal and dura.

Its motor fibres are branchial efferent (SVE) to muscles of pharynx and larynx, not true GSE, which supply extraocular and tongue muscles only.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Emotional prosody of speech is mainly a function of which area of the brain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior superior temporal gyrus

Emotional prosody refers to the emotional tone, rhythm, stress, and intonation of speech that conveys feelings such as happiness, sadness, or anger. It is primarily mediated by the right posterior superior temporal gyrus (the right-sided homolog of Wernicke’s area), which is responsible for comprehension of emotional prosody.

• Posterior superior temporal gyrus (right hemisphere) processes the emotional content and intonation of speech (receptive affective language).

Why not the other options?

• A. Cingulate gyrus: Involved in emotion, motivation, and behavior, but not the primary cortical area for emotional prosody.
• C. Posterior inferior parietal gyrus: Involved in multimodal sensory integration and spatial attention.
• D. Precentral gyrus: Primary motor cortex responsible for voluntary motor movements.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Glymphatics is the lymphatic like structure of which system?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Central Nervous System

The glymphatic system is a lymphatic-like waste clearance pathway of the central nervous system (CNS). It facilitates the exchange of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with interstitial fluid (ISF) through perivascular spaces, allowing the removal of metabolic waste products from the brain.

The system is dependent on astrocytic aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels and is most active during sleep.

• The glymphatic system is unique to the CNS and functions as the brain’s waste clearance mechanism.
• It removes:

• β-amyloid
• Tau protein
• Other metabolic waste products

• Impaired glymphatic function has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease, traumatic brain injury, and other neurodegenerative disorders.

Why not the other options?

• B. Respiratory system: Does not possess a glymphatic system.
• C. Renal system: Has lymphatics but no glymphatic pathway.
• D. Gastrointestinal system: Has a conventional lymphatic system, not a glymphatic system.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In a lesion at the sensory decussations, which nuclei are affected? 1. Lateral vestibular nucleus 2. Nucleus gracilis 3. Spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve 4. Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus 5. Hypoglossal nucleus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3, 4, 5

The sensory decussation occurs in the caudal (closed) medulla, where the internal arcuate fibers arising from the gracile and cuneate nuclei cross to form the medial lemniscus. A lesion at this level affects nuclei located in the caudal medulla but spares structures situated more rostrally.

Nuclei affected at the level of sensory decussation:

• Nucleus gracilis ✓
• Spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve ✓
• Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus ✓
• Hypoglossal nucleus ✓

Thus, the correct combination is 2, 3, 4, 5.

Why not the other options?

• 1. Lateral vestibular nucleus: Located in the rostral medulla/caudal pons, not at the level of the sensory decussation.
• Options A, B, and D either omit affected nuclei or incorrectly include the lateral vestibular nucleus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Loss of hand-eye coordination is associated with which of the following brain areas?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parietal lobe

The parietal lobe, particularly the posterior parietal cortex (parietal association cortex), integrates visual, proprioceptive, and somatosensory information to guide hand– eye coordination and goal-directed movements. Lesions in this region impair visuospatial processing and motor planning, resulting in optic ataxia (difficulty reaching for objects under visual guidance).

• Parietal lobe integrates sensory inputs necessary for accurate hand movements guided by vision.

Why not the other options?

• A. Temporal lobe: Involved in memory, hearing, and object recognition (“what” pathway).
• C. Occipital lobe: Primary visual processing; lesions cause visual deficits rather than impaired visuomotor coordination.
• D. Frontal lobe: Responsible for motor execution and planning but relies on parietal sensory integration for hand– eye coordination.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: New neurons are formed in which of the following areas of the central nervous system?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dentate gyrus

Adult neurogenesis occurs primarily in two regions of the brain:

• Dentate gyrus of the hippocampus (important for learning and memory)
• Subventricular zone (SVZ) lining the lateral ventricles (with migration to the olfactory bulb in many mammals)

Among the given options, the dentate gyrus is the only recognized site of ongoing neuronal generation in adults.

Why not the other options?

• B. Anterior horn of spinal cord: Motor neurons do not undergo physiological regeneration or neurogenesis.
• C. Locus ceruleus: Contains noradrenergic neurons but is not a site of adult neurogenesis.
• D. Substantia nigra: Dopaminergic neurons do not regenerate under normal physiological conditions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Olfactory sensation is transmitted by all of the following nerves, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypoglossal nerve

CN XII is a purely motor nerve supplying intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, with no sensory component.

Trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves contribute general sensory input (irritant, pungent stimuli) that modulates perceived olfactory sensation, but CN XII has no such role.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Structure lying in the floor of inferior horn of lateral ventricle are all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tail of caudate nucleus

The correct answer is Tail of caudate nucleus.

The floor of the inferior (temporal) horn of the lateral ventricle is formed by the hippocampus, fimbria, and collateral eminence.

The tail of the caudate nucleus runs in the roof of the inferior horn, along with the stria terminalis, and therefore is not a floor structure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The lesion in Broadmann’s area 22 causes:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Receptive aphasia

Brodmann area 22 corresponds to Wernicke’s area in the dominant temporal lobe, responsible for language comprehension.

Lesions here cause fluent but meaningless speech with impaired understanding, i.e., receptive aphasia.

Expressive aphasia is due to Broca’s area (areas 44–45), while repetition and naming deficits depend on other language network components.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve is not the content of superior orbital fissure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. II

The correct answer is Optic nerve (CN II).

CN II passes through the optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure.

The superior orbital fissure transmits CN III, CN IV, CN VI, and the ophthalmic division of CN V (V1) along with sympathetic fibres.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following findings is characteristic of Frey’s syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sweating & flushing over preauricular region

Frey’s syndrome occurs due to aberrant regeneration of auriculotemporal nerve fibers after parotid gland injury or surgery.

Parasympathetic fibers meant for salivation instead stimulate sweat glands, causing gustatory sweating and flushing over the preauricular area.

The other options describe features of Horner syndrome, not Frey’s syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which one of the following is the myelinating cell of Central Nervous System?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Oligodendrocyte

Oligodendrocytes are the myelinating cells of the central nervous system (CNS). They produce the myelin sheath around axons in the brain and spinal cord, allowing rapid saltatory conduction of nerve impulses between the nodes of Ranvier.

Why not the other options?

• A. Astrocyte: Provides structural and metabolic support, maintains the blood-brain barrier, regulates extracellular potassium, and participates in repair after CNS injury (gliosis). It does not produce myelin.
• B. Microglia: The resident macrophages of the CNS, responsible for phagocytosis and immune defense.
• C. Schwann cell: The myelinating cell of the peripheral nervous system (PNS). Each Schwann cell myelinates only one segment of a single axon.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which type of sensation is carried by the 2nd order neuron of the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pain

| Sensory Nucleus | Location | Function

| --------------- | -------- | --------

| Mesencephalic Nucleus of Trigeminal Nerve (MNT) | Midbrain | Proprioception from jaw muscles and teeth

| Chief Sensory Nucleus of Trigeminal Nerve (CNT) | Pons | Touch and pressure sensation from face

| Spinal Nucleus of Trigeminal Nerve (SNT) | Medulla | Pain and temperature sensation from face

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 4-year-old child inhaled a small toy while playing. X-ray reveals the toy to be on the right side of the chest. Which of the following is the anatomical basis for these findings? 1. Right bronchus is in direct line with the trachea 2. Right bronchus is wider 3. Right bronchus is longer 4. Right lung has 3 lobes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 2

The right main bronchus is the most common site for aspiration of inhaled foreign bodies because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical (more in direct continuation with the trachea) than the left main bronchus. As a result, aspirated objects are more likely to enter the right bronchial tree.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Right bronchus is in direct line with the trachea
• 2. Right bronchus is wider

Why not the other options?

• 3. Right bronchus is longer: The right main bronchus is shorter, not longer.
• 4. Right lung has 3 lobes: Although true anatomically, the number of lobes does not influence the site of foreign body aspiration.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient accidentally swallowed a fish bone and presented with choking. On examination, the bone was found to be impacted in the esophagus at the level of T4 vertebra. Which of the following structures is responsible for the obstruction at this level?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arch of aorta

The esophagus has physiological constrictions, one of which occurs at the T4 vertebral level due to the arch of aorta crossing anterior to the esophagus.

This site is a common location for foreign body impaction, especially fish bones.

The cricopharyngeal junction lies at C6, the left bronchus crosses at T5–T6, and the diaphragm constriction is at T10.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient complains of decreased sensation in the lateral 3 ½ fingers of the palmar side of the right hand along with difficulty moving the upper phalanx of the thumb. Associated thenar atrophy is also present. What is the associated nerve injury in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High median nerve

• Sensory loss over the lateral 3½ fingers (palmar side) with thenar muscle atrophy indicates a proximal median nerve lesion.
• Difficulty moving the upper phalanx of the thumb reflects weakness of thenar muscles (OP, APB, FPB) supplied by median nerve.
• Ulnar and radial nerves have different sensory distributions, while anterior interosseous nerve is purely motor and spares sensation and thenar eminence.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with shoulder pain following a hyperextension injury during exercise. On examination, there is evidence of avulsion of the long head of the triceps. What is the site of avulsion of triceps?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Infraglenoid tubercle

The long head of triceps brachii originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, crossing the shoulder joint.

A hyperextension injury can avulse this tendon at its origin.

The shaft of humerus gives origin to the lateral and medial heads, supraglenoid tubercle is for the long head of biceps, and deltoid tuberosity is for deltoid insertion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An elderly woman reports difficulty in buttoning her shirt and increased clumsiness in performing daily activities. On examination, the clinician asked her to make an 'O' using her thumb and index finger, which she was unable to do. Which of the following muscles is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flexor pollicis longus

Inability to make an “O” sign indicates weakness of flexion at the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, which is the primary action of flexor pollicis longus.

This muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve (median nerve branch), and its paralysis produces the classic positive pinch sign.

Opponens pollicis and abductor pollicis brevis mediate opposition and abduction, while palmar interossei act on digits, not the thumb IP joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Choose the true statement regarding breast.
options: Superior & medial quadrant has more tissue
Axillary tail of Spence crosses anterior axillary fold
Nipple is located at 4th intercostal space in most of the females
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Axillary tail of Spence crosses anterior axillary fold

The correct answer is Axillary tail of Spence crosses the anterior axillary fold.

The axillary tail is a superolateral extension of breast tissue that passes into the axilla across the anterior axillary fold, making it clinically important in breast examination and surgery. The axillary tail is an extension of upper outer quadrant, it passes through the foramen of Langer, enters the axilla and lies along the lateral border of pectoralis major.

The superolateral quadrant (not superomedial) has maximum breast tissue, breasts have 15–20 lobules, and the nipple is usually at the 4th intercostal space in males, not consistently in females.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Common site for congenital diaphragmatic hernia is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Posterolateral

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia most commonly occurs through the foramen of Bochdalek, a posterolateral defect of the diaphragm.

It results from failure of closure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane, leading to herniation of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity.

Anterior defects (foramen of Morgagni) are less common and usually right-sided.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Posterior interosseous nerve injury causes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of extension at finger

The correct answer is loss of extension at fingers.

The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) supplies the finger and thumb extensors.

Wrist extension is largely preserved due to extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, so wrist drop does not occur.

Supination is mainly by biceps brachii and supinator, which are not significantly affected.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a tributary of the inferior vena cava?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left inferior phrenic vein

The inferior vena cava (IVC) directly receives the inferior phrenic veins, including the left one.

In contrast, the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins drain into the left renal vein, not directly into the IVC.

The ascending lumbar veins contribute to the azygos system, not the IVC.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not a tributary of the thoracic duct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right jugular trunk

The thoracic duct is the main lymphatic channel of the body and drains lymph from both lower limbs, abdomen, left thorax, left upper limb, and the left side of the head and neck before emptying into the left venous angle (junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins). Its major tributaries include:

• Right and left lumbar trunks (via cisterna chyli)
• Intestinal trunk
• Left jugular trunk
• Left subclavian trunk
• Left bronchomediastinal trunk

The right jugular trunk does not drain into the thoracic duct. Instead, it usually drains into the right lymphatic duct or directly into the right venous angle.

Why Not the Other Options?

• Left lumbar trunk → Contributes to formation of the cisterna chyli.
• Right lumbar trunk → Contributes to formation of the cisterna chyli.
• Left jugular trunk → Drains into the thoracic duct near its termination.
• Right jugular trunk → Drains into the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve? 1. 3rd lumbrical 2. 4th Dorsal interossei 3. Opponens digiti minimi 4. Flexor carpi ulnaris
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3

The ulnar nerve divides into superficial and deep branches as it enters the hand. The deep branch of the ulnar nerve is responsible for supplying most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 40-year-old man with raised intracranial pressure develops horizontal diplopia. On examination, the right eye shows failure of abduction, suggesting involvement of the nerve which is particularly vulnerable to stretching as it bends over the petrous apex beneath the petrosphenoidal ligament. Compression of this nerve occurs in a small osteofibrous tunnel before it enters the cavernous sinus. Which of the following structures transmits this nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dorello’s canal

The nerve described is the abducens nerve (CN VI).

Key clues in the question:

• Failure of abduction of eye → Lateral rectus palsy → CN VI
• Passes over petrous apex under petrosphenoidal (Gruber’s) ligament

This segment of the nerve passes through Dorello’s canal before entering the cavernous sinus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles are ectoderm-derived?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ciliaris

Why Ciliaris?

The ciliaris muscle is derived from neural crest cells. It is an intraocular smooth muscle that controls lens accommodation.

Why the Others Are Wrong

| Option | Embryological Origin | Why Wrong

| ------ | -------------------- | ---------

| A — Cardiac muscle | Mesoderm (splanchnic/lateral plate) | Completely mesodermal

| B — Smooth muscle of gut | Mesoderm (splanchnic lateral plate) | Not ectoderm

| C — Erector pili | Mesoderm | Common trap — it's a skin muscle but still mesodermal

| D — Ciliaris | Neural crest | Correct

The two key ones to remember:

• Ciliaris — accommodation (Neural crest)
• Sphincter and dilator pupillae — neuroectoderm

Erector pili is the classic distractor — students assume "skin = ectoderm," but the smooth muscle itself comes from mesoderm (specifically, mesenchyme).
